docs.title: torchtsetlin
docs.text:
GPU-enabled, PyTorch-native Tsetlin machines.

Latest release: torchtsetlin 0.7.1

pip install torchtsetlin==0.7.1. See the changelog for what's new.

torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family — the propositional-logic learning algorithm introduced by Ole-Christoffer Granmo — as ordinary torch.nn.Module objects. The automata states live in tensors, so a model moves between CPU and GPU with .to(device), is saved with state_dict(), and learns from mini-batches with a single model.update(x, y) call. Everything a Tsetlin machine workflow needs is included: Booleanization of data, training and evaluation loops, metrics, rule extraction, feature importance and plots.

import torchtsetlin as tt

x_train, y_train = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(5000, noise=0.4)          # Boolean features, int labels
x_test, y_test = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(2000, noise=0.0, seed=1)

model = tt.TsetlinMachine(n_features=12, n_classes=2, n_clauses=20, T=15, s=3.9).to("cuda")

trainer = tt.Trainer(model, batch_size=10, callbacks=[tt.EarlyStopping(patience=20)])
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=100, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
print(trainer.evaluate((x_test, y_test)))       # {'accuracy': 0.99}
print(model.rules()[:3])                        # ['IF x0 AND NOT x1 THEN 1', ...]

docs.title: Why a Tsetlin machine?
docs.text:
• Interpretable by construction. Every clause is a conjunction of literals (x0 AND NOT x1) that votes for or against a class. The whole model is the explanation.
  • Bit-level efficient. Inputs are Booleans and the learned state is a matrix of small integers; inference is an AND over included literals plus a vote count.
  • Universal approximator with summation-based decisions, like a neural network, but learned without gradients through reward/penalty feedback to learning automata.

  • Why it learns what it learns — the book's Markov-chain analysis: what s, n_states and T do to the learned clauses.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text: The algorithms implemented here follow the Tsetlin machine literature by Granmo and colleagues (the original TM, the convolutional TM, the weighted TM, the coalesced TM, drop-clause, clause-size constraints, closed-form interpretability, TM composites and confidence) and the textbook An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (tsetlinmachine.org). See the concept pages for references.

Adding a version
docs.text:
pip install -e .                    # the version to measure
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh      # writes benchmarks/results/versions/<version>/

Each run writes to the folder of the installed library version, so the results of older versions are never overwritten. The driver then regenerates CPU vs GPU for the newest version and this page for all of them; python benchmarks/plot_history.py rebuilds this page alone.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
All numbers below were measured with torchtsetlin 0.1.0, PyTorch 2.10 / CUDA 12.8 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090, with the whole Boolean dataset resident on the GPU. They are meant to show the throughput of the batched update and that accuracy is on par with the literature after a few epochs — not to be state-of-the-art results (those need hundreds of epochs and larger clause budgets).

The systematic CPU-vs-GPU sweep — throughput against batch size, clause budget and feature count, the model zoo, and where the time inside one update() goes — lives on its own page: CPU vs GPU. That page is generated end to end by benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh, so you can replace its numbers with your own hardware's. Results are kept per library version, and Version history puts every release's numbers side by side.

How torchtsetlin is compared with the other Tsetlin-machine libraries (pyTsetlinMachine and its parallel and CUDA variants, tmu, green-tsetlin) — data, training, testing and what is measured — is set out in the benchmarking guideline.

For what the papers report, see Literature results. It covers every dataset and reported result from 55 Tsetlin-machine papers, with filtering, the best value per dataset or other grouping, the best TM result per dataset, and an in-browser SQL console over the SQLite catalog.

The 500-clause flat machine reaches 95.8 % after 5 epochs; the literature reports ≈ 98 % for 2000 clauses per class after 400 epochs and ≈ 99 % for convolutional machines with 8000 clauses per class. The cost of a batched update is dominated by per-clause work (n_clauses × 2F element-wise passes), so larger batches are almost free: going from batch 32 to 100 triples the throughput of the flat model.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
The accuracy numbers above come from the example scripts:

python examples/mnist_flat.py --clauses 500 --T 25 --epochs 5 --batch-size 100
python examples/mnist_conv.py --clauses 200 --T 100 --epochs 3 --batch-size 32
python examples/noisy_xor.py --batch-size 10

The throughput numbers on CPU vs GPU come from the benchmark driver, which runs every suite, writes benchmarks/results/versions/<version>/cpu_vs_gpu.json for the installed torchtsetlin version, and regenerates the figures, tables and that page, plus the Version history page comparing every version on disk. A run never touches another version's results:

./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh                  # every suite, cpu + cuda:0 (~20-25 min)
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh --quick          # ~1 min smoke test, docs untouched
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh -s batch models  # a subset
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh --plots-only     # re-render from the results already on disk
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh --plots-only -V 0.5.0  # re-render one older version's tables
./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh --help           # every option

Fix: out of memory on large models when counting included literals. Every refresh of include_count (the dense CUDA commit, apply_feedback* with a clause budget, and the full include-cache refresh after loading or moving a model) summed state >= N in one go, which makes an int64 copy of the whole state: 8 bytes per automaton, a 7.5 GiB spike at 64,000 clauses per class on flat MNIST (640,000 x 1,568 automata). Flat MNIST at that size ran out of memory on a 24 GB RTX 3090 for batches of 64 and more. The new functional.count_included counts in row blocks (at most ~0.6 GiB of scratch, same speed, same result) and is used at every such site. Found by the batch-size x clause-count experiments (experiments/mnist_batch_clauses/, gap MBC-1; also toolbox_cifar10 TB-1).

Notebooks in the documentation, runnable in Google Colab. The example notebooks (examples/notebooks/) are rendered under Examples → Notebooks (mkdocs-jupyter, added to the docs extra; docs/examples/notebooks is a symlink to them). They are stored without outputs, nothing is executed during the docs build, and every notebook was re-run on 0.7.0 with its text updated to the results it now produces. Each notebook has an Open in Colab badge and a first cell that installs torchtsetlin from PyPI when it runs in Colab; MNIST and CIFAR-10 download to data/ there. New notebook 06_graph_tsetlin.ipynb: the graph Tsetlin machine on the paper's three-A's task (four readable clauses, explain_node), run lengths, the padded CUDA fast path, and MNIST as depth-1 graphs learning bit for bit like ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine. New notebook 07_segmentation_tsetlin.ipynb: SegmentationTsetlinMachine on generated street scenes (the segmentation example), with the row-prior floor, position literals and the OR-pooled pyramid, explain_pixel, a patches_per_commit sweep and class-balanced feedback. The segmentation example, guide and concept pages now show the numbers measured on 0.7.0 (e.g. single scale 0.818 mIoU, was 0.798; pyramid + position 0.954, was 0.959).

The C-RTM notebook (04_convolutional_regression_tsetlin.ipynb) no longer recovers the planted mask with the paper's 15 clauses (0 of 12 restarts, was 9 of 12 on 0.1.x). Side experiments trace this to the two 0.5.0 rule changes together: weights floored at 1 and the squared regression feedback (either one alone still breaks it, putting both back restores it). The notebook now uses 8 weighted clauses, 400 epochs and batches of 16, which is exact on 8 of 12 restarts.

New: graph Tsetlin machine (GraphTsetlinMachine, torchtsetlin.data.GraphBatch, torchtsetlin.data.SymbolTable; Granmo et al., arXiv:2507.14874; issue #8, plans/graph-tm.md). Deep clauses over graphs with typed edges: one clause component per layer, connected by messages that clauses send to neighbouring nodes. Random, double-hashed or one-hot messages, node types, batched and sequential feedback, and clause decoding in the paper's right1:0 notation. At depth 1 on GraphBatch.from_images graphs it learns bit for bit like ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine (tested). The Trainer accepts a GraphBatch wherever it takes a tensor. A specificity per layer (s=(s0, s1, ...), as the reference implementation allows; new functional.apply_feedback_blocks), explain_node (traces a clause at one node back to the symbols of the neighbours that sent its messages) and rules(symbols=...).

Graph TM on the CUDA fast paths (plans/graph-tm-fast-paths.md). GraphBatch.pad(max_nodes, max_edges) gives a fixed-shape layout (edges as a (B, E, 2) array with a mask) whose slices have static shapes and never synchronise with the host. Batched updates run in events mode (the fused Triton commit) for flat and padded batches. Padded batches also take the compiled single-example commit in sequential mode and are replayed from CUDA graphs. Sequence example on an RTX 3090 (smoke): sequential 4.8 → 0.065 ms per graph, batched 0.23 → 0.013 ms per graph. models/base.py and the Triton kernels are unchanged.

Depth-1 graphs on the convolutional kernel. A depth-1 graph clause is a convolutional clause over the node features, so batches whose graphs all have the full node count (GraphBatch.full_nodes, set by from_images and from_graphs, kept by slicing) evaluate and draw their feedback nodes with _triton.conv_eval on bit-packed literals, never forming the (B, P, C) match tensor. On CUDA such a model learns bit for bit like ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine (tested). This makes the paper-scale image experiments feasible: Fashion-MNIST with 40,000 clauses trains in ~12 s per epoch on an RTX 3090.

CoalescedTsetlinMachine.rules forwards extra keyword arguments to clause_expression.

Paper reproduction (plans/graph-tm-reproduction.md, experiments/paper_experiments/results/graphtm/REPORT.md, 5 seeds each): three consecutive A's 100.00 (paper 100); MNIST GraphTM 98.07 (98.42), CoTM 98.49 (98.93); Fashion-MNIST GraphTM 88.59 (89.49), CoTM 90.70 (91.05). All within tolerance, and the paper's ordering CoTM > GraphTM holds. CIFAR-10 and multivalue noisy XOR were skipped (no comparable published number).

Fix: sequential convolutional models on CUDA predicted from a stale include mask (gap G25, experiments/paper_experiments/LIBRARY_GAPS.md). In 0.6.0, once all of a sequential model's 64-example update blocks were replayed from CUDA graphs, nothing marked the bit-packed include mask stale, so predict() / forward() on a Conv* model trained with feedback_mode="sequential" kept using the mask from its last eager update. Learning itself was correct; the predictions froze (2-D Noisy XOR: 78.5 +- 13.4% over 5 seeds against 100% on 0.5.1). A replay now re-applies the Python-side flags its captured update set. Batched updates, flat models and the CPU were not affected. On 0.6.0, model.cuda_graphs = False or TORCHTSETLIN_CUDA_GRAPHS=0 avoids it.

The CUDA path is rebuilt around two Triton kernels and CUDA graphs (gaps G15-G24 of the low-level kernel audit, experiments/paper_experiments/LIBRARY_GAPS.md). What a model learns is unchanged in distribution, and CUDA-graph replays are bit-identical to eager execution. Same GPU (RTX 3080), per update() against 0.5.1: flat MNIST batch 32 4.7 -> 1.1 ms, batch 100 5.1 -> 1.7 ms; IMDb-sized flat model 20.7 -> 6.6 ms; convolutional MNIST batch 16 5.0 -> 1.5 ms, batch 100 22.7 -> 7.6 ms; Noisy XOR sequential 17x and 2-D Noisy XOR sequential 12x faster; convolutional prediction 4.7x faster.

  • Fused commit kernel (torchtsetlin._triton.fused_commit; G15, G16, G17, G22). A batched CUDA update that fits one chunk records its events instead of count tensors; one kernel computes the Type Ia / Type II counts per tile (tensor cores for flat models, a gather of each clause's random matching patch for convolutional ones), samples them (inverse CDF, walked arithmetically for small counts), and writes the state, the include cache, the bit-packed include mask and the include counts. No (C, 2F) count buffer is allocated, saving 12 bytes per automaton.
  • Fused convolutional evaluation (_triton.conv_eval; G20, G21, G24). Clauses are evaluated on bit-packed literals with the OR over patches in registers; while learning the kernel also draws each clause's random matching patch for Type Ia and, independently, Type II. Conv literals are float16 on CUDA. ConvTsetlinMachine.patch_clause_outputs keeps the dense evaluation.
  • No host synchronisation in an update (G18). Labels already on a CUDA device are checked by a device-side assertion (utils.class_targets); labels from the host are checked there before the copy. Feedback selection uses scatter_, the CDF table is cached per device, and the table width comes from the batch size instead of a read-back.
  • CUDA graphs (G19). On CUDA, an update shape seen for the third time (sequential mode: blocks of 64 examples) is captured and replayed. Off with model.cuda_graphs = False or TORCHTSETLIN_CUDA_GRAPHS=0; not used with clause or literal dropout.
  • functional.commit_dense and functional.commit_single_example update include_count in place; commit_dense takes max_events and no longer sums the include counts inside the compiled kernel (half its time). TORCHTSETLIN_TRITON=0 disables the Triton kernels.
  • Start-up: the first update of a process takes 2.2 s cold / 0.7 s warm (was 5.2 / 2.1 s, G23).

Faster GPU training, and two CPU slow paths removed (gaps G10-G14 of the cross-library benchmark, experiments/paper_experiments/LIBRARY_GAPS.md). Learning is unchanged in distribution; clause evaluation on CUDA is bit-identical. Times are per update() on an RTX 3090 / Ryzen 9 3950X after warm-up, MNIST-sized models (20k clauses).

  • Fused dense commit on CUDA (G10). A batched GPU update applies its feedback with one torch.compile kernel (functional.commit_dense) that draws the binomials inside the kernel (inverse CDF by bisection over a fixed table), writes the state and the include cache, and zeroes the counts for reuse, instead of ~20 full passes over the automata. Flat MNIST: batch 32 7.2 -> 3.9 ms, batch 100 7.6 -> 4.1 ms. Hard budgets and counts above 255 per automaton keep the eager commit.
  • Clauses are evaluated in float16 on CUDA (G11). The include cache is float16 on CUDA (tensor-core matmul). The evaluation only tests whether a count of violated literals is zero, which half precision decides exactly, so clause outputs, votes and every random draw are unchanged. compute_dtype still sets the literals and the feedback counts; the CPU keeps it.
  • Convolutional batches are no longer split into tiny chunks (G12). The chunk size counted the worst-case random-patch draw (every clause selected for every example), which split a batch of 16 MNIST images into 4 chunks. It now follows the largest real intermediate, the (P, C) evaluation block, and the patch draw is bounded separately by blocks of events (_event_block). With G10/G11, conv MNIST batch 16: 9.6 -> 4.1 ms on CUDA.
  • Sequential mode on CUDA: small models and convolutional models use the fused kernel (G13). Whether to compile is decided on the work of the whole update() call, not one step, and ConvTsetlinMachine records each example's per-clause random matching patch for functional.commit_single_example, which now accepts (C, 2F) literals (and literals_ii). Noisy XOR: 3.1 -> 0.55 ms per example; 2-D Noisy XOR (conv): 3.6 -> 0.73 ms.
  • CPU: two slow paths removed (G14). Clause-major evaluation is used only for up to 256 rows: for the thousands of patch rows of a convolutional batch it was 3x slower (conv MNIST batch 16, 16 threads: 619 -> 258 ms per update). Counts beyond the CPU kernels' 64 x 32 table (large batches, small s) now bisect the wide table instead of falling back to the eager geometric sampler (coalesced MNIST, 2000 clauses, s=3, batch 100: 2047 -> 110 ms).

Learning follows the reference implementations, and training is much faster. A configuration audit against pyTsetlinMachine, pyTsetlinMachineParallel, PyTsetlinMachineCUDA, tmu and green-tsetlin (experiments/paper_experiments/LIBRARY_GAPS.md) found nine gaps; eight are closed here, and CPU training is the one still open (14x faster, but still slower than pyTsetlinMachine on one core). G1, G3 and G4 change what a model learns, so results measured with 0.4.0 on weighted, regression or focused-sampling models are not directly comparable.

  • Behaviour change: clause weights floor at 1, not 0 (G1). TsetlinMachine(weighted=True) and RegressionTsetlinMachine(weighted=True) used to let Type II drive a weight to 0, which silences the clause. pyTsetlinMachine and tmu keep every weight at least 1.
  • Behaviour change: regression feedback probability is the squared error (G3), ((v* - v)/T)**2, as in pyTsetlinMachine, pyTsetlinMachineParallel and tmu. It was |v* - v|/T.
  • Behaviour change: focused negative sampling uses the reference rule (G4). A non-target class is drawn with probability proportional to (T + clip(v_k, -T, T)) / 2T, as in tmu and green-tsetlin. It was proportional to v_k - min(v) + 1. functional.sample_negative_classes takes a new T argument and raises without it when focused=True.
  • Behaviour change: automaton states are 8-bit by default (G6). state_dtype=None picks uint8 when 2 * n_states - 1 <= 255 (the default n_states=128), else int16 / int32, so a model and its checkpoint are 4x smaller, the same 8 bits per automaton the reference implementations use. Commits form the new state in a wider buffer, so narrow dtypes cannot wrap. Checkpoints saved with int32 states load unchanged. Cast before doing arithmetic on ta_state yourself (model.ta_state.long() - N).
  • Faster CPU training and sequential mode (G8, G9). On the CPU and in sequential mode the commit is row-sparse (functional.apply_feedback_rows): Type Ia / Type II counts are kept only for the clauses that matched and were selected, Type Ib forgetting is drawn by geometric gaps (functional.sample_forget_events, exact), and the include caches are refreshed only where the state changed. The count buffers are reused between updates. Same distribution as before. MNIST-sized model (20k clauses, batch 32): CPU 2.2x faster with 16 threads (and it now scales with threads, 2.7x from 1 to 16), GPU sequential mode 2.8x faster. Batched GPU training keeps the dense commit and is unchanged.
  • torch.compile kernels for the update (G8, G9). On the CPU, Type Ib forgetting and the binomial draws of the row-sparse commit run as exact inverse-CDF kernels with the random numbers drawn inside the kernel, and clause evaluation is computed clause-major. In sequential mode on CUDA, flat models (TsetlinMachine, CoalescedTsetlinMachine, RegressionTsetlinMachine) commit each example with one fused kernel (functional.commit_single_example). MNIST-sized model, one epoch from initialisation: CPU batch 32 with 16 threads 1,259 s -> 91 s, GPU sequential mode 406 s -> 36 s (including compilation). The compiled paths are used only for large enough work, never with an explicit generator=, and fall back to the eager code (with one warning) where torch.compile does not work. functional.set_compile(False) or TORCHTSETLIN_COMPILE=0 turns them off. Compiled and eager runs consume random numbers differently, so a seeded run reproduces only under the same setting. The first update of a session pays the compilation (seconds; cached on disk).
  • max_weight caps clause weights (G2): TsetlinMachine, RegressionTsetlinMachine and (on the magnitude) CoalescedTsetlinMachine.
  • clamp_prediction_votes is now a constructor argument (G7), for pyTsetlinMachine's clamped argmax.
  • Documented (G5): a clause over the literal budget still gets its weight updated, as in tmu; pyTsetlinMachine skips that increment.

Training now matches the reference implementation (tmu) on the TM Composites benchmark. Reproducing TMComposites (Granmo, 2023) on CIFAR-10 turned up two library gaps. Both are fixed here. With 0.4.0, torchtsetlin reproduces 8 of the 9 rows of the paper's Table 2, against 1 of 9 with 0.3.2 (experiments/multi_convtm/REPORT.md). Two behaviour changes, so check results you compare against 0.3.x:

  • Behaviour change: the clause budget is soft again by default (budget_mode="soft", MC-2). max_included_literals now follows the reference implementation (tmu): the budget only gates Type Ia, so a clause may overshoot it and is then pruned by Type Ib until it shrinks back.
  • Why: the 0.3.x hard cap reverted every inclusion beyond the budget, so no clause ever exceeded it and the Type Ia -> Type Ib switch never fired. Clauses froze at exactly the budget.
  • Effect on the TM Composites CIFAR-10 reproduction (batch 50, 3 seeds): the 3x3 / 4x4 colour-thermometer specialists go from about 51% to 61.5-61.7%, matching tmu. The four-specialist composite goes from 68.6% to 73.3% (experiments/multi_convtm/REPORT.md).
  • Compatibility: budget_mode="hard" restores 0.3.x. Every model trained with max_included_literals learns differently, so results measured with 0.3.x and a budget are not directly comparable. Experiments in experiments/ that recorded results under 0.3.x pass no budget_mode, so re-running them now uses the soft rule.
  • Classifier predictions no longer clamp vote sums (MC-1). Learning still clamps each class sum to [-T, T], because the feedback probability is defined on it. forward() and predict() used the clamped sum too, so every class that reached +T tied for the argmax, and ties went to the lowest class index. forward() now returns the raw class sums, as the reference implementations do.
  • Measured on the TM Composites CIFAR-10 specialists, the clamp had cost 0.6-3.9 pp of test accuracy (experiments/multi_convtm/REPORT.md).
  • predict_proba() and confidence() still clamp, so the probabilities they return are unchanged.
  • RegressionTsetlinMachine keeps the clamp (new class attribute clamp_prediction_votes = True), because its output is the clamped sum rescaled to the target range.
  • This is a behaviour change: a classifier whose class sums exceed T predicts differently from 0.3.2, almost always better.

A segmentation memory fix, and documentation for the Tsetlin-machine literature. There are no API changes, and every non-segmentation model behaves exactly as in 0.3.1.

  • Segmentation: committed updates are budgeted per commit window (LG-001). With patches_per_commit set, the chunk budget now counts only the (P, 2L) literals per image plus one commit window, rather than every intermediate per image. Before, 128-px images with a few hundred clauses were processed one image per chunk, so a commit could never mix pixels from different images. forward() and patches_per_commit=None keep the per-image bound.
  • Segmentation: opt-in pixel_order="shuffle" permutes a chunk's pixels before committing. Returned votes stay in row-major (image, patch) order. The default is unchanged.
  • Docs: new Benchmarks → Literature results page. It lists every dataset and reported result from 55 Tsetlin-machine papers (128 datasets, 3,295 numbers). Filtering, grouping and best-per-group ranking run as SQL in the browser over a SQLite catalog. The page also has a best-per-dataset leaderboard, dataset and paper tables, and a SQL console. The catalog's source of truth is benchmarks/literature/papers/*.json, rebuilt by benchmarks/literature/build_catalog.py. The same data is served by a Hugging Face Space.
  • Docs: the changelog page renders again; it was missing the pymdownx.snippets extension. The site now uses the white paper's orange palette, with an automata-grid logo and favicon (scripts/make_logo.py). The concept figures are recoloured to match, and the current release is shown site-wide.

3D convolution. Clauses can now slide through volumes: MRI/CT stacks, or frame sequences with time as depth.

  • New models: Conv3dTsetlinMachine, Conv3dCoalescedTsetlinMachine and Conv3dRegressionTsetlinMachine take (B, Z, D, H, W) Boolean volumes with a kd × kh × kw window and depth/row/column thermometer position literals. Clause evaluation and the random-matching-patch feedback are the 2D code, unchanged. With D = kd = 1, the literals and the whole training run are bit-identical to ConvTsetlinMachine.
  • Patch-axis blocking: when one volume would exceed max_chunk_elements, the patch axis is split into blocks (or set patches_per_chunk). The output is identical, and the patch draw has the same distribution.
  • clause_patch returns (Z, kd, kh, kw), clause_region adds a "d" range, and patch_clause_outputs returns (B, Pd, Ph, Pw, C). viz.plot_conv_clause(s) draws 3D clauses slice by slice and takes depth= to show one slice.
  • data.make_3d_shapes: two shapes that differ only in the order of their slices. examples/shapes_conv3d.py gets 1.000 on it, against 0.83–0.98 for the 2D model on slices stacked as channels and 0.73–0.80 for a flat machine.
  • Docs: a "3D volumes" section with two new figures in Convolution, a conv3d benchmark suite on the CPU-vs-GPU page, and the design and proofs in plans/conv3d.md.

The clause-size budget is now a hard limit. This is a behaviour change: models trained with max_included_literals will learn differently from 0.2.0.

  • max_included_literals caps clause growth in every feedback mode (issue #1). Before, the budget was only checked at the start of a commit. One batched commit aggregates many Type Ia and Type II events, and Type II was never gated, so a clause under budget could end the commit far over it: 41% of rules exceeded a budget of 6, and segmentation models averaged about 200 literals against a budget of 32. Now, after each commit, a clause that would exceed the budget keeps only a random subset of its newly included literals and the rest return to just below the include boundary. Oversized clauses still get forgetting-only feedback and can only shrink. Results measured with a budget under 0.2.0 are not directly comparable.
  • Fixed: SegmentationTsetlinMachine crashed on GPU when class_feedback_p was set before .to(device) (issue #1). It is now a non-persistent buffer, so it moves with the model; checkpoints are unchanged and 0.2.0 checkpoints still load.

Semantic segmentation. Dense, per-pixel prediction is now a supported task rather than something to rebuild in a notebook.

  • New models: SegmentationTsetlinMachine and CoalescedSegmentationTsetlinMachine (models/segmentation.py). A convolutional TM takes the disjunction over patch positions — matches.any(dim=1) — which gives it translation tolerance and makes a dense output impossible: afterwards it knows a pattern occurred, not where. The dense models keep the patch axis and fold it into the batch axis instead (B' = B·P), so vote sums, Type I / Type II selection, feedback counting and apply_feedback all apply unchanged. predict returns a (B, H, W) label map, vote_map a (B, K, H, W) vote surface, and forward the folded (B·P, K) votes that keep Trainer / metrics / interpret working. padding="same" with stride=1 preserves the input resolution; ignore_index handles the void class of CamVid / Cityscapes / VOC; multi-label mode takes (B, K, H, W) mask stacks.
  • patches_per_commit (default 128). One batch of 8 images at 32×32 is 8 192 pixel-examples, and committing their feedback at once is a mini-batch of 8 192 — far past where batched feedback stops matching the classical algorithm. Measured over 3 seeds on make_segmentation_shapes: mIoU 0.749 at 128 against 0.527 at 4 096, and the variance grows with the commit size too (sd 0.009 → 0.073), so a large-commit run can look fine once and collapse the next time. feedback_mode="sequential" is patches_per_commit=1.
  • Context, measured. A k × k patch cannot decide classes that need global structure. Two TM-native fixes ship: thermometer-encoded patch-position literals (position_encoding, now also an int to bound the feature count on large images) and data.PyramidEncoder, an OR-pooled multi-scale stack built on the new functional.boolean_pool and functional.thermometer_cast. On generated CamVid-like scenes, building IoU goes 0.505 with neither → 0.699 (pyramid) → 0.894 (position) → 0.921 (both), and mIoU 0.798 → 0.959. No float parameter and no gradient anywhere.
  • Imbalance: class_feedback_p plus data.balanced_class_probabilities. A Tsetlin machine has no loss to reweight, so the lever is which pixels produce feedback. It is a rescue, not a default — it lifts a pyramid-only run 0.874 → 0.927 mIoU but costs 0.05 once position literals are on.
  • Metrics: pixel_accuracy, iou, mean_iou, dice, boundary_f1, segmentation_confusion_matrix, segmentation_metrics and segmentation_report, all accepting vote maps, label maps or folded votes. Absent classes get NaN IoU rather than 0, and mean_iou skips them. confusion_matrix gained ignore_index.
  • Trainer detects a dense model, logs pixel accuracy / mIoU / mean Dice / per-class IoU, and accumulates the confusion matrix batch by batch instead of keeping (B, K, H, W) vote tensors for a whole test set.
  • Interpretability: interpret.explain_pixel lists the clauses that decided one pixel, decoded over absolute image coordinates (p[1,21,13] = "plane 1 of pixel (21, 13)"), so a dense prediction can be audited pixel by pixel rather than attributed by a saliency heuristic. Plus model.clause_map, model.pixel_feature_names, clause_patch and clause_region for the dense geometry.
  • Data: make_scenes (CamVid-like street scenes with a wavy horizon, per-class texture and CamVid-like class imbalance), make_segmentation_shapes (a fast toy where the classes are only separable from the neighbourhood), load_segmentation_boolean and load_voc_segmentation_boolean — the latter resize masks with nearest interpolation, since bilinear invents class indices that do not exist.
  • Visualisation: viz.plot_segmentation (image / truth / prediction / error panels) and viz.plot_vote_map, plus viz.segmentation_palette.
  • _ConvMixin.patch_clause_outputs exposes the per-patch match tensor (B, Py, Px, C) that previously had no public accessor — useful for plotting where a clause fires and for stacking blocks, though learning a dense output still needs the segmentation models.
  • Benchmarks: a segmentation suite in bench_device.py reporting pixels per second, with a figure, table and page section. Measured on a 16-core CPU: ~35 000 px/s training and ~1 090 000 px/s predicting at the default commit size; patches_per_commit=None is 4.2× faster and measurably worse.
  • Docs: new concepts/segmentation.md, guides/segmentation.md and examples/segmentation.md, with every number above reproduced from examples/segmentation_scenes.py. They also report the row-prior baseline — a classifier that sees no image content and still scores 0.876 pixel accuracy on these scenes — because pixel accuracy on a layout-driven dataset is a weak claim.
  • Internal: TsetlinMachineBase._accumulate_chunk split into _accumulate_literals so models that encode once and commit several times do not re-encode. No behaviour change.

• Fixed / faster (convolutional models): the random matching patch used for Recognize and Reject feedback was drawn in _ConvMixin._evaluate, which builds a (B, P, C) rand tensor on every call — including forward() / predict() / evaluate_clauses(), where the draw is discarded. _evaluate now returns the per-patch match tensor as its feedback context and _feedback_counts draws from it, over the selected feedback events only. Prediction is RNG-free: on a 400-clause 10x10-window MNIST config, predict() went 885 -> 180 ms and update() 914 -> 216 ms per 64 images (4.9x / 4.2x). Each feedback event now also draws its own patch; a ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine clause that takes Type Ia and Type II in the same update (16% of feedback pairs in a 4-output probe, 43% multi-label) was sharing one. Learning is unchanged for ConvTsetlinMachine, where the two feedback types never coincide.
  • Verified the convolutional implementation against chapter 4 of An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines — patch layout, the OR over patches, the thermometer position bits (P-1 per axis, bit k = coord >= k+1) and Recognize / Erase / Reject feedback all match the theory. Three new tests pin those semantics against a brute-force reference.
  • Examples: three new convolutional scripts — examples/shapes_conv.py (2-D clauses vs a flat machine, and what position_encoding costs on a translation-invariant task), examples/conv1d_ramps.py (Conv1dTsetlinMachine on thermometer-encoded signals) and examples/conv_regression_blobs.py (ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine). examples/mnist_conv.py gained --stride, --no-position-encoding, --coalesced and --max-samples, keeps the encoder on the compute device, and prints the clauses it learned. New examples/README.md indexes all of them.
  • Docs: new Convolution on generated data example page (docs/examples/convolution.md) in the Examples nav, a runnable-examples table on the Convolution concept page, and measured --stride / --coalesced / position_encoding comparisons on the MNIST example page.

• Fixed (silent data corruption on GPU): as_bool_tensor / as_long_tensor / as_float_tensor moved tensors with non_blocking=True regardless of direction. A device-to-host copy issued that way returns before the transfer completes, so a CPU-resident BooleanEncoder handed a CUDA tensor thresholded stale memory and returned roughly 40% wrong bits — with no error, just a quietly worse model. All three now route through utils._to_device, which uses non_blocking=True only when the destination is CUDA; Trainer used the same pattern and is fixed too.
  • Added: two notebooks working through the Tsetlin-machine segmentation literature — examples/notebooks/04_convolutional_regression_tsetlin.ipynb (C-RTM, ICMLT 2021) and examples/notebooks/05_ctm_unet_segmentation.ipynb (CTM-UNet, ISTM 2025), the latter including a dense per-pixel Tsetlin segmentation head built on TsetlinMachine.

• Fixed: the 0.1.0 wheel on PyPI was missing the torchtsetlin.data subpackage (it had been excluded from git by an over-broad .gitignore rule), which made import torchtsetlin fail. 0.1.0 should not be used.
  • The publish workflow now runs the test-suite and smoke-imports the built wheel before uploading.

First public release.

  • Models: TsetlinMachine (multi-class, optional integer clause weights), CoalescedTsetlinMachine (shared clauses, multi-class / multi-label), RegressionTsetlinMachine, convolutional variants (ConvTsetlinMachine, ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine, ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine, Conv1dTsetlinMachine).
  • Learning options: specificity s, vote margin T, memory depth n_states, boosted true-positive feedback, clause size constraint (max_included_literals), drop-clause and drop-literal regularisation, focused negative sampling, batched or exact sequential feedback.
  • Data preparation: thermometer / one-hot / bit-plane / adaptive-threshold / colour thermometer / hypervector encoders, synthetic datasets, torchvision helpers.
  • Training: Trainer with DataLoader support, callbacks (early stopping, checkpoints, CSV logging, hyper-parameter schedules), metrics.
  • Interpretation: rule extraction, clause activity/precision, closed-form global and local feature importance, per-example explanations.
  • Visualisation: memory plots, automata heat-maps, convolutional clause patches, confusion matrices, trustworthiness curves.
  • Documentation site (MkDocs) and examples.

docs.title: Building the PDFs
docs.text: Both documents are LaTeX sources in whitepaper/, sharing one theme, the figures and data files: make builds the white paper (main.pdf), and make summary builds the report (summary.pdf). Their benchmark charts read the repository's benchmark records. Their literature counts and charts come from the literature database, via python whitepaper/data/regen_literature.py. The documentation build copies both committed PDFs into the site.

docs.title: CPU vs GPU
docs.text:
Every number on this page comes from one run of benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh on a single machine:

CPU AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-Core Processor (32 logical cores, torch using 16 threads) GPU 0 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU 1 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128 / CUDA 12.8 torchtsetlin 0.7.0 Python 3.10.11 measured 2026-11-08 11:20:01

How to read these

Each point is the median of three timed blocks of steady-state calls, after a warm-up, with the device synchronised once per block. The micro-benchmarks use synthetic Boolean data at 20 % density, resident on the device unless stated otherwise. Reproduce — or replace these numbers with your own hardware's — with:

./benchmarks/run_benchmarks.sh          # ~20-25 min, rewrites this page

These are the numbers of torchtsetlin 0.7.0. Benchmark history puts the same suites side by side for every earlier version.

docs.title: Throughput vs batch size
docs.text:
One update() call touches every automaton in the machine, so its cost depends far more on the size of the machine than on how many examples are in the batch. Feeding the GPU more examples per call is therefore nearly free: training throughput rises from 4,031 examples/s at batch 1 to 249,073 at batch 4096. At batch 256 the same model trains 139,188 examples/s on the GPU against 3,905 on the CPU (36×).

The Noisy-XOR scale machine in the bottom row is the counter-example: 20 clauses over 12 features is less work than a kernel launch, so only past batch 1 does the GPU pull ahead. Small machines belong on the CPU.

Batch size — MNIST scale (784 features, 500 clauses/class) batch CPU train ex/s GPU train ex/s train speedup CPU infer ex/s GPU infer ex/s infer speedup 1 225 4,031 17.9× 556 3,875 7.0× 2 545 7,665 14.1× 2,287 7,717 3.4× 4 797 16,170 20.3× 4,267 15,420 3.6× 8 876 31,433 35.9× 4,672 30,802 6.6× 16 1,309 60,008 45.8× 8,545 61,359 7.2× 32 1,883 112,329 59.7× 13,671 124,002 9.1× 64 2,319 200,348 86.4× 17,768 251,979 14.2× 128 2,276 297,589 130.7× 27,588 501,384 18.2× 256 3,905 139,188 35.6× 32,747 982,760 30.0× 512 4,881 207,829 42.6× 52,307 1,975,241 37.8× 1,024 5,421 278,420 51.4× 51,315 2,421,505 47.2× 2,048 6,311 309,807 49.1× 31,769 2,414,376 76.0× 4,096 515 249,073 483.6× 30,876 2,521,657 81.7× Batch size — Noisy-XOR scale (12 features, 10 clauses/class) batch CPU train ex/s GPU train ex/s train speedup CPU infer ex/s GPU infer ex/s infer speedup 1 890 4,339 4.9× 8,627 3,970 0.5× 4 3,076 17,259 5.6× 30,259 15,875 0.5× 16 11,995 70,193 5.9× 116,475 62,771 0.5× 64 46,409 278,789 6.0× 443,445 249,983 0.6× 256 148,050 206,397 1.4× 1,503,227 1,002,328 0.7× 1,024 326,535 826,193 2.5× 4,363,726 4,010,677 0.9×

docs.title: How much the GPU buys you
docs.text: The speedup is not one number. It grows with batch size because the CPU pays the per-clause cost serially while the GPU hides it, peaks at about 484× around batch 4096, and holds from there. Inference behaves differently again: the CPU forward pass is already cheap, so the gap there tops out at 82× — worth having, but not the same kind of difference.

docs.title: Throughput vs model size
docs.text:
Both axes cost the same thing — the update is n_clauses × 2 × n_features element-wise work — so both curves fall roughly as 1/x. The CPU falls off immediately; the GPU stays flat until the machine is big enough to fill it, which is why the gap widens with model size: 36× at 50 clauses/class against 43× at 4000; 19× at 128 features against 34× at 8192. Big machines are exactly the ones worth moving to a GPU.

Clause budget (784 features, batch 256) clauses/class CPU train ex/s GPU train ex/s train speedup CPU infer ex/s GPU infer ex/s infer speedup 50 5,460 195,700 35.8× 243,556 979,627 4.0× 100 11,864 187,060 15.8× 156,753 998,623 6.4× 250 5,640 158,336 28.1× 64,086 997,053 15.6× 500 3,888 143,801 37.0× 34,817 993,030 28.5× 1,000 1,674 91,596 54.7× 14,958 1,013,655 67.8× 2,000 798 47,954 60.1× 5,776 630,410 109.1× 4,000 556 24,180 43.5× 2,001 262,502 131.2× Feature count (500 clauses/class, batch 256) features CPU train ex/s GPU train ex/s train speedup CPU infer ex/s GPU infer ex/s infer speedup 128 9,965 188,356 18.9× 90,189 969,794 10.8× 256 9,386 180,257 19.2× 66,429 1,013,269 15.3× 512 5,119 158,938 31.0× 42,099 997,063 23.7× 1,024 3,180 131,877 41.5× 24,237 982,130 40.5× 2,048 1,484 77,297 52.1× 13,558 975,955 72.0× 4,096 846 42,867 50.7× 7,780 606,706 78.0× 8,192 633 21,845 34.5× 3,734 330,901 88.6×

docs.title: The model zoo
docs.text:
Weighted and coalesced variants cost about what the plain machine costs: they change the output layer and the feedback policy, not the per-clause work that dominates. The convolutional models are the outlier at 6× the cost of the flat machine per example — a 10×10 patch over a 28×28 image is 361 patches, and every patch is evaluated against every clause.

Model zoo (784 features, batch 128) model CPU train ex/s GPU train ex/s train speedup CPU infer ex/s GPU infer ex/s infer speedup GPU peak memory TsetlinMachine 2,255 275,431 122× 27,768 490,389 18× 55 MB TsetlinMachine (weighted) 2,979 291,915 98× 27,059 450,997 17× 56 MB CoalescedTsetlinMachine 1,930 197,180 102× 22,869 490,858 21× 64 MB RegressionTsetlinMachine 3,235 312,991 97× 26,172 516,131 20× 56 MB ConvTsetlinMachine 630 48,580 77× 632 56,779 90× 167 MB ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine 505 47,277 94× 633 56,698 90× 167 MB

docs.title: Where an update goes
docs.text:
apply_feedback — the stochastic increment/decrement of the whole (n_clauses, 2F) automaton state — is the expensive part of an update: on the CPU it is 25 % of the 57.3 ms call; on the GPU it is 28 % of the 1.9 ms call. A standalone torch.binomial draw of the same (C, 2F) shape costs 267.70 ms on the CPU and 0.21 ms on the GPU — the single most expensive op in the commit. Everything before the commit (encoding, clause evaluation, the vote sums and the feedback count matmuls) is comparatively cheap. That is also why batching pays: a batched update draws once per commit, a sequential one draws once per example.

Update cost breakdown (5 000 clauses, 784 features, batch 256) stage cpu (ms) cuda:0 (ms) encode 0.063 0.039 evaluate 7.495 0.108 votes+select 7.483 0.439 feedback_counts 15.419 0.670 accumulator_alloc 3.691 0.117 coerce_targets 0.009 0.053 apply_feedback 14.205 0.534 refresh_include 15.515 0.226 commit 29.730 0.813 torch.binomial (C x 2F) 267.704 0.209 update() total 57.298 1.882

docs.title: CPU thread scaling
docs.text:
More CPU threads buy surprisingly little in training: 2.5× going from 1 to 32 threads. The batched update is a chain of large element-wise ops over the state, and the binomial draw that dominates it does not thread. Inference scales much better (6.5× over the same range): the forward pass is one big matmul-shaped reduction. If a CPU run is too slow, the lever is the clause budget or the batch size, not torch.set_num_threads.

CPU thread scaling (5 000 clauses, 784 features, batch 256) threads train ex/s infer ex/s 1 742 4,703 2 1,586 9,067 4 2,131 11,250 8 3,952 24,998 16 4,817 34,143 32 1,818 30,741

docs.title: Batched vs sequential feedback
docs.text:
feedback_mode="sequential" is the exact per-example algorithm: it commits once per example, so a mini-batch of 32 pays 32 commits instead of one. Measured at batch 32 that is 7-393× slower than the batched update, depending on the model scale and the device. Batching is the default for that reason — but it is an approximation, and its fidelity degrades as the batch grows. See Batched vs sequential feedback for the accuracy side of this trade.

Batched vs sequential feedback scale feedback_mode batch device examples/s ms / update call mnist-1k batch 1 cpu 461 2.17 mnist-1k batch 1 cuda:0 4,332 0.23 mnist-1k batch 32 cpu 3,054 10.48 mnist-1k batch 32 cuda:0 139,652 0.23 mnist-1k batch 256 cpu 17,457 14.66 mnist-1k batch 256 cuda:0 189,512 1.35 mnist-1k sequential 1 cpu 403 2.48 mnist-1k sequential 1 cuda:0 1,326 0.75 mnist-1k sequential 32 cpu 446 71.77 mnist-1k sequential 32 cuda:0 18,568 1.72 xor batch 1 cpu 883 1.13 xor batch 1 cuda:0 4,395 0.23 xor batch 32 cpu 23,785 1.35 xor batch 32 cuda:0 140,583 0.23 xor batch 256 cpu 132,340 1.93 xor batch 256 cuda:0 208,458 1.23 xor sequential 1 cpu 982 1.02 xor sequential 1 cuda:0 358 2.79 xor sequential 32 cpu 880 36.38 xor sequential 32 cuda:0 357 89.51

docs.title: Where the data lives
docs.text:
Keeping the Boolean dataset in host memory and copying each mini-batch across costs at most 2 % of throughput here — the update is long enough to hide the transfer. So stream a dataset that does not fit in VRAM without worrying, but do hand the model a device tensor: see Choosing a device for the one copy that does bite (Booleanization encoders keep their thresholds on the CPU).

docs.title: Dense segmentation
docs.text:
Dense prediction evaluates one patch per pixel, so throughput is quoted in pixels per second rather than examples per second — one 32×32 image is 1 024 examples.

  • A 3×3 dense model on 32×32 inputs runs at 20,713 px/s training and 1,058,131 px/s predicting on CPU — prediction is roughly 51× cheaper, because it never draws feedback or touches the automata.
  • patches_per_commit is the price of fidelity: committing once per batch reaches 46,876 px/s against 20,713 at the default 128, a 2.3× speedup that costs real accuracy (see the segmentation guide's ablation).

docs.title: 3D convolution
docs.text:
A 3D convolutional machine evaluates every clause at every window position of a volume, so the cost scales with the number of positions P = Pd·Ph·Pw. Throughput is quoted in volumes per second.

  • On GPU (RTX 3090), a cardiac-sized 12×64×64 volume with a 3×7×7 window has 33,640 window positions and trains at 1,288.3 volumes/s; an in-plane stride of 2 cuts that to 8,410 positions and runs at 1,168.4 volumes/s (0.9×).
  • With 2 000 clauses one such volume no longer fits max_chunk_elements, so the patch axis is split automatically into blocks of 18,982 positions: peak memory 247 MB at 305.96 volumes/s, against 268 MB at 347.91 volumes/s when it is forced into one block. The output is identical (the OR over patches and the random-patch draw are exact under the split); with fewer clauses, ordinary batch chunking already respects the budget and blocking buys nothing.

docs.title: End to end: MNIST
docs.text:
Synthetic micro-benchmarks flatter whichever device wins the micro-benchmark, so here is the whole thing end to end, Trainer.fit included:

  • ConvTsetlinMachine 200/class 10x10 — 0.2 s/epoch on the GPU vs 16 s on the CPU (65×), 82.8% test accuracy
  • TsetlinMachine 500/class — 0.4 s/epoch on the GPU vs 12 s on the CPU (34×), 95.4% test accuracy

Accuracy matches across devices to within run-to-run noise, as it should — only the wall clock moves. These are short runs at a modest clause budget; see Benchmarks for what longer runs reach.

docs.title: How the ranking works
docs.text:
★ Highlighted values are the best in their group. Rows are compared only when they share the grouping you chose and the same metric, unit and split, and a group needs at least two such rows. A train-set accuracy is never ranked against a test-set one, and nJ never against µJ. Rows whose paper states no split (mostly hardware measurements) are ranked with test rows. "Best" means highest for accuracy, F1, AUC, IoU, correlations, speed-ups, throughput and efficiency, and lowest for errors (MAE, RMSE, ECE), time, latency, energy, power, area, memory and model size; the ↑ / ↓ next to each value says which. A few count-type metrics, such as the number of clusters, are never ranked.

Before comparing across papers

Papers use different splits, Booleanizations, clause budgets and epoch counts, and some report the peak test accuracy over training rather than a final one. Click a row to see the config, source table and notes behind a number. Papers marked ⚠ have a specific reliability problem; for example, the Pre-Sorted TM's top MNIST and Kuzushiji-MNIST accuracies are likely optimistic. Results from other implementations, or measured before torchtsetlin 0.3.0 made the clause budget a hard cap, are not directly comparable to torchtsetlin runs.

docs.title: torchtsetlin.data.encoders
docs.text:
Booleanization: turning continuous, categorical and image data into Boolean features.

All encoders are torch.nn.Module objects so they can be moved to a device, saved in a state_dict and composed with :class:torchtsetlin.data.Compose. They follow the scikit-learn fit / transform protocol on top of forward (transform is an alias of forward; fit_transform chains both).

docs.title: ThermometerEncoder
docs.text:
ThermometerEncoder(n_bits: int = 8, strategy: str = 'quantile', thresholds: Optional[Tensor] = None, value_range: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None, flatten: bool = True)

Bases: BooleanEncoder

Thermometer (ordinal) encoding of continuous features.

Each feature v becomes n_bits Booleans [v >= t_1, ..., v >= t_n] for increasing thresholds t_k. Clauses can then express ranges with two literals (x>=t_a AND NOT x>=t_b). Thresholds are learned by :meth:fit (quantiles by default) or given explicitly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_bits int

thresholds per feature.

8 strategy str

threshold strategy (see :func:thermometer_thresholds).

'quantile' thresholds Optional[Tensor]

explicit (F, n_bits) thresholds (skips fitting).

None value_range Optional[Sequence[float]]

(lo, hi) for the uniform strategy (e.g. (0, 255) for images).

None flatten bool

return (N, F*n_bits) instead of (N, F, n_bits).

True Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    n_bits: int = 8,
    strategy: str = "quantile",
    thresholds: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    value_range: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None,
    flatten: bool = True,
) -> None:
    super().__init__()
    self.n_bits = int(n_bits)
    self.strategy = strategy
    self.value_range = tuple(value_range) if value_range is not None else None
    self.flatten = bool(flatten)
    if thresholds is not None:
        self.register_buffer("thresholds", torch.as_tensor(thresholds, dtype=torch.float32))
    else:
        self.register_buffer("thresholds", torch.empty(0))

docs.title: feature_names
docs.text:
feature_names(names: Sequence[str]) -> List[str]

Names of the Boolean outputs, e.g. "age>=30.0".

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def feature_names(self, names: Sequence[str]) -> List[str]:
    """Names of the Boolean outputs, e.g. ``"age>=30.0"``."""
    thr = self.thresholds
    if thr.shape[0] == 1:
        thr = thr.expand(len(names), -1)
    return [f"{n}>={float(thr[i, k]):.4g}" for i, n in enumerate(names) for k in range(self.n_bits)]

docs.title: decode_range
docs.text:
decode_range(feature: int, included_pos: Iterable[int], included_neg: Iterable[int])

Range (lo, hi) implied by included positive/negated bits of one feature.

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def decode_range(self, feature: int, included_pos: Iterable[int], included_neg: Iterable[int]):
    """Range ``(lo, hi)`` implied by included positive/negated bits of one feature."""
    thr = self.thresholds[feature if self.thresholds.shape[0] > 1 else 0]
    lo = max((float(thr[k]) for k in included_pos), default=-float("inf"))
    hi = min((float(thr[k]) for k in included_neg), default=float("inf"))
    return lo, hi

docs.title: AdaptiveThresholdEncoder
docs.text:
AdaptiveThresholdEncoder(block_size: int = 11, C: float = 2.0, method: str = 'gaussian')

Bases: BooleanEncoder

Adaptive (local) thresholding for grayscale / multi-channel images, as used to booleanize MNIST/CIFAR for convolutional Tsetlin machines.

bit = pixel > local_mean(pixel) - C where the local mean is computed over a block_size x block_size window, either uniformly (method="mean") or with a Gaussian kernel (method="gaussian", OpenCV ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C).

Input (N, C, H, W) (or (N, H, W)) -> Boolean of the same shape.

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def __init__(self, block_size: int = 11, C: float = 2.0, method: str = "gaussian") -> None:
    super().__init__()
    if block_size % 2 == 0 or block_size < 3:
        raise ValueError("block_size must be odd and >= 3")
    if method not in ("gaussian", "mean"):
        raise ValueError("method must be 'gaussian' or 'mean'")
    self.block_size = int(block_size)
    self.C = float(C)
    self.method = method
    if method == "gaussian":
        sigma = 0.3 * ((block_size - 1) * 0.5 - 1) + 0.8  # OpenCV's default sigma
        ax = torch.arange(block_size, dtype=torch.float32) - (block_size - 1) / 2
        g1 = torch.exp(-(ax**2) / (2 * sigma**2))
        g1 = g1 / g1.sum()
        kernel = torch.outer(g1, g1)
    else:
        kernel = torch.full((block_size, block_size), 1.0 / block_size**2)
    self.register_buffer("kernel", kernel.view(1, 1, block_size, block_size))

docs.title: ColorThermometerEncoder
docs.text:
ColorThermometerEncoder(n_bits: int = 8, value_range: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 255.0))

Bases: BooleanEncoder

Per-channel thermometer encoding of images: each pixel channel becomes n_bits planes [v >= k * 255/(n_bits+1)]. (N, C, H, W) -> (N, C*n_bits, H, W).

value_range defaults to (0, 255); use (0, 1) for float images.

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def __init__(self, n_bits: int = 8, value_range: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 255.0)) -> None:
    super().__init__()
    lo, hi = float(value_range[0]), float(value_range[1])
    steps = torch.arange(1, n_bits + 1, dtype=torch.float32) / (n_bits + 1)
    self.register_buffer("thresholds", lo + (hi - lo) * steps)
    self.n_bits = int(n_bits)

docs.title: HypervectorEncoder
docs.text:
HypervectorEncoder(vocab_size: int, dim: int = 1024, n_bits: int = 8, bind_position: bool = False, seed: int = 0)

Bases: BooleanEncoder

Sparse binary hypervector encoding of discrete tokens (Halenka et al., 2024).

Every token id t < vocab_size owns a fixed random hypervector with n_bits ones among dim positions. A sample (a set / sequence of token ids) is bundled with bitwise OR. Optionally each position p is bound by cyclically shifting the token's hypervector by p (bind_position=True), so word order is preserved.

Input: (N, L) long tensor of token ids (padding id -1 is ignored). Output: (N, dim) Boolean.

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, dim: int = 1024, n_bits: int = 8, bind_position: bool = False, seed: int = 0) -> None:
    super().__init__()
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    table = torch.zeros(vocab_size, dim, dtype=torch.bool)
    for t in range(vocab_size):
        idx = torch.randperm(dim, generator=g)[:n_bits]
        table[t, idx] = True
    self.register_buffer("table", table)
    self.dim = int(dim)
    self.bind_position = bool(bind_position)

docs.title: PyramidEncoder
docs.text:
PyramidEncoder(scales: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 4), patch: int = 3, mode: str = 'or')

Bases: BooleanEncoder

Stack each pixel's neighbourhood at several resolutions into extra Boolean planes.

A k x k patch is all a dense Tsetlin machine sees of a pixel, and some classes simply are not decidable from it — a patch of building interior and a patch of road look alike once illumination varies; telling them apart needs to know where the horizon is. This is the gap an encoder-decoder closes in a CNN, and it can be closed natively here: OR-pool the Boolean planes to build a pyramid, take the same k x k patch at each level, and resample every level back to full resolution. A clause then reads a pixel's immediate neighbourhood and the coarse structure around it, with no float parameter and no gradient anywhere.

Feed the result to a model with patch_size=1: the neighbourhood is already in the planes, and asking for a second one on top multiplies the feature count for nothing.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default scales Sequence[int]

downsampling factors, ascending. 1 is the full-resolution level.

(1, 2, 4) patch int

neighbourhood side length taken at each level.

3 mode str

pooling mode for the pyramid (see :func:torchtsetlin.functional.boolean_pool).

'or' Shape
  • input: (B, Z, H, W) Boolean.
  • output: (B, Z * patch * patch * len(scales), H, W) Boolean.
Example

enc = PyramidEncoder(scales=(1, 2, 4), patch=3) planes = enc(x) # (B, Z93, H, W) model = SegmentationTsetlinMachine(4, 300, T=60, patch_size=1)

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def __init__(self, scales: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 4), patch: int = 3, mode: str = "or") -> None:
    super().__init__()
    self.scales = tuple(int(s) for s in scales)
    self.patch = int(patch)
    self.mode = str(mode)
    if min(self.scales) < 1 or self.patch < 1:
        raise ValueError("scales and patch must be >= 1")

docs.title: thermometer_thresholds
docs.text:
thermometer_thresholds(x: Tensor, n_bits: int, strategy: str = 'quantile', value_range: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None) -> Tensor

Per-feature thresholds (F, n_bits) for thermometer encoding.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x Tensor

(N, F) training data (only needed for "quantile"/"unique" or when value_range is None).

required n_bits int

thresholds per feature.

required strategy str

"quantile" (equal-frequency), "uniform" (equal-width) or "unique" (evenly spaced ranks of the unique training values).

'quantile' value_range Optional[Sequence[float]]

optional global (lo, hi) for the uniform strategy.

None Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/encoders.py 
def thermometer_thresholds(
    x: Tensor,
    n_bits: int,
    strategy: str = "quantile",
    value_range: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None,
) -> Tensor:
    """Per-feature thresholds ``(F, n_bits)`` for thermometer encoding.

    Args:
        x: ``(N, F)`` training data (only needed for ``"quantile"``/``"unique"`` or when
            ``value_range`` is ``None``).
        n_bits: thresholds per feature.
        strategy: ``"quantile"`` (equal-frequency), ``"uniform"`` (equal-width) or
            ``"unique"`` (evenly spaced ranks of the unique training values).
        value_range: optional global ``(lo, hi)`` for the uniform strategy.
    """
    x = x.to(torch.float32)
    Fn = x.shape[1]
    if strategy == "uniform":
        if value_range is not None:
            lo = torch.full((Fn,), float(value_range[0]), device=x.device)
            hi = torch.full((Fn,), float(value_range[1]), device=x.device)
        else:
            lo, hi = x.min(dim=0).values, x.max(dim=0).values
        steps = torch.arange(1, n_bits + 1, device=x.device, dtype=torch.float32) / (n_bits + 1)
        return lo.unsqueeze(1) + (hi - lo).unsqueeze(1) * steps.unsqueeze(0)
    if strategy == "quantile":
        q = torch.arange(1, n_bits + 1, device=x.device, dtype=torch.float32) / (n_bits + 1)
        return torch.quantile(x, q, dim=0).transpose(0, 1).contiguous()
    if strategy == "unique":
        out = torch.empty(Fn, n_bits, device=x.device)
        for f in range(Fn):
            u = torch.unique(x[:, f])
            if u.numel() > 1:
                u = u[1:]  # ``x >= min`` is always True — drop it
            if u.numel() >= n_bits:
                idx = torch.linspace(0, u.numel() - 1, n_bits, device=x.device).round().long()
                out[f] = u[idx]
            else:  # pad by repeating the max (bits that are never on for training data)
                pad = u.max().repeat(n_bits - u.numel()) if u.numel() else torch.zeros(n_bits)
                out[f] = torch.cat([u, pad.to(u.device)])
        return out
    raise ValueError("strategy must be 'quantile', 'uniform' or 'unique'")

docs.title: torchtsetlin.data.graphs
docs.text:
Graph-structured input for :class:~torchtsetlin.models.GraphTsetlinMachine.

A :class:GraphBatch holds a batch of directed multigraphs whose nodes carry Boolean feature vectors and whose edges carry an integer type. Node features are usually sparse hypervectors of symbols, built by a :class:SymbolTable (Halenka et al., 2024; Granmo et al., 2025, arXiv:2507.14874), but any Boolean vector works: an image patch with its position bits is a node, so a graph without edges is the input of a convolutional Tsetlin machine.

Storage is padded: features (B, P, F) with P the largest node count of the batch and a (B, P) node mask. Edges are kept per graph, sorted by graph, with local node indices, so that slicing a batch (batch[idx]) is cheap and keeps every edge inside its graph.

:meth:GraphBatch.pad gives the fixed-shape layout: a fixed node count P and edges as a (B, E, 2) array with an edge mask. Slicing it never looks at the data (no host synchronisation, and the shape of a slice depends only on how many graphs it holds), which is what the CUDA fast paths of :class:~torchtsetlin.models.GraphTsetlinMachine need.

docs.text:
SymbolTable(symbols: Iterable, dim: int = 128, bits: int = 2, encoding: str = 'random', seed: int = 0)

Map symbol names to sparse hypervector positions (the node properties of a graph).

Every symbol owns bits positions out of dim. A node's feature vector is the OR (bundle) of its symbols' positions. The three encodings follow the reference GraphTsetlinMachine (Graphs in graphs.py):

  • "random": bits distinct random positions per symbol (seeded);
  • "double_hashing": positions i mod dim and p - (i mod p) with p the largest prime below dim (always 2 bits);
  • "one_hot": dim = len(symbols) and symbol i owns position i. This is a plain Boolean feature per symbol, and it makes decoding exact.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default symbols Iterable

the symbol names (any hashable values).

required dim int

hypervector size (ignored for "one_hot").

128 bits int

positions per symbol (ignored for "double_hashing" and "one_hot").

2 encoding str

"random", "double_hashing" or "one_hot".

'random' seed int

seed of the random positions.

0 Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/graphs.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    symbols: Iterable,
    dim: int = 128,
    bits: int = 2,
    encoding: str = "random",
    seed: int = 0,
) -> None:
    self.symbols = list(symbols)
    if len(set(self.symbols)) != len(self.symbols):
        raise ValueError("symbol names must be unique")
    self.index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(self.symbols)}
    n = len(self.symbols)
    if encoding == "one_hot":
        dim, bits = n, 1
        pos = torch.arange(n).unsqueeze(1)
    elif encoding == "double_hashing":
        bits = 2
        p = _prev_prime(dim)
        i = torch.arange(n)
        pos = torch.stack([i % dim, p - (i % p)], dim=1)
    elif encoding == "random":
        if not 1 <= bits <= dim:
            raise ValueError("bits must lie in [1, dim]")
        g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(int(seed))
        pos = torch.stack([torch.randperm(dim, generator=g)[:bits] for _ in range(n)]) if n else \
            torch.zeros(0, bits, dtype=torch.long)
    else:
        raise ValueError("encoding must be 'random', 'double_hashing' or 'one_hot'")
    self.dim = int(dim)
    self.bits = int(bits)
    self.encoding = encoding
    self.positions: Tensor = pos.long()  # (n_symbols, bits)

def vector(self, symbols: Iterable) -> Tensor:
    """``(dim,)`` Boolean hypervector of a set of symbols (their bundle)."""
    out = torch.zeros(self.dim, dtype=torch.bool)
    for s in symbols:
        out[self.positions[self.index[s]]] = True
    return out

def encode(self, nodes: Sequence[Iterable]) -> Tensor:
    """``(n, dim)`` Boolean feature matrix, one row per node's symbol set."""
    if not len(nodes):
        return torch.zeros(0, self.dim, dtype=torch.bool)
    return torch.stack([self.vector(s) for s in nodes])

def decode(self, vector: Tensor) -> List:
    """Symbols whose positions are all set in ``vector`` (``(dim,)`` Boolean)."""
    v = as_bool_tensor(vector).flatten()
    hit = v[self.positions].all(dim=1)
    return [self.symbols[i] for i in torch.nonzero(hit).flatten().tolist()]

def __init__(
    self,
    node_features: Tensor,
    n_nodes: Tensor,
    edges: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    edge_type: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    edges_per_graph: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    node_type: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    n_edge_types: Optional[int] = None,
    n_node_types: Optional[int] = None,
    edge_type_names: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None,
) -> None:
    x = as_bool_tensor(node_features)
    if x.dim() != 3:
        raise ValueError("node_features must have shape (B, P, F)")
    dev = x.device
    B, P, _ = x.shape
    n_nodes = torch.as_tensor(n_nodes, dtype=torch.long, device=dev).reshape(-1)
    if n_nodes.numel() != B:
        raise ValueError("n_nodes must hold one count per graph")
    if B and (int(n_nodes.min()) < 0 or int(n_nodes.max()) > P):
        raise ValueError("node counts must lie in [0, P]")
    if edges is None:
        edges = torch.zeros(0, 2, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
    edges = torch.as_tensor(edges, dtype=torch.long, device=dev).reshape(-1, 2)
    E = edges.shape[0]
    edge_type = (torch.zeros(E, dtype=torch.long, device=dev) if edge_type is None
                 else torch.as_tensor(edge_type, dtype=torch.long, device=dev).reshape(-1))
    if edge_type.numel() != E:
        raise ValueError("edge_type must hold one type per edge")
    if edges_per_graph is None:
        if E and B != 1:
            raise ValueError("edges_per_graph is required for a batch of several graphs")
        edges_per_graph = torch.full((B,), E, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
    edges_per_graph = torch.as_tensor(edges_per_graph, dtype=torch.long, device=dev).reshape(-1)
    if edges_per_graph.numel() != B or int(edges_per_graph.sum()) != E:
        raise ValueError("edges_per_graph must hold one count per graph and sum to E")
    if E:
        graph = torch.repeat_interleave(torch.arange(B, device=dev), edges_per_graph)
        if int(edges.min()) < 0 or bool((edges >= n_nodes[graph].unsqueeze(1)).any()):
            raise ValueError("an edge refers to a node outside its graph")
        if int(edge_type.min()) < 0:
            raise ValueError("edge types must be non-negative")
    if node_type is not None:
        node_type = torch.as_tensor(node_type, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
        if node_type.shape != (B, P):
            raise ValueError("node_type must have shape (B, P)")
    self.node_features = x
    self.n_nodes = n_nodes
    self._edges: Optional[Tensor] = edges
    self._edge_type: Optional[Tensor] = edge_type
    self._edges_per_graph: Optional[Tensor] = edges_per_graph
    self._padded: Optional[Tuple[Tensor, Tensor, Tensor]] = None
    #: every graph has exactly ``P`` nodes (no padding rows). Set by the builders on the
    #: host and carried by slicing; it lets depth-1 models use the bit-packed kernel.
    self.full_nodes = False
    self.node_type = node_type
    inferred_et = int(edge_type.max()) + 1 if E else 1
    self.n_edge_types = int(n_edge_types) if n_edge_types is not None else inferred_et
    if E and inferred_et > self.n_edge_types:
        raise ValueError("an edge type is >= n_edge_types")
    inferred_nt = int(node_type.max()) + 1 if node_type is not None and node_type.numel() else 1
    self.n_node_types = int(n_node_types) if n_node_types is not None else inferred_nt
    if inferred_nt > self.n_node_types:
        raise ValueError("a node type is >= n_node_types")
    self.edge_type_names = None if edge_type_names is None else [str(n) for n in edge_type_names]
    if self.edge_type_names is not None and len(self.edge_type_names) != self.n_edge_types:
        raise ValueError("edge_type_names needs one name per edge type")

docs.text:
pad(max_nodes: Optional[int] = None, max_edges: Optional[int] = None) -> GraphBatch

The fixed-shape layout: nodes padded to max_nodes, edges stored as a (B, max_edges, 2) array with an edge mask (defaults: this batch's maxima).

Slicing a padded batch keeps max_nodes and max_edges and never inspects the data, so it is free of host synchronisation and its shape depends only on the number of graphs. That is what lets :class:~torchtsetlin.models.GraphTsetlinMachine use the CUDA fast paths (events mode, fused sequential commits, CUDA graphs). Pad a whole dataset to one size: every distinct (max_nodes, max_edges) is compiled and captured separately. Results are the same as with the flat layout.

Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/graphs.py 
def pad(self, max_nodes: Optional[int] = None, max_edges: Optional[int] = None) -> GraphBatch:
    """The fixed-shape layout: nodes padded to ``max_nodes``, edges stored as a
    ``(B, max_edges, 2)`` array with an edge mask (defaults: this batch's maxima).

    Slicing a padded batch keeps ``max_nodes`` and ``max_edges`` and never inspects the
    data, so it is free of host synchronisation and its shape depends only on the number
    of graphs. That is what lets :class:`~torchtsetlin.models.GraphTsetlinMachine` use the
    CUDA fast paths (events mode, fused sequential commits, CUDA graphs). Pad a whole
    dataset to one size: every distinct ``(max_nodes, max_edges)`` is compiled and captured
    separately. Results are the same as with the flat layout.
    """
    if self._padded is not None and max_nodes is None and max_edges is None:
        return self
    B, P0, F_ = self.shape
    dev = self.device
    per = self.edges_per_graph
    need_p = int(self.n_nodes.max()) if B else 0
    need_e = int(per.max()) if B and per.numel() else 0
    P = need_p if max_nodes is None else int(max_nodes)
    E = need_e if max_edges is None else int(max_edges)
    if P < need_p:
        raise ValueError(f"max_nodes={P} is below the largest graph ({need_p} nodes)")
    if E < need_e:
        raise ValueError(f"max_edges={E} is below the largest graph ({need_e} edges)")
    P = max(P, 1)
    feats = torch.zeros(B, P, F_, dtype=torch.bool, device=dev)
    k = min(P, P0)
    feats[:, :k] = self.node_features[:, :k]
    ntype = None
    if self.node_type is not None:
        ntype = torch.zeros(B, P, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
        ntype[:, :k] = self.node_type[:, :k]
    edges = torch.zeros(B, E, 2, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
    etype = torch.zeros(B, E, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
    mask = torch.zeros(B, E, dtype=torch.bool, device=dev)
    flat_e, flat_t = self.edges, self.edge_type
    if flat_e.shape[0]:
        graph = self.edge_graph
        start = torch.cumsum(per, 0) - per
        slot = torch.arange(flat_e.shape[0], device=dev) - start[graph]
        edges[graph, slot] = flat_e
        etype[graph, slot] = flat_t
        mask[graph, slot] = True
    return self._keep_full(GraphBatch._from_padded(feats, self.n_nodes, edges, etype, mask, ntype,
                                                   self.n_edge_types, self.n_node_types,
                                                   self.edge_type_names))

def unpad(self) -> GraphBatch:

def copy_(self, other: GraphBatch) -> GraphBatch:
    """Copy a padded batch of the same shape into this one, in place (CUDA-graph inputs)."""
    if self._padded is None or other._padded is None:
        raise ValueError("copy_ needs padded batches (GraphBatch.pad)")
    if (self.shape != other.shape or self._padded[0].shape != other._padded[0].shape
            or (self.node_type is None) != (other.node_type is None)):
        raise ValueError("copy_ needs batches of the same padded shape")
    self.node_features.copy_(other.node_features)
    self.n_nodes.copy_(other.n_nodes)
    for a, b in zip(self._padded, other._padded):
        a.copy_(b)
    if self.node_type is not None:
        self.node_type.copy_(other.node_type)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    return self

@staticmethod
def cat(batches: Sequence[GraphBatch]) -> GraphBatch:
    """Concatenate batches along the graph axis (padding to the largest node count).
    Padded batches give a padded batch (to the largest ``max_nodes`` and ``max_edges``)."""
    if not batches:
        raise ValueError("nothing to concatenate")
    out = GraphBatch._cat(batches)
    out.full_nodes = all(b.full_nodes and b.shape[1] == out.shape[1] for b in batches)
    return out

def flat_edges(self) -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor, Tensor]:
    """``(src, dst, type)`` with node indices into the flattened ``B * P`` node axis. For a
    padded batch these include the unused edge slots; :meth:`flat_edge_mask` tells them
    apart."""
    P = self.node_features.shape[1]
    if self._padded is not None:
        e, t, _ = self._padded
        base = (torch.arange(e.shape[0], device=e.device) * P).unsqueeze(1)
        return (base + e[..., 0]).reshape(-1), (base + e[..., 1]).reshape(-1), t.reshape(-1)
    base = self.edge_graph * P
    return base + self.edges[:, 0], base + self.edges[:, 1], self.edge_type

@classmethod
def from_graphs(
    cls,
    node_features: Sequence,
    edges: Optional[Sequence] = None,
    edge_types: Optional[Sequence] = None,
    node_types: Optional[Sequence] = None,
    n_edge_types: Optional[int] = None,
    n_node_types: Optional[int] = None,
    edge_type_names: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None,
) -> GraphBatch:
    """Build a batch from per-graph lists.

    Args:
        node_features: per graph, an ``(n_i, F)`` Boolean array.
        edges: per graph, an ``(E_i, 2)`` array of ``(source, destination)`` local node
            indices (or ``None`` / empty for no edges).
        edge_types: per graph, an ``(E_i,)`` array of edge types (default: all ``0``).
        node_types: per graph, an ``(n_i,)`` array of node types (default: none).
    """
    feats = [as_bool_tensor(f) for f in node_features]
    if not feats:
        raise ValueError("no graphs")
    F_ = feats[0].shape[1] if feats[0].dim() == 2 else 0
    n = torch.tensor([f.shape[0] for f in feats], dtype=torch.long)
    P = max(1, int(n.max()))
    X = torch.zeros(len(feats), P, F_, dtype=torch.bool)
    for i, f in enumerate(feats):
        if f.dim() != 2 or f.shape[1] != F_:
            raise ValueError("every graph needs (n_i, F) node features with the same F")
        X[i, : f.shape[0]] = f.cpu()
    E_list, T_list, per = [], [], []
    for i in range(len(feats)):
        e = edges[i] if edges is not None else None
        e = torch.zeros(0, 2, dtype=torch.long) if e is None else torch.as_tensor(e, dtype=torch.long).reshape(-1, 2)
        t = edge_types[i] if edge_types is not None else None
        t = torch.zeros(e.shape[0], dtype=torch.long) if t is None else torch.as_tensor(t, dtype=torch.long).reshape(-1)
        E_list.append(e)
        T_list.append(t)
        per.append(e.shape[0])
    nt = None
    if node_types is not None:
        nt = torch.zeros(len(feats), P, dtype=torch.long)
        for i, t in enumerate(node_types):
            t = torch.as_tensor(t, dtype=torch.long).reshape(-1)
            nt[i, : t.numel()] = t
    g = cls(X, n, torch.cat(E_list), torch.cat(T_list), torch.tensor(per, dtype=torch.long), nt,
            n_edge_types, n_node_types, edge_type_names)
    g.full_nodes = bool((n == P).all())  # on the host, while building
    return g

@classmethod
def from_sequences(
    cls,
    sequences: Sequence[Sequence],
    symbols: SymbolTable,
    edge_types: Tuple[str, str] = ("left", "right"),
    unknown: str = "ignore",
) -> GraphBatch:
    """One node per sequence element, chained in both directions.

    Node ``k`` sends to ``k - 1`` over edge type 0 (named ``edge_types[0]``) and to
    ``k + 1`` over type 1, as in the reference ``SequenceClassificationDemo``. An element
    may be a single symbol or a set of symbols. Symbols missing from the table are
    ignored (``unknown="ignore"``) or rejected (``"error"``).
    """
    if unknown not in ("ignore", "error"):
        raise ValueError("unknown must be 'ignore' or 'error'")
    feats, edges, types = [], [], []
    for seq in sequences:
        nodes = []
        for el in seq:
            group = el if isinstance(el, (set, frozenset, list, tuple)) else [el]
            kept = [s for s in group if s in symbols.index]
            if unknown == "error" and len(kept) != len(group):
                raise KeyError(f"unknown symbol in {group!r}")
            nodes.append(kept)
        feats.append(symbols.encode(nodes) if nodes else torch.zeros(0, symbols.dim, dtype=torch.bool))
        L = len(nodes)
        k = torch.arange(L)
        left = torch.stack([k[1:], k[:-1]], dim=1)   # k -> k-1, type 0
        right = torch.stack([k[:-1], k[1:]], dim=1)  # k -> k+1, type 1
        edges.append(torch.cat([left, right]))
        types.append(torch.cat([torch.zeros(max(L - 1, 0), dtype=torch.long),
                                torch.ones(max(L - 1, 0), dtype=torch.long)]))
    return cls.from_graphs(feats, edges, types, n_edge_types=2, edge_type_names=edge_types)

from_images(images: Any, patch_size: Union[int, Tuple[int, int]], stride: Union[int, Tuple[int, int]] = 1, position_encoding: bool = True) -> GraphBatch

One node per image patch and no edges (paper Sec. 3.2, "disconnected nodes").

Node features are the Z * kh * kw patch pixels followed by thermometer-coded patch coordinates, exactly the patch features of :class:~torchtsetlin.models.ConvTsetlinMachine with the same arguments. A depth-1 graph machine on these graphs is therefore the convolutional coalesced machine.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default images Any

Boolean (B, Z, H, W) (or (B, H, W)) images.

required Source code in src/torchtsetlin/data/graphs.py 
@classmethod
def from_images(
    cls,
    images: Any,
    patch_size: Union[int, Tuple[int, int]],
    stride: Union[int, Tuple[int, int]] = 1,
    position_encoding: bool = True,
) -> GraphBatch:
    """One node per image patch and no edges (paper Sec. 3.2, "disconnected nodes").

    Node features are the ``Z * kh * kw`` patch pixels followed by thermometer-coded
    patch coordinates, exactly the patch features of
    :class:`~torchtsetlin.models.ConvTsetlinMachine` with the same arguments. A depth-1
    graph machine on these graphs is therefore the convolutional coalesced machine.

    Args:
        images: Boolean ``(B, Z, H, W)`` (or ``(B, H, W)``) images.
    """
    x = as_bool_tensor(images)
    if x.dim() == 3:
        x = x.unsqueeze(1)
    if x.dim() != 4:
        raise ValueError("images must have shape (B, Z, H, W) or (B, H, W)")
    kh, kw = (patch_size, patch_size) if isinstance(patch_size, int) else patch_size
    sh, sw = (stride, stride) if isinstance(stride, int) else stride
    B, Z, H, W = x.shape
    Py, Px = (H - kh) // sh + 1, (W - kw) // sw + 1
    if Py < 1 or Px < 1:
        raise ValueError("image smaller than the patch")
    patches = torch.nn.functional.unfold(x.float(), kernel_size=(kh, kw), stride=(sh, sw))
    patches = patches.transpose(1, 2) > 0.5  # (B, P, Z*kh*kw)
    if position_encoding:
        ys = torch.arange(Py, device=x.device).repeat_interleave(Px)
        xs = torch.arange(Px, device=x.device).repeat(Py)
        pos = torch.cat([ys.unsqueeze(1) > torch.arange(Py - 1, device=x.device).unsqueeze(0),
                         xs.unsqueeze(1) > torch.arange(Px - 1, device=x.device).unsqueeze(0)], dim=1)
        patches = torch.cat([patches, pos.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1)], dim=2)
    P = Py * Px
    n = torch.full((B,), P, dtype=torch.long, device=x.device)
    g = cls(patches, n, None, None, torch.zeros(B, dtype=torch.long, device=x.device), None, 1, 1)
    g.full_nodes = True  # every image has the same patches
    return g
