    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.figure.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)
    return ax

docs.title: Batched vs sequential feedback
docs.text:
The classical Tsetlin machine processes one example at a time: evaluate the clauses, give feedback, update the automata, move on. On a GPU that leaves most of the hardware idle, so torchtsetlin offers two ways to consume a mini-batch.

Sequential feedback updates the memory after every example. A mini-batch looks at all its examples against the same memory, adds up their feedback and commits it once — far fewer, larger steps, which is what makes the GPU fast. The price: the examples of a batch do not see each other's updates.

docs.title: feedback_mode="batch" (default)
docs.text:
All B examples of the batch are evaluated against the current automata. For every (example, clause) pair the algorithm decides whether the clause gets Type I or Type II feedback exactly as in the sequential algorithm. The resulting feedback events are then counted per (clause, literal):

  • n_true[j, k] — Type Ia events where literal k was True (memorise candidates),
  • n_false[j, k] — Type Ia events where literal k was False (forget candidates),
  • n_ib[j] — Type Ib events (forget everything),
  • n2[j, k] — Type II events where literal k was False.

These counts are two small matrix products, and the stochastic transitions become binomial draws: Binomial(n_true, (s-1)/s) increments, Binomial(n_false + n_ib, 1/s) decrements, and min(n2, N - state) deterministic Type II increments (an automaton is never pushed past the include boundary by Type II, exactly as in the sequential algorithm where the clause stops matching once a literal is included). The automata are updated once per batch.

With B = 1 this is the classical algorithm. For B > 1 it is an approximation in the same sense as mini-batch SGD: the examples of a batch do not see each other's updates. Empirically (Noisy XOR, 20 clauses, T=15, s=3.9, N=50, 2000 training examples, 3 seeds):

batch size epochs updates test accuracy 1 (sequential) 40 80 000 0.95 – 0.99 10 100 20 000 0.93 – 0.99 50 200 8 000 0.88 – 0.99 200 400 4 000 0.77 – 0.89

Small and medium batches (≈ 8–64) keep the accuracy of the sequential algorithm while running one to two orders of magnitude faster on a GPU; very large batches need more epochs. Clause weights (weighted and coalesced models) change by at most the number of events in the batch, so also prefer moderate batch sizes there.

docs.title: feedback_mode="sequential"
docs.text:
model = tt.TsetlinMachine(..., feedback_mode="sequential")
# or per call
model.update(x, y, sequential=True)

Examples are processed one by one (still vectorised over all clauses and literals, so it is fast for large models on a GPU, just not as fast as batching). Use it when you want the exact reference dynamics, for small data, or to validate a batched configuration.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text: Independently of the feedback mode, a batch is split into chunks so that the intermediate tensors ((chunk, patches, clauses) for convolutional models) respect max_chunk_elements. Chunking never changes the result of a batched update; it only bounds memory.

docs.title: Practical guidance
docs.text:
• Start with a batch size of 16–64 for flat models and 8–32 for convolutional models.
  • If accuracy lags the sequential algorithm, halve the batch size or increase the number of epochs before touching T and s.
  • The update() return value (vote sums before the update) gives you a free running training accuracy; the Trainer logs it as batch_accuracy.

docs.title: Booleanization
docs.text: Tsetlin machines consume Boolean features. Turning raw data into Booleans is the single most important modelling decision, because the literals are the vocabulary of the learned rules. torchtsetlin.data provides encoders that follow the scikit-learn fit / transform protocol and are nn.Modules (they move to the GPU and are saved in state_dict()).

docs.title: Continuous features: thermometer encoding
docs.text:
ThermometerEncoder(n_bits, strategy) turns each value v into bits [v >= t_1, …, v >= t_n] for increasing thresholds. Two literals then express a range: age>=30 AND NOT age>=50.

Thermometer encoding: each bit answers “is the value at least this much?”, so the 1s fill up from the left as the value grows. Any range is then just two literals. 
enc = tt.data.ThermometerEncoder(n_bits=8, strategy="quantile").fit(x_train_float)
xb = enc(x_train_float)                       # (N, F * 8) bool
model.feature_names = enc.feature_names(column_names)   # readable rules

Strategies: "quantile" (equal-frequency, robust default), "uniform" (equal-width, pass value_range=(0, 255) for images), "unique" (evenly spaced ranks of the unique training values, like tmu's StandardBinarizer).

docs.title: Categorical features
docs.text: OneHotEncoder produces one Boolean per category (menopause=ge40), as in the book's breast cancer example. BitPlaneEncoder gives the binary digits of integers when you want compact codes (even numbers are NOT bit0).

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
• Binarizer(0.3) — fixed threshold (the original MNIST recipe: pixel > 0.3).
  • AdaptiveThresholdEncoder(block_size=11, C=2, method="gaussian") — local thresholding (OpenCV's ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C), used for MNIST/Fashion-MNIST in the convolutional TM papers.
  • ColorThermometerEncoder(n_bits=8) — per-channel thermometer, (N, 3, H, W) → (N, 24, H, W), the standard CIFAR encoding for TM composites.
  • BitPlaneEncoder(8) — 8 place-value planes per channel.

load_mnist_boolean / load_torchvision_boolean apply any of these to a torchvision dataset and return Boolean tensors ready for the GPU.

docs.title: Text and sets
docs.text: Bag-of-words presence bits are the classical text encoding. HypervectorEncoder maps token ids to sparse random hypervectors and bundles them with OR (optionally binding word position with a cyclic shift), a compact alternative for large vocabularies.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
pipeline = tt.data.Compose(tt.data.ThermometerEncoder(4), tt.data.Flatten())
xb = pipeline.fit_transform(x)
pipeline.output_size(n_columns)

docs.title: Decoding rules
docs.text: ThermometerEncoder.decode_range and ConvTsetlinMachine.clause_region translate included bits back to intervals, and interpret.aggregate_literal_importance sums literal importances over the bits of one original feature.

docs.title: Confidence and composites
docs.text: A Tsetlin machine's vote sum is more than a decision: it says how strongly the clauses agree. This page follows Chapter 7 of Granmo's An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines. It covers how to read confidence from the votes, how to tell whether that confidence can be trusted, and how several machines with different skills can be combined into a composite by trusting whichever one is confident.

docs.title: Confidence is the size of the vote sum
docs.text:
Take the book's example: predicting whether a student passes a course from three facts, with three clauses.

  • Lectures votes for Pass.
  • Textbook votes for Pass.
  • NOT Assignments votes for Fail.

A student who followed the lectures and read the book gets two votes for Pass and none against, so v = +2. Every clause that fired agrees, and the machine is confident. A student who only read the book but skipped the assignments gets one vote each way, so v = 0. The clauses disagree, and the machine is uncertain. A large negative sum is confident too, in the other class.

book definition library one binary machine abs(v) — multi-class machine max_k v_k, the winning class's vote sum model.confidence(x) = (clip(max_k v_k, -T, T) + T) / 2T

The library rescales the winning vote sum to [0, 1] so that machines with different T can be compared. Below T the order is the book's. Every prediction whose winning vote reaches T gets confidence 1, so to rank the most confident predictions use the raw votes from model(x), which are not clipped.

docs.title: Trustworthy confidence
docs.text:
High confidence is only useful if it comes with high accuracy. The book's 2 × 2 table:

low accuracy high accuracy high confidence overconfident justifiably confident low confidence justifiably uncertain underconfident

A model's confidence is trustworthy when accuracy rises with it. To check, sort the test predictions by confidence and measure the accuracy of those above each threshold. On the six students of the book's example:

confidence at least +0 +1 +2 correct 5 of 6 5 of 5 2 of 2 accuracy 83 % 100 % 100 %

Acting only on confident predictions removes the one mistake. The book's CIFAR-100 machine shows the same shape at scale: accuracy climbs from about 34 % for the least confident images to 100 % for the most confident.

votes = model(x_test)                                     # raw vote sums, eval() mode
curve = tt.metrics.trustworthiness_curve(votes, y_test)   # accuracy and coverage per level
tt.viz.plot_trustworthiness(curve)

trustworthiness_curve uses the winning raw vote sum as confidence and places its thresholds at quantiles of it. Read the coverage entry next to accuracy: it is the fraction of examples a threshold keeps.

docs.title: Composites: let the confident machine decide
docs.text:
Different machines can have different skills. Two hospitals may train on different patient populations. One machine may read blood samples and another the images. On CIFAR-10, one may see adaptive-threshold edges, another colour thermometers, and another histograms of gradients. A Tsetlin machine composite combines them without retraining:

  1. Each member runs on its own input as usual, but outputs its vote sums instead of a class. Any kind of Tsetlin machine can take part.
  2. Normalise. Members differ in clause count, T and data, so their raw vote sums are on different scales. Each member computes its own factor once, the spread of the vote sums it produces on a reference set: alpha = max(v) - min(v). It divides its votes by that factor.
  3. Add the normalised vote sums of all members and take the arg-max, as for a single machine.

A confident member has a large normalised sum and dominates. An uncertain member sums to about zero and barely affects the result. In the book's breast-cancer example, the Recurrence machine votes +2 (normalised +1) and the Non-recurrence machine does not fire (0), so the composite predicts Recurrence.

Fix the factor once per member

alpha belongs to the member, not to the batch. Computing max - min over each batch you happen to predict makes one example's prediction depend on the other examples in its batch, and changes results with the batch size. Fit the factors once on a reference set, such as a validation split, and reuse them. The TM Composites paper uses the test set's 10 000 images, as does our reproduction.

The combination is plug-and-play: no member is retrained and members can be added later. In this repository's reproduction of the CIFAR-10 composite (experiments/multi_convtm/, three seeds on library version 0.3.2), four specialists reached 68.6 % against 56.8 % for the best single specialist. That gain of about 12 points matches the paper's. The absolute numbers are lower than the paper's, which the report attributes mainly to the 0.3.x hard clause budget; see experiments/multi_convtm/REPORT.md.

How to build one in code is in Evaluation and metrics.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• O.-C. Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Chapter 7, tsetlinmachine.org.
  • O.-C. Granmo, TMComposites: Plug-and-Play Collaboration Between Specialized Tsetlin Machines, arXiv:2309.04801 (2023).

docs.title: Convolution
docs.text: A convolutional Tsetlin machine (Granmo et al., 2019; book chapter 4) lets clauses look for patterns anywhere in an image, sequence or volume instead of memorising absolute pixel positions.

docs.title: Why convolution
docs.text: Take 4 × 4 black-and-white images of circles and crosses that can appear in any of the four corners (the book's example). A flat Tsetlin machine sees 16 pixel features, so the same circle in a different corner is a different pattern: it needs one clause per position, four for the circle and four for the cross. A convolutional machine looks at the image through a 3 × 3 window and uses the window's 9 pixels as features, so the features are the same wherever the window is. One clause per shape is enough, and it stays one clause when the image grows; a larger image only adds window positions.

docs.title: Patches and position literals
docs.text:
An input image (Z, H, W) of Boolean planes is cut into every kh × kw window (with a stride). Each window becomes a patch with

  • Z * kh * kw pixel features, followed by
  • thermometer-encoded coordinates: P_y - 1 bits [y > k] and P_x - 1 bits [x > k], where P_y, P_x are the number of window positions along each axis (position_encoding=True).

A clause that includes y > 2 AND NOT y > 5 therefore only matches windows in rows 3–5, i.e. it can learn where a pattern is allowed to appear — or ignore position entirely.

Position matters when the same local pattern means different things in different places. The book's example is a horizontal stroke: at the top of a digit it is the bar of a 7, at the bottom it is the base of a 2. A clause that restricts the stroke to the upper rows stops matching the 2. Thermometer bits are used because two of them express a range, so a clause can describe a rectangular region with at most four position literals.

Position literals are thermometer bits too. Including y > 2 and NOT y > 5 restricts the clause to window rows 3–5; including none of them lets it match anywhere.

docs.title: Evaluation and learning
docs.text:
A clause is True for an image if it matches at least one patch (OR over patches). Vote sums, T and the Type I / Type II selection are unchanged. When a matching clause receives Type Ia or Type II feedback, one matching patch is drawn uniformly at random and its literals are used for the update; Type Ib (no match) needs no patch.

For a clause selected for feedback, the four cases are:

clause matches some patch clause matches no patch example of the clause's class Type Ia (Recognize) on one random matching patch Type Ib (Erase), no patch needed example of another class Type II (Reject) on one random matching patch no feedback

Different clauses end up specialising on different parts of an image: one on a wheel, one on the ground below it, one on a window. The image's class is decided by their summed votes. This cooperation is what T buys. With the book's T = 2 from Chapter 1, two matching clauses already satisfy the margin, so few clauses ever learn about a class. A larger T keeps feedback flowing until many clauses agree, so more of them learn to recognise different parts. That is why convolutional models use a much larger T relative to their clause count than flat ones (see Hyper-parameters).

A 3 × 3 clause is checked at every window position; the OR over positions makes it true for the image if it matches anywhere. That is why one clause can find a shape no matter where it appears.

torchtsetlin implements this with torch.nn.functional.unfold for the patches, a single matmul for all (patch, clause) matches and a gather of the randomly chosen patch rows for the feedback counts. The draw happens in _feedback_counts, over the selected feedback events only, so prediction costs one matmul and an OR — no randomness at all — and each event draws its own patch (a coalesced clause can take Type Ia and Type II in the same update). Memory is bounded by chunking the batch (see Batched vs sequential feedback).

model = tt.ConvTsetlinMachine(
    n_classes=10, n_clauses=200, T=100, s=10, patch_size=10, weighted=True,
).to("cuda")
model.update(images, labels)          # images: (B, 1, 28, 28) Boolean
model.clause_patch(0)                 # (Z, kh, kw) map: 1 = must be on, -1 = off, 0 = free
model.clause_region(0)                # allowed window rows/columns of clause 0
tt.viz.plot_conv_clauses(model, range(16))

Variants: ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine (shared clauses, multi-label capable), ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine, Conv1dTsetlinMachine for sequences (B, Z, L), and the 3D models below for volumes (B, Z, D, H, W).

docs.title: 3D volumes
docs.text:
Nothing in the algorithm above depends on the patches coming from a 2D grid. Evaluation is an OR over a set of patches, and feedback draws one matching patch from that set. A 3D machine changes only how the set is built:

  • the window is kd × kh × kw and slides along depth, rows and columns, giving P = Pd · Ph · Pw positions, with P_a = ⌊(N_a − k_a) / s_a⌋ + 1 per axis;
  • each patch has Z · kd · kh · kw voxel features;
  • position literals use three thermometers, d > k, y > k and x > k. A clause's position literals therefore describe an axis-aligned box of window positions, and clause_region returns it as {"d": …, "y": …, "x": …}.
The window covers three consecutive slices and visits every position along x, y and depth. There is one match map per depth offset, and the OR over all of them is the clause output.

Conv3dTsetlinMachine reuses the 2D clause evaluation and feedback code unchanged, because that code only ever sees a (B, P, 2F) tensor of patch literals. A consequence that the tests pin: with D = kd = 1, the 3D model builds bit-for-bit the literals of ConvTsetlinMachine and, under the same seed, trains to the same automata.

Why not just stack the slices as channels? That works, and it equals a 3D machine whose window spans the whole depth (kd = D). But such a window cannot slide along depth, so a pattern that can occur at any depth needs one clause per depth offset. A window with kd < D covers all offsets with a single clause. For the concept "some voxel is on" in a depth-D column, the stacked model provably needs at least D clauses, while the 3D model needs one.

The two classes of make_3d_shapes use the same slices in a different order. A kd = 3 window learns the order once and slides it through depth; a 2D model on stacked slices sees all five at once and has to learn each depth offset as a separate clause. 
model = tt.Conv3dTsetlinMachine(
    n_classes=2, n_clauses=20, T=15, s=10, patch_size=3, position_encoding=False,
)
model.update(volumes, labels)         # volumes: (B, Z, D, H, W) Boolean
model.clause_patch(0)                 # (Z, kd, kh, kw): 1 = on, -1 = off, 0 = free
model.clause_region(0)                # {"d": (lo, hi), "y": ..., "x": ...}
model.patch_clause_outputs(volumes)   # (B, Pd, Ph, Pw, C) match maps
tt.viz.plot_conv_clauses(model, range(8))   # each clause drawn slice by slice

Conv3dCoalescedTsetlinMachine and Conv3dRegressionTsetlinMachine are the 3D versions of the coalesced and regression variants. Use it for MRI or CT stacks (slices, H, W), or put time on the depth axis for cine sequences (frames, H, W).

Memory. The cost scales with P, and volumes have many positions: a 12 × 64 × 64 stack with a 3 × 7 × 7 window has 33 640. When one volume would exceed max_chunk_elements, which happens with many clauses, the model splits the patch axis into blocks. This is exact: the OR over patches is the OR of the per-block ORs, and the random matching patch is the best of the per-block winners, so the draw has the same distribution. Set patches_per_chunk to choose the block size yourself. An in-plane stride such as stride=(1, 2, 2) is the cheaper lever, since it cuts P four-fold. Measured numbers are in CPU vs GPU.

docs.title: Runnable examples
docs.text:
Walked through in Convolution on generated data and MNIST:

script model what it demonstrates examples/shapes_conv.py ConvTsetlinMachine one clause beats a flat machine that has to memorise every position (1.000 on every seed, against 0.55–0.91), and what position_encoding costs on a translation-invariant task examples/conv1d_ramps.py Conv1dTsetlinMachine a motif anywhere in a thermometer-encoded signal; the clauses print as the ramp they detect examples/conv_regression_blobs.py ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine reading a continuous quantity (a square's side length) off an image examples/shapes_conv3d.py Conv3dTsetlinMachine shapes that differ only in their slice order: the 3D model scores 1.000 on every seed, stacking slices as channels 0.83–0.98, a flat TM 0.73–0.80 examples/mnist_conv.py ConvTsetlinMachine, ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine the real thing: 10×10 windows, adaptive thresholding, --stride, --coalesced

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Booleanize images with AdaptiveThresholdEncoder (MNIST-like) or ColorThermometerEncoder (RGB) — see Booleanization.
  • Typical MNIST settings from the literature: 10 × 10 windows, 2000–8000 clauses per class, T around 1.25–12.5 × clauses-per-class, s 5–10, weighted clauses.
  • Set position_encoding=False for tasks that are fully translation invariant; position literals otherwise make clauses more specific and slower to generalise on small data. This holds in 3D too: on make_3d_shapes, accuracy drops from 1.000 to 0.48 with them on.

docs.title: Graph Tsetlin machines
docs.text: A graph Tsetlin machine (GraphTM; Granmo et al., 2025, arXiv:2507.14874) learns clauses over graph-structured input: sequences, grids, relations, or several views of one example. It generalises the convolutional machine. Where a convolutional clause looks at one window at a time, a graph clause looks at one node and at what the node's neighbours reported, and through several layers of such reports it can describe a whole sub-graph.

docs.title: The input: nodes, symbols and typed edges
docs.text:
A graph is a set of nodes with directed, typed edges between them. Each node carries a Boolean feature vector, usually the bundle (bitwise OR) of the sparse hypervectors of its symbols (properties), as in the hypervector TM (Halenka et al., 2024): a letter, a pixel value, a coordinate. Edges have a type, such as "left" and "right" in a sequence or "parent" and "measurement" in a medical record. A node hears from the nodes that have an edge into it.

In torchtsetlin a batch of graphs is a GraphBatch, and SymbolTable turns symbol names into hypervector positions.

docs.title: Deep clauses
docs.text:
A GraphTM clause has one component per layer:

C = C⁰ ∧ C¹ ∧ … ∧ C^(D-1)
  • C⁰ is an ordinary clause over the node's own features.
  • C^i (i ≥ 1) is a clause over the node's inbox of layer i. The inbox holds a message (clause k, edge type t) for every in-neighbour, reached over an edge of type t, at which clause k's components 0 … i-1 all match.

So a node first checks its own properties. A clause that matches there tells the neighbours, and the next layer can then require "and my left neighbour matched clause 3, and my right neighbour matched clause 0". Each layer reaches one hop further. A clause is True for the graph when its deep clause holds at some node: the same OR over positions that makes a convolutional clause translation tolerant.

Three consecutive A's with a depth-2 clause, the paper's worked example. Clause 0's first component C⁰ = A matches at X1–X3, and each match is sent to both neighbours, labelled with the edge it travels along. The second component asks for a match on both sides, so the deep clause holds only at X2.

docs.title: Messages are symbols too
docs.text:
An inbox is a Boolean vector of M bits (message_size). Clause k owns message_bits positions in it, and a message arriving over an edge of type t sets those positions shifted cyclically by t. This binds the message to the edge type: "clause 3 via left" and "clause 3 via right" set different bits. The inbox is the OR of all messages received, so a clause component over it is an ordinary clause over Boolean literals, and the whole machinery of literals, automata and feedback applies unchanged.

Three encodings are available (message_encoding):

Encoding Bits per message Collisions Readable as "random" (default, as the reference code) message_bits random positions out of M possible decoded when unambiguous "double_hashing" 2 (k mod M, p − (k mod p)) possible decoded when unambiguous "one_hot" 1, M = n_clauses · n_edge_types none right1:0 exactly

Hashed messages keep the inbox small however many clauses there are, at the price of collisions: when many clauses share few bits, a message literal can no longer tell them apart. The paper sees accuracy fall from 1,000 to 2,000 clauses at a fixed message size on its multivalue XOR task, and attributes it to such collisions. model.message_collision_rate() reports the fraction of messages whose bits are all shared with others. One-hot messages never collide but grow with the clause count, which suits small and medium models and makes every clause readable.

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
Voting is the coalesced machine's: one pool of clauses with a signed integer weight per class. Feedback is the convolutional machine's, applied to the deep clause. For each feedback event, one node where the whole clause matches is drawn at random, and every layer's component is updated against that node's input of that layer: its own features for C⁰, its inbox of layer i for C^i. A clause that matches nowhere receives only forgetting (Type Ib). The literal budget max_included_literals counts the included literals of all layers together. As in the reference implementation, s may be one value per layer, s=(s0, s1, …): s0 for the node features, s_i for the inbox of layer i.

The budget matters more than in a flat machine. At the start every clause is empty, matches at every node and so sends messages from everywhere; a boosted Type Ia event then includes every message literal of the drawn node at once. Without a budget, clauses can settle on "nothing special here, and everything matched around me", which is True in every graph. On the sequence example (examples/graph_sequence.py) depth 2 without a budget stays at chance, and with max_included_literals=8 it reaches 100% on every seed tried.

An empty component matches (it constrains nothing), in learning and in prediction: messages are the next layer's input, and a clause can learn to rely on those of an empty clause, which say no more than "a neighbour exists on that side". Only an entirely empty clause's own vote is dropped when predicting, as in every torchtsetlin model.

docs.title: How torchtsetlin implements it
docs.text:
Concatenate a node's per-layer inputs into one row, [H⁰ | H¹ | … | H^(D-1)]. A clause is then a single row of automata over that row, and:

  1. The deep clause is the row's AND. AND is associative: the AND over all included literals of the row is the AND, over layers, of each component on its own input. An empty component contributes True.
  2. The feedback is the convolutional feedback on that row. Drawing one matching node and updating every layer from it is exactly what the convolutional machine does with one matching patch and its literal row. (The code sums the drawn rows as one sparse product of "events per clause and node" with the node inputs, which gives the same counts without copying a row per event.)

So a GraphTsetlinMachine stores one ta_state of shape (C, 2·(F + (D−1)·M)), like every other model, and reuses the convolutional feedback code. Only evaluation is new, because an inbox depends on the previous layer's matches at the neighbours. It runs layer by layer: match component i on the inputs of layer i, AND it into the running match, and send the result along the edges (a scatter-OR, then a matrix product with the shifted message positions). The derivation is in plans/graph-tm.md.

Two consequences:

  • Depth 1 is the convolutional coalesced machine. With no message layers and the graphs of GraphBatch.from_images (one node per patch, no edges), a GraphTsetlinMachine given the same automata, weights and random stream learns bit for bit like ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine. The test suite checks this.
  • Batched feedback works as for other models (batching). A batch of graphs is padded to its largest node count and evaluated in one pass; feedback_mode="sequential" is the reference implementation's one graph at a time.
  • The CUDA fast paths of the convolutional machine apply: with nodes for patches, the fused Triton commit and the compiled single-example commit take the graph's literal rows and the drawn nodes unchanged. Datasets padded to one shape (GraphBatch.pad) are also replayed from CUDA graphs (guide).

docs.title: Where torchtsetlin differs from the reference code
docs.text: Point Reference GraphTsetlinMachine torchtsetlin default To match the reference Random node per clause one per (graph, clause), shared by all classes and by Type I and II one per feedback event shared_node_draw=True Negative classes every class, scaled by q / (K−1) the target and one sampled negative class multi_label=True, one-hot targets, negative_scale = q / (K−1) Order one graph at a time batched feedback_mode="sequential" Empty clause when predicting votes does not vote; its messages still flow —

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Relations matter more than positions. In a sequence, "an A whose left and right neighbours are A" is one depth-2 clause, wherever it occurs. A flat machine needs one clause per position, and a convolutional one needs a window wide enough to hold the whole pattern.
  • Several views of one example. Different encodings of the same data can be different nodes with their own symbols, so one graph can carry, say, a thresholded image and a colour thermometer side by side. The paper attributes its CIFAR-10 result (70.28% vs 66.42% for the convolutional machine, both at depth 1) to this.
  • Variable-size input. Graphs in a batch may have different numbers of nodes and edges.

Depth costs time. Every extra layer adds a pass over the edges and M automata per clause; keep depth at the number of hops a pattern really needs.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• O.-C. Granmo et al. The Tsetlin Machine Goes Deep: Logical Learning and Reasoning With Graphs. arXiv:2507.14874, 2025 (v2 2026). Reference implementation: cair/GraphTsetlinMachine.
  • O.-C. Granmo, S. Glimsdal, L. Jiao, M. Goodwin, C. W. Omlin, G. T. Berge. The Convolutional Tsetlin Machine. arXiv:1905.09688, 2019.
  • S. Glimsdal, O.-C. Granmo. Coalesced Multi-Output Tsetlin Machines with Clause Sharing. arXiv:2108.07594, 2021.
  • V. Halenka et al. Exploring Effects of Hyperdimensional Vectors for Tsetlin Machines. arXiv:2406.02648, 2024.

docs.title: Hyper-parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning Typical values n_clauses clauses per class (flat/conv) or shared clauses (coalesced) 20 (XOR) … 2000–8000 (MNIST) T vote margin: how many net votes a class should reach ≈ 0.5–2 × clauses/class for flat, up to 10 × for convolutional s specificity: 1/s forget probability 2–4 for small/tabular, 5–15 for images, 2–8 for text n_states memory depth N per action 50–128 (256 states); deeper = slower forgetting boost_true_positive deterministic memorisation of True literals True weighted integer clause weights True for images, often False for tiny problems max_included_literals clause size budget (soft by default; budget_mode) 8–32 for concise rules drop_clause_p fraction of clauses dropped per batch/epoch 0.25 (images) – 0.75 (text) focused_negative_sampling pick confusable negative classes True for many classes feedback_mode "batch" or "sequential" "batch" with batch size 8–64

Reference configurations from the literature:

Task clauses T s notes Noisy XOR (12 bits) 20 15 3.9 100 states, ~200 epochs MNIST, flat 2000/class 50 10 pixel > 0.3, 256 states, 400 epochs MNIST, conv 10×10 8000/class 10 000 5 weighted, adaptive Gaussian threshold Fashion-MNIST, conv 10×10 8000/class 10 000 10 weighted CIFAR-10, conv 3×3 colour thermometer 2000/class 1500 2.5 composites IMDb bag-of-words 10 000 8000 2.0 drop clause 0.75 Specificity s. Literals that do not help are forgotten with probability 1/s: a small s keeps rules short and general, a large s lets them grow long and specific.

What each core parameter does, from the Markov-chain analysis in Why a Tsetlin machine learns what it learns:

  • s is a frequency threshold: a literal stays in a clause roughly when it is true in more than 1/s of the examples that train the clause.
  • n_states sets how sharp each include/exclude decision is: every extra state makes the automaton exponentially more likely to sit firmly on one side.
  • T makes clauses divide the work: without a margin, clauses for the same class converge to the same pattern.

Rules of thumb:

  • Raise T together with the number of clauses; the ratio matters more than either value.
  • If clauses stay empty or tiny, raise s; if they memorise noise, lower s.
  • Use HyperparameterSchedule to anneal s or grow drop_clause_p over epochs.
  • Track model.state_summary() (mean included literals, empty clauses) with StateSummaryLogger.

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text: Semantic segmentation asks for a label at every pixel. This page explains why a convolutional Tsetlin machine cannot produce one, what torchtsetlin does instead, and which of the available context mechanisms actually move the numbers.

docs.title: Why a convolutional TM cannot segment
docs.text:
In a convolutional TM a clause is a filter that slides over the image, and the clause's output for the image is the disjunction over all patch positions (Granmo et al., 2019):

\[c_j \;=\; \bigvee_{b=1}^{B} c_j^{\,b}\]

That OR is exactly what gives a CTM its translation tolerance, and exactly what destroys a dense output: afterwards the model knows a pattern occurred somewhere, not where. In the code it is one line — matches.any(dim=1) at the end of _ConvMixin._evaluate. Every published TM aggregates patches this way, and CTM-UNet (Liu & Abeyrathna, ISTM 2025) is the only paper that works around it, by keeping the block output as a vote map.

If you want the unreduced tensor for a convolutional model — to plot where a clause fires, or to stack blocks — use model.patch_clause_outputs(x), which returns (B, Py, Px, C). It is an inspection tool: it does not make the model learn a dense output, because the feedback path still collapses the patch axis.

docs.title: The dense head
docs.text:
SegmentationTsetlinMachine keeps the patch axis instead. Every pixel contributes one kh × kw neighbourhood of the Boolean planes, and that neighbourhood is an ordinary example of a flat Tsetlin machine whose label is the pixel's class:

(B, Z, H, W)  --unfold, pad--> (B·P, Z·kh·kw)  --> clause outputs (B·P, C) --> votes (B·P, K)
                                                                              --> (B, K, H, W)

Folding the patch axis into the batch axis is the whole trick: with B' = B·P the vote sums, the Type I / Type II selection, the feedback counting and functional.apply_feedback all apply unchanged. A dense segmenter is a convolutional TM with padding="same", stride=1, no OR-pooling and a per-patch label taken from the centre pixel.

Left: the OR over windows gives one answer for the whole picture — it knows that there is a building, not where. Right: the dense head gives every pixel its own window and its own vote, and the votes form the label map.

This is CTM-UNet's CTM2D block without the disjunction, and the paper's K parallel machines are the K clause banks of one TsetlinMachine.

model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(
    n_classes=4, n_clauses=300, T=60, s=10.0, patch_size=3,
).to("cuda")
model.update(x, labels)        # x: (B, Z, H, W) Boolean, labels: (B, H, W) long
model.eval()
model.predict(x)               # (B, H, W) label map
model.vote_map(x)              # (B, K, H, W) per-pixel vote sums

forward() returns the folded votes (B·P, K), which is what keeps Trainer, metrics and interpret working unchanged; vote_map and predict are the segmentation-facing views.

docs.title: Commit granularity is a real hyper-parameter
docs.text:
One batch of 8 images at 32×32 is 8 192 pixel-examples. Committing all of their feedback at once is a mini-batch of 8 192 — far past the point where batched feedback stops matching the classical algorithm (see Batched vs sequential feedback, which puts the onset at a couple of hundred on Noisy XOR). patches_per_commit bounds it.

Measured on make_segmentation_shapes (16×16, 3 classes, 100 clauses/class, 12 epochs, mean ± sd over 3 seeds):

patches_per_commit pixel accuracy mIoU relative time 64 0.938 ± 0.001 0.741 ± 0.002 21× 128 (default) 0.940 ± 0.002 0.749 ± 0.009 11× 256 0.909 ± 0.019 0.659 ± 0.056 5.7× 512 0.898 ± 0.034 0.620 ± 0.097 3.0× 1024 0.886 ± 0.012 0.591 ± 0.029 1.7× 4096 0.814 ± 0.094 0.527 ± 0.073 1×

Two things to read off it. Quality is flat up to ~128 and then falls away; and the variance grows with the commit size, so a single large-commit run can look fine and the next one collapse. feedback_mode="sequential" is equivalent to patches_per_commit=1 — the exact classical algorithm, one pixel at a time, and correspondingly slow.

docs.title: Context: what a k × k patch cannot know
docs.text:
A 3×3 patch of building interior and a 3×3 patch of road look alike once illumination varies; separating them needs to know where the horizon is, which is information that does not exist inside the window. This is the gap an encoder–decoder closes in a CNN, and there are two TM-native ways to close it here.

Position literals (position_encoding=8) append thermometer-encoded patch coordinates, so a clause can say y > 12 AND NOT y > 18 — "only in these rows". Pass an integer to bound the feature count on large images; True uses one bit per row and column, which is fine at 32 px and ruinous at 512.

A multi-scale pyramid (data.PyramidEncoder) OR-pools the Boolean planes, takes the same k × k patch at each level and resamples every level back to full resolution, so a clause reads the pixel's neighbourhood and the coarse structure around it. Feed the result to a model with patch_size=1. No float parameter and no gradient anywhere — the pooling is functional.boolean_pool and the machinery to pass one machine's votes into another as ordered Boolean planes is functional.thermometer_cast.

Why the pyramid helps. On the full image, a 3 × 3 window inside the building sees only wall; on coarser copies the same window reaches the sky and the road. (The encoder OR-pools Boolean planes; the colours here are for readability.)

Measured on make_scenes (32×32, 4 classes, 220 train / 80 test, 300 clauses/class, 8 epochs, 4-bit colour thermometer):

pixel acc. mIoU sky building tree road row prior, no image content 0.876 0.410 0.715 0.000 0.000 0.923 single scale 3×3 0.945 0.818 0.997 0.526 0.833 0.915 pyramid 1×/2×/4× 0.987 0.925 0.998 0.837 0.884 0.981 single scale + position 0.989 0.935 0.999 0.865 0.893 0.984 pyramid + position 0.993 0.954 0.999 0.919 0.906 0.990

Building IoU is the column that matters: 0.526 with no context, 0.837 with the pyramid, 0.865 with position literals, 0.919 with both. Both mechanisms work and they compose.

Read mIoU, not pixel accuracy

The first row is a classifier that has never seen a pixel — it labels each pixel by the most common class in its row — and it already reaches 0.876 pixel accuracy, because these scenes have a stable vertical layout. It scores 0.410 mIoU, and zero on two of the four classes. Any dataset with a consistent layout has a floor like this; report it alongside your numbers. It is the same objection that applies to CTM-UNet's headline 96.35%, which is a binary sky-vs-background task.

A corollary for the model: position literals are so effective here partly because the layout is fixed. On data where the structure moves — cardiac MRI at varying slice positions, microscopy — expect them to help much less, and lean on the pyramid instead.

docs.title: Class imbalance
docs.text:
Background dominates every real segmentation set, and a Tsetlin machine has no loss to reweight. The only lever is which pixels produce feedback, which is class_feedback_p: a per-class probability that a pixel takes part in an update. data.balanced_class_probabilities(labels, K, floor=0.05) computes the equalising choice.

It is a rescue, not a default. On the scenes above it lifts the pyramid-only run from 0.925 to 0.950 mIoU (building 0.837 → 0.914), and costs about 0.03 mIoU once position literals are on, because by then the model can separate the classes anyway and throwing away 95% of the road pixels is pure loss. Reach for it when a specific class is being lost, and check the per-class IoU afterwards.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Dense evaluation is H·W clause evaluations per image — roughly 1000× a flat classifier on a 32×32 input. Measured on a 16-core CPU, 4 planes, 4 classes, 100 clauses/class, batch of 8 images: about 35 000 px/s training and 1 090 000 px/s predicting, so prediction is ~30× cheaper than learning. Above ~64 px, use a GPU. _chunk_elements_per_example scales the chunk size with P · (8C + 4F); if you override it, get it right or chunking collapses into many tiny chunks.

docs.title: What not to build
docs.text: CTM-UNet puts trainable Conv2D layers in front of each CTM block. No gradient can cross a Tsetlin machine, so by the paper's own account those layers are a frozen random projection; measured in examples/notebooks/05_ctm_unet_segmentation.ipynb they cost 5.5 points of pixel accuracy, because they mix the bit planes and the thresholding that follows discards the ordering the thermometer encoding was built to preserve. A clause can only refer to the bits it is handed. Use the Boolean pyramid instead.

docs.text:

docs.title: How a Tsetlin machine learns
docs.text:
This page summarises the algorithm implemented by torchtsetlin, using the vocabulary of Granmo's textbook An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines and the original paper (Granmo, 2018). If you know the book, the mapping is:

Book Paper / code Memorize / Forget value (s-1)/s and 1/s (specificity s) Recognize feedback Type Ia feedback Erase feedback Type Ib feedback Reject feedback Type II feedback Vote margin threshold T memory position 1…2N automaton state 0…2N-1, included when >= N Memorize Value + Forget Value = 1 (Chapter 1, e.g. 0.1 / 0.9) (s-1)/s and 1/s, or memorize with probability 1 (boost_true_positive=True, the default, which is also the book's choice from Chapter 2 on)

The machine combines three strategies, one per part of the algorithm:

  1. Frequent pattern mining. Type Ia and Type Ib feedback make a clause describe what is typical of its class, for example "most cars have four wheels".
  2. Discrimination. Type II feedback makes the clause reject look-alikes from other classes, for example "cars have no wings".
  3. Data dissection. The vote margin T spreads the clauses over different sub-patterns, so together they cover the whole class instead of all describing its most common case.

It is rule-based like a decision tree, adds up evidence like logistic regression, and works on bits, which keeps inference cheap and the learned rules readable.

docs.title: Literals, clauses and votes
docs.text:
An example is a vector of F Boolean features. Its literals are the features and their negations, [x, NOT x] (length 2F). A clause is an AND of a subset of literals; it matches an example when all its literals are True. Each clause belongs to a class and has a polarity: positive clauses vote for the class, negative clauses vote against it.

The class sum (vote sum) is

\[v_k = \sum_{j \in \text{pos}(k)} w_j c_j(x) - \sum_{j \in \text{neg}(k)} w_j c_j(x), \qquad \hat y = \arg\max_k \operatorname{clip}(v_k, -T, T)\]

with w_j = 1 for the standard TM (integer weights for the weighted TM).

In everyday terms: the machine turns the input into a list of yes/no facts, each clause is a small checklist that fires only when every item on it is true, and the class with the most net votes wins.

Deciding “beach day?” for a sunny, windy weekend. Each clause is an AND of literals; it votes only if all of its literals are true. Two clauses vote for, one against, so the total is +1 and the answer is yes.

While learning, an empty clause (no included literals) evaluates to True so that it can start memorising; while predicting it evaluates to False.

A clause may include both x and NOT x. Such a clause can never match, so it receives only Type Ib (forget) feedback until one of the two literals is dropped. Contradictions disappear without a special rule.

docs.title: Memory: Tsetlin automata
docs.text:
Every (clause, literal) pair owns a Tsetlin automaton whose state is an integer in [0, 2N-1]. States >= N mean the literal is included (memorised) in the clause, states < N mean it is excluded (forgotten). N (n_states) is the memory depth: deep states are hard to change, states near the boundary flip easily. Automata start just below the boundary (N-1), "about to be memorised but currently forgotten". The starting point does not decide where learning ends up: the outcome is a probability distribution over clauses that does not depend on the initial state (see Why a Tsetlin machine learns what it learns). init="random" is therefore a valid alternative to the default init="boundary".

Think of each automaton as a token on a track: rewards push it towards remember, penalties towards forget, and the literal is part of the clause only while the token sits on the remember side. A token deep in either half needs many consistent signals to change its mind — that is what makes learning robust to noise.

One Tsetlin automaton with N = 4 (8 states). The token starts just left of the line (N-1); each step right is a reward, each step left a penalty. Sunny is in the clause only while the token is on the right.

docs.title: Feedback
docs.text:
For a training example of class y:

  1. Evaluate all clauses and compute the clamped vote sums.
  2. Draw a random negative class q != y.
  3. Each clause of class y receives feedback with probability \((T - v_y) / 2T\): Type I if it is positive, Type II if it is negative.
  4. Each clause of class q receives feedback with probability \((T + v_q) / 2T\): Type II if it is positive, Type I if it is negative.

The probabilities implement the vote margin: once a class already wins by T votes, its clauses stop being updated, which frees them to specialise on other examples (resource allocation).

The vote margin T. The class of the example is taught with probability (T - v)/2T — always when it clearly says no, never once it wins by T. A randomly drawn wrong class is corrected with probability (T + v)/2T.

Type I feedback makes a clause recognise frequent patterns:

  • If the clause matches the example (Type Ia / Recognize): every True literal is memorised (state +1) with probability (s-1)/s — or with probability 1 when boost_true_positive=True, the default — and every False literal is forgotten (-1) with probability 1/s.
  • If the clause does not match (Type Ib / Erase): all literals are forgotten with probability 1/s.

Type II feedback makes a clause reject examples of other classes: if the clause matches, every False literal that is currently excluded moves one step towards inclusion (deterministically). As soon as one such literal is included the clause no longer matches.

The same clause, Sunny, under each kind of feedback. Type I (an example of its own class): true literals step towards remember, false ones occasionally towards forget. Type II (a look-alike from another class): false literals step towards remember, so the clause stops matching. Both end at Sunny AND Weekend by different routes.

docs.title: Specificity as a frequency threshold
docs.text:
Larger s means forgetting is rarer, so clauses keep more literals and become more specific. The book's breast-cancer example shows the arithmetic. Take a literal that is true for 2 of 3 patients of the clause's class, and a memorise/forget pair of 0.2/0.8. Per pass over the three patients it moves up 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 steps and down 1 × 0.8 = 0.8 steps on average, so it drifts out of the clause. With 0.5/0.5 it moves up 1.0 and down 0.5, so it stays. In the library's terms: a literal survives in a clause roughly when it is true in more than about 1/s of the examples that train the clause. Why a Tsetlin machine learns what it learns makes this exact.

T controls how many clauses cooperate on each example; larger T needs more clauses.

docs.title: How clauses coordinate
docs.text:
No clause knows about the others. They coordinate only through the shared vote sum, and the book's Section 1.6 lists three effects:

  • Examples are prioritised by how far they are from the margin. With T = 2, the probability that a clause of the example's class gets feedback is (T - v)/2T:

    vote sum v of the true class -2 -1 0 1 2 chance each clause is updated 1 0.75 0.5 0.25 0

    Misclassified examples get the most attention; solved ones get none. * Type II only reaches clauses that voted wrongly. A clause that does not match an example of another class is left alone, so correct clauses are shielded. * Good clauses are memorised deepest. A clause that matches most of its class and never votes wrongly gets the most Type Ia and no Type II, so its literals sit far from the boundary. Clauses that keep being disrupted stay shallow, which leaves them free to move to a better pattern. Duplicate clauses are not waste: two copies of a good clause add their votes and help the class reach the margin.

docs.title: Variants implemented
docs.text:
• Weighted / integer-weighted TM (weighted=True): each clause has an integer weight that grows by 1 on Type Ia and shrinks by 1 on Type II feedback.
  • Coalesced TM (CoalescedTsetlinMachine): one pool of clauses shared by all outputs, each with a signed integer weight per output. Weights move away from zero on Type I and towards zero on Type II, so a clause can change sides. Supports multi-label targets.
  • Regression TM (RegressionTsetlinMachine): all clauses positive, v in [0, T] mapped linearly to the target range; Type I when the prediction is too low, Type II when too high, with probability proportional to the error.
  • Convolutional TM — see Convolution.
  • Graph TM (GraphTsetlinMachine): deep clauses over graph input, one component per layer, connected by messages along typed edges — see Graph Tsetlin machines.
  • Clause size constraint (max_included_literals): clauses above the budget receive only forgetting feedback until they shrink (Abeyrathna et al., 2023). By default (budget_mode="soft", the reference implementation's rule) a clause may overshoot the budget and is then pruned, which keeps its contents changing. budget_mode="hard" also reverts every inclusion beyond the budget. With that, no clause ever exceeds it, the pruning never triggers, and clauses freeze at exactly the budget. On the TM Composites CIFAR-10 colour-thermometer specialists that cost 10-11 pp (experiments/multi_convtm/REPORT.md).
  • Drop clause / drop literal (drop_clause_p, drop_literal_p): randomly excluded clauses neither vote nor learn for one batch or epoch (Sharma et al., 2023).
  • Focused negative sampling: choose the negative class proportionally to its current vote sum, i.e. correct confusions first.

docs.title: Where each piece lives
docs.text: Step Function / method literals functional.to_literals clause evaluation functional.clause_outputs (one matmul + comparison) vote sums functional.vote_sums, model._votes feedback probabilities functional.feedback_probabilities which clause gets which feedback model._select_feedback counting feedback events over a batch functional.type_i_counts, functional.type_ii_counts moving the automata functional.apply_feedback

docs.text:

  • O.-C. Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, tsetlinmachine.org.

docs.title: Why a Tsetlin machine learns what it learns
docs.text:
How a Tsetlin machine learns describes the algorithm. This page explains what it converges to, following Chapter 2 of Granmo's An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines. The argument is short. Every automaton is a random walk, so learning is a Markov chain, and its long-run behaviour can be computed exactly. Doing so shows why s acts as a frequency threshold, why more automaton states make the decisions sharper, and why the vote margin T keeps clauses from getting stuck in bad configurations.

Every number and figure on this page is computed exactly from the book's chains by scripts/make_concept_figures.py. --check prints them next to the values in the book, and they agree.

Scope

The analysis covers the classical algorithm: one example at a time, unweighted clauses, no clause budget. It also follows the book's convention that a True literal of a matching clause is always memorised (boost_true_positive=True, the library default). Batched feedback, clause weights and max_included_literals are outside it; see Batched vs sequential feedback for how far batching moves away from this picture.

docs.title: One literal is a Markov chain
docs.text:
Look at a single literal L in a clause for class Y, and let the clause contain nothing else. Each training example is one of four kinds, and each kind moves the literal's automaton in a fixed way:

example feedback what happens to L L true, class Y Recognize (Type Ia) one step towards memorized L false, class Y Recognize or Erase (Type Ia / Ib) one step towards forgotten, probability 1/s L false, other class Reject (Type II) one step towards memorized, only while forgotten L true, other class none stays

The next position depends only on the current one and on the example drawn, so the position is a Markov chain. Its transition probabilities follow from how often each kind of example occurs: P(L | Y) P(Y), P(not L | Y) P(Y) and so on.

The chain of one literal with four memory positions. Reject feedback pushes a literal up only while it is forgotten, so it can add a literal to a clause but never makes it stick.

A Markov chain of this kind settles into a stationary distribution: the fraction of time it spends in each state in the long run. The distribution does not depend on where the chain started. For the literal it is the answer to "how likely is L to be part of the clause after learning?".

docs.title: What the stationary distribution says
docs.text:
The book solves the four-state chain in closed form (its Table 2.1). Each state's probability is a product of factors, and each factor is one property of the learned clause:

  • Frequent literals are memorised. The higher P(L | Y), the more mass sits on the memorized side.
  • Infrequent literals are forgotten. The higher P(not L | Y), the more mass sits on the forgotten side.
  • s moves the threshold. Forgetting happens with probability 1/s, so a larger s lets rarer literals survive. Roughly, a literal is kept when it is true in more than 1/s of the class's examples.
  • Discriminative literals are preferred. A literal that is often true for Y and often false for the other classes gets pushed up by both Recognize and Reject feedback.
  • Each extra memory state sharpens the decision exponentially. Every factor appears once per step away from the boundary. With more states the distribution piles up at the ends, and the literal is either clearly in or clearly out.
The book's four single-literal scenarios. A literal true in only 10 % of its class is dropped at s = 1 and kept at s = 15. A discriminative literal is kept almost surely, and doubling the memory concentrates the mass at the deepest position.

The four scenarios, in numbers:

scenario share of class Y L true within Y L false within other classes s positions P(included) rare literal, carries no information 0.9 0.1 0.9 1 4 0.04 the same, slower forgetting 0.9 0.1 0.9 15 4 0.87 discriminative literal 0.82 0.99 0.5 15 4 > 0.999 the same, deeper memory 0.82 0.99 0.5 15 8 > 0.999

In the first two rows the literal is independent of the class. Whether it is kept depends only on whether it clears the 1/s frequency threshold.

docs.title: Literals play a game
docs.text:
With two literals in one clause, each literal still moves on its own, but the feedback it receives depends on the other one, because the clause matches only if every included literal is true. The book frames this as a game in the style of the Prisoner's Dilemma. Each literal decides, without communicating, whether to be part of the clause, and the payoff depends on both decisions. The joint position of the two literals is again a Markov chain, now with 8 × 8 = 64 states for 8 memory positions each.

Where two literals settle. Left: only Literal Two predicts the class, and the clause keeps Literal Two alone. Middle: either literal predicts the class with precision 0.9, and at s = 1 the clause alternates between them. Right: the same data at s = 4, and the clause keeps both, reaching precision 0.99.

Four outcomes, from the book's Tables 2.5 to 2.8:

  1. It selects informative literals. When only one literal carries information about the class, that one is memorised and the other is forgotten.
  2. It keeps alternatives alive. When two literals are equally good on their own, the distribution has two peaks. During one long run the clause visits both.
  3. It picks the best literal. When one literal is better than the other, the peak sits on the better one.
  4. It combines literals for precision. Raising s allows rarer, more specific patterns. The pair L1 AND L2 is true less often but predicts the class with precision 0.99, and at s = 4 it becomes the most likely clause.

No literal ever sees the others. Coordination emerges from the three feedback types alone, which is why the learning rule is so short.

docs.title: Clauses interact through the vote margin
docs.text:
The last step is several clauses. The book's example is Y = x1 OR x2 with 10 % label noise, learned by two clauses for Y. The only correct pair is one clause x1 and one clause x2. The clause x1 AND x2 is also correct whenever it fires, but it misses every example in which only one of the two literals is true.

Without a vote margin, every clause gets feedback on every example, so each clause learns independently and both converge to the same thing. Here that is x1 AND x2, a local optimum that fires on only one of the three input patterns for which Y holds.

With T = 2, a clause gets feedback with a probability that depends on how many clauses already vote. Once one clause covers an example, the other one is less likely to be trained on it, so the two clauses spread over different parts of the data.

Two clauses learning x1 OR x2. Without a vote margin, both clauses become x1 AND x2 about two thirds of the time. With T = 2, that configuration almost disappears and the correct pair dominates. pair of clauses after learning no vote margin T = 2 x1 AND x2 twice (local optimum) 68.7 % 0.3 % x1 and x2 (the solution) 4.6 % 81.3 %

The book does not state s for this example. s = 5 reproduces its peak probabilities (0.31 without the margin and 0.16 with it, against 0.306 and 0.154 computed). The book describes the bad configuration as having zero probability with the margin; the exact chain gives it 0.3 %.

docs.title: Learning never stops
docs.text:
All three results share one property. The outcome of learning is a probability distribution over clauses, not a single clause, and it does not depend on the initialisation. A Tsetlin machine keeps moving between the configurations that distribution favours. That has practical consequences:

  • runs with different seeds end at different, equally good, rule sets;
  • the clause set keeps changing late in training, so a single epoch's rules are a snapshot;
  • the end of training is a valid starting point for further training on new data.

docs.title: What to take away
docs.text:
result parameter practical reading a literal is kept when it is true in more than about 1/s of the class s raise s for longer, more specific clauses; lower it if clauses memorise noise more memory states sharpen every decision exponentially n_states deeper memory makes clauses more stable but slower to change their mind combining literals only pays once rare patterns are allowed s precise multi-literal rules need a large enough s the vote margin steers clauses away from shared local optima T raise T with the number of clauses so they keep covering different sub-patterns

See also Hyper-parameters.

docs.title: Convolution on generated data
docs.text: Four small scripts that each take a minute or less and need no download. They cover the convolutional models that MNIST does not: 1-D sequences, 3-D volumes and convolutional regression, plus a controlled look at what position_encoding actually does. See Convolution for the algorithm.

docs.title: Translation invariance
docs.text:
Full script: examples/shapes_conv.py.

A hollow 3 × 3 circle or a 3 × 3 cross sits at a random position in a 12 × 12 image — 100 possible positions. A flat machine has to memorise all of them; a convolutional one learns one clause.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

tt.seed_everything(0)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
x_train, y_train = tt.data.make_shapes(2000, size=12, seed=0)   # (N, 1, 12, 12) Boolean
x_test, y_test = tt.data.make_shapes(1000, size=12, seed=1)

model = tt.ConvTsetlinMachine(2, n_clauses=40, T=15, s=3.9, patch_size=3,
                              position_encoding=False, n_states=100)
model.class_names = ["circle", "cross"]
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=16)
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=10, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
print(trainer.test((x_test, y_test)))           # {'test_accuracy': 1.0}

# Clauses 0..39 vote for 'circle', 40..79 for 'cross'; rank them by how often they are right.
score = tt.interpret.clause_precision(model, x_test, y_test)
cross = (model.clause_class == 1) & (model.clause_polarity > 0) & (score["support"] > 0.05)
best = int(torch.where(cross, score["precision"], torch.zeros_like(score["precision"])).argmax())

print(model.clause_patch(best))                 # 1 = pixel on, -1 = off, 0 = don't care
print(model.clause_region(best))                # {'y': (0, 9), 'x': (0, 9)} — matches anywhere

The winner is not the whole cross but a fragment of it — and that is the point. The script prints it with # = pixel must be on, . = must be off, blank = don't care:

clause 40 of 'cross': fires on 43% of images, 100% of them class 'cross'
  allowed window rows y=(0, 9), columns x=(0, 9)
|###|
|.# |
|...|

Three horizontally adjacent on pixels never occur in a hollow circle (.#. / #.# / .#.), so the cross's arm plus an empty row below already separates the classes perfectly, and the window range says the clause may match at any of the 100 positions. Nothing forces a clause to learn the complete template when a shorter one is already precise.

Run python examples/shapes_conv.py --flat to train both models on the same images. The convolutional one scored 1.000 on every seed tried; the flat one, with the same clause budget, lands anywhere between 0.55 and 0.91.

Position literals are not free

position_encoding=True lets a clause demand where it matches. On a task where the shape can sit anywhere that is only a way to overfit: accuracy drops from 1.000 to about 0.5 (--position-encoding). Digits are the opposite case — see MNIST — so check this flag before suspecting the feedback code.

docs.title: Sequences and signals
docs.text:
Full script: examples/conv1d_ramps.py.

Conv1dTsetlinMachine expects (B, Z, L): Z Boolean channels over L timesteps. A thermometer encoder with flatten=False produces (N, L, n_bits), so one permute puts the bit planes where the channels belong.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

# 48-sample signals of uniform noise with one 8-sample ramp hidden at a random offset:
# rising = class 1, falling = class 0 (see make_ramps() in the script).
x_train, y_train = make_ramps(3000, seed=0)
x_test, y_test = make_ramps(1000, seed=1)

enc = tt.data.ThermometerEncoder(n_bits=8, strategy="uniform",
                                 value_range=(0.0, 1.0), flatten=False)
b_train = enc(x_train).permute(0, 2, 1).contiguous()    # (N, 8, 48)
b_test = enc(x_test).permute(0, 2, 1).contiguous()

model = tt.Conv1dTsetlinMachine(2, n_clauses=50, T=30, s=5.0, kernel_size=8,
                                position_encoding=False, n_states=100)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=32)
trainer.fit((b_train, y_train), epochs=10, val_data=(b_test, y_test))
print(trainer.test((b_test, y_test)))           # {'test_accuracy': 0.996} from the script

A clause is a (n_bits, 1, kernel_size) pattern, so printing its bit planes with the highest threshold on top draws the waveform it detects — here, a rising staircase:

clause 51 of 'rising': fires on 12% of signals, 100% of them class 'rising'
  ........
  .......#
   .....##
  #....###
  #....###
  #...####
  #..#####
  #.######

docs.title: Volumes (3D)
docs.text:
Full script: examples/shapes_conv3d.py.

make_3d_shapes puts a 3 × 3 × 3 shape at a random position in an 8 × 12 × 12 volume. Class 0, the spindle, stacks the slices plus, dot, plus. Class 1, the 3D cross, stacks dot, plus, dot. Every slice is a plus or a dot in both classes, so only the order along depth tells them apart.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

x_train, y_train = tt.data.make_3d_shapes(2000, size=(8, 12, 12), seed=0)  # (N, 1, 8, 12, 12)
x_test, y_test = tt.data.make_3d_shapes(1000, size=(8, 12, 12), seed=1)

model = tt.Conv3dTsetlinMachine(2, n_clauses=20, T=15, s=10, patch_size=3,
                                position_encoding=False, n_states=100)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=16)
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=10, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
print(trainer.test((x_test, y_test)))           # {'test_accuracy': 1.0}

--baselines trains two alternatives with the same clause budget. One is the 2D machine on the slices stacked as channels, (8, 12, 12), whose window spans the whole depth. The other is a flat machine. Over training seeds 0–4:

model test accuracy Conv3dTsetlinMachine, 3 × 3 × 3 window 1.000 on all five seeds ConvTsetlinMachine, depth as channels 0.828 – 0.984 TsetlinMachine (1 152 features) 0.726 – 0.796

The stacked model has to learn every shape once per depth offset (six here); the 3D window learns it once. The script prints each class's most precise clause slice by slice (# = must be on, . = must be off). The spindle's clause is the lower half of a plus, a dot, and the lower half of a plus again, which is a fragment of the spindle that never occurs in a 3D cross:

clause 0 of 'spindle': fires on 47% of volumes, 100% of them 'spindle'  region={'d': (0, 5), 'y': (0, 9), 'x': (0, 9)}
  d=0     d=1     d=2
  |...|   |...|   |...|
  |.#.|   |...|   |.#.|
  |###|   |.#.|   |###|

--plot saves the same patches with tt.viz.plot_conv_clauses, which draws a 3D clause as its kd slices side by side. With --position-encoding accuracy falls to 0.48, the same trap as in 2D.

docs.title: Convolutional regression
docs.text:
Full script: examples/conv_regression_blobs.py.

ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine maps the vote sum linearly onto y_range instead of taking an argmax. Here each image holds one solid square of side 2–6 and the target is that side length — a quantity that does not depend on position, so position_encoding=False again.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

x_train, y_train = make_squares(4000, seed=0)   # (N, 1, 12, 12) Boolean, float targets
x_test, y_test = make_squares(1000, seed=1)

model = tt.ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine(
    n_clauses=400, T=400, s=5.0, patch_size=7,  # the window must be wider than the square
    position_encoding=False,
    weighted=True,                              # one clause can vote several times
    y_range=(2.0, 6.0), n_states=100,
)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=16)
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=30, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
print(trainer.test((x_test, y_test)))
# {'test_mae': 0.20, 'test_rmse': 0.27, 'test_r2': 0.96} from the script

Each clause adds weight * (y_max - y_min) / T to the prediction when it matches — 0.01 per unit of weight at T=400 over a range of 4 — and its patch shows what it is keying on. The heaviest clause of a default run requires a three-pixel vertical run in one column and every other pixel of the 7 × 7 window to be off — a three-tall edge with nothing else beside it:

clause 379: weight 47, 3 pixels required on, 46 required off
  #......
  #......
  #......
  .......
  .......
  .......
  .......

Read the next few and the tidiness stops: clauses 274 and 89 carry almost as much weight on a scatter of unrelated pixels. A regression TM spreads its answer over hundreds of clauses, and only some of them are individually legible.

weighted and T have to be chosen together

At these settings weighted=True is not a refinement but a requirement. Unweighted clauses each contribute at most 1, so 400 of them can only reach a vote sum of 400 if every clause fires — and with T=400 the same run collapses to R² −0.19. Either keep the weights, or drop T to roughly half the clause count (unweighted with T=200 reaches R² 0.83).

docs.title: MNIST
docs.text: Full scripts: examples/mnist_flat.py and examples/mnist_conv.py (require torchvision).

docs.title: Flat Tsetlin machine
docs.text:
import torchtsetlin as tt

x_train, y_train = tt.data.load_mnist_boolean("./data", train=True, threshold=0.3, device="cuda")
x_test, y_test = tt.data.load_mnist_boolean("./data", train=False, threshold=0.3, device="cuda")

model = tt.TsetlinMachine(784, 10, n_clauses=2000, T=50, s=10.0, weighted=True)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device="cuda", batch_size=32,
                     callbacks=[tt.ModelCheckpoint("mnist_flat.pt"), tt.StateSummaryLogger()])
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=30, val_data=(x_test, y_test))

With 500 clauses per class the model reaches about 95.8 % test accuracy after 5 epochs (1.5–5 s per epoch on an RTX 3090 depending on the batch size, see Benchmarks); the literature reports ~98 % for 2000 clauses per class after hundreds of epochs.

docs.title: Convolutional Tsetlin machine
docs.text:
enc = tt.data.AdaptiveThresholdEncoder(block_size=11, C=2)          # book/paper recipe
x_train, y_train = tt.data.load_mnist_boolean("./data", train=True, encoder=lambda x: enc(x * 255), device="cuda")
x_test, y_test = tt.data.load_mnist_boolean("./data", train=False, encoder=lambda x: enc(x * 255), device="cuda")

model = tt.ConvTsetlinMachine(10, n_clauses=2000, T=2500, s=10.0, patch_size=10, weighted=True)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device="cuda", batch_size=32)
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=30, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
tt.viz.plot_conv_clauses(model, range(32))                          # what the clauses look for

Images are (N, 1, 28, 28) Boolean tensors; each 10 × 10 window plus its thermometer-encoded position forms a 136-feature patch (272 literals), and a 28 × 28 image has 19 × 19 = 361 such windows. Adaptive thresholding turns the flat background on and the strokes off (as in the reference implementations), which starts slower than a plain pixel > 0.3 threshold (≈ 74 % vs 96 % after one epoch with 200 clauses/class) but is the recipe used for the best published results. examples/mnist_conv.py reaches 97.9 % with its defaults (200 clauses per class, 10 epochs, ≈ 80 s on an RTX 3090).

docs.title: Variations the script exposes
docs.text:
python examples/mnist_conv.py --stride 2                 # 100 windows instead of 361, ~1.5x faster
python examples/mnist_conv.py --no-position-encoding     # translation invariant clauses
python examples/mnist_conv.py --coalesced --clauses 1000 # one shared clause pool, class weights

--coalesced builds a ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine: instead of n_clauses clauses per class, all classes share one pool and each clause carries an integer weight per class, so --clauses is the total budget. Keep T proportional to the pool a class effectively uses. Note that coalesced clauses are weighted by construction — there is no weighted argument.

Sharing pays here: --coalesced --clauses 1000 --T 500 reaches 98.5 % in 50 s, against 97.9 % in 80 s for the 2000 per-class clauses of the default run (10 epochs each, same RTX 3090).

Position literals earn their keep on MNIST — 97.2 % with them against 95.9 % without, after three epochs of the default configuration. That is the opposite of a task where the pattern can appear anywhere; examples/shapes_conv.py shows that side.

docs.title: Noisy XOR
docs.text:
The benchmark of the original paper: 12 Boolean inputs, y = x0 XOR x1, 40 % label noise in the training set. Full script: examples/noisy_xor.py.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

tt.seed_everything(0)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
x_train, y_train = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(5000, noise=0.4, seed=0)
x_test, y_test = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(5000, noise=0.0, seed=1)

model = tt.TsetlinMachine(12, 2, n_clauses=20, T=15, s=3.9, n_states=50)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=10,
                     callbacks=[tt.EarlyStopping(patience=30)])
trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=200, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
print(trainer.test((x_test, y_test)))
for rule in model.rules():
    print(rule)

Expected output (the two XOR patterns per class, plus their negations):

IF x0 AND NOT x1 THEN 1
IF x1 AND NOT x0 THEN 1
IF x0 AND x1 THEN NOT 1
IF NOT x0 AND NOT x1 THEN NOT 1
...

Try feedback_mode="sequential" to compare with the classical one-example-at-a-time algorithm, or max_included_literals=2 to force minimal rules.

  • The Colab links open the notebooks from the main branch on GitHub.

docs.title: Running locally
docs.text:
pip install torchtsetlin jupyterlab        # or pip install -e ".[dev]" in a checkout
