      f"= {states.numel() / 8 / 2**20:.3f} MB"
      f"   <- {states.element_size() * 8}x smaller than the training state")
def block_bytes(n_clauses, in_planes, patch=3, state_bytes=4): """TA-state memory of one CTM block: n_clauses x 2 x (planes*k*k) literals.""" return n_clauses * 2 * in_planes * patch * patch * state_bytes rows = [] for name, in_planes, clauses, paper_mb in [("Block 1 (24->64)", 24, 256, 0.007), ("Block 2 (64->128)", 64, 512, 0.028), ("Block 3 (128->256)", 128, 1024, 0.111), ("Block 4 (256->512)", 256, 2048, 0.442)]: rows.append({"CTM block": name, "input planes": in_planes, "clauses (~4x channels)": clauses, "paper Table IV, MB": paper_mb, "TA states int32, MB": round(block_bytes(clauses, in_planes) / 2 ** 20, 2), "TA states int8, MB": round(block_bytes(clauses, in_planes, state_bytes=1) / 2 ** 20, 2)}) tab = pd.DataFrame(rows) tab["understated by"] = (tab["TA states int8, MB"] / tab["paper Table IV, MB"]).round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + "x" print(tab.to_string(index=False)) states = single.tm.ta_state print("\nmeasured, this notebook's single-scale head:") print(f" training state : ta_state {tuple(states.shape)} x {states.element_size()} B " f"= {states.numel() * states.element_size() / 2**20:.3f} MB (state_dtype={single.tm.state_dtype})") print(f" with int8 states " f"= {states.numel() / 2**20:.3f} MB") print(f" inference only : 1-bit include mask " f"= {states.numel() / 8 / 2**20:.3f} MB" f" <- {states.element_size() * 8}x smaller than the training state")

Even at one byte per automaton, a CTM block's state costs roughly 15–20× more than the paper's per-block figure — because that figure prices the convolution the block replaces (its Parameters column is U-Net's own parameter count, re-quoted at 1 bit), not the machine that replaces it. A TM's memory advantage is real: one-byte states (torchtsetlin's default uint8 here) are 4× smaller than int32, and inference needs only the 1-bit include mask rather than the counters — another 8×. But it is an advantage that has to be measured on the automata, and Tables III and IV do not measure it.

torchtsetlin note: ta_state is the trainable state, while include / include_count are non-persistent caches derived from it. At inference time only the include mask matters, which is the 1-bit-per-literal figure; training needs the full counters.

docs.title: CTM-UNet — Tsetlin machines for semantic segmentation¶
docs.text:
Paper. Yi Liu, K. Darshana Abeyrathna, CTM-UNet: Integrating Convolutional Tsetlin Machines with U-Net Architecture for Semantic Segmentation, ISTM 2025. doi:10.1109/ISTM67926.2025.00013 · code: github.com/yiliu-coding/CTM-UNet (PDF in source_documents/papers/03_segmentation/)

This is, as far as the repository's literature survey could establish, the only paper that puts a Tsetlin machine into a segmentation architecture. A title/abstract search over a 422-paper arXiv TM corpus for segmentation, unet, mask, pixel-wise and delineat returns no other match. So this notebook is less "here is a well-trodden technique" and more "here is the entire state of the art, and here is what is actually load-bearing in it".

What CTM-UNet does. U-Net's convolution blocks are replaced by CTM blocks — Conv2D → binarise → CTM2D → integer votes → cast to float — so ordinary float tensors still flow between levels and the encoder/decoder/skip structure is untouched. RGB is booleanised as 8 place-value bits per channel (H×W×3 → H×W×24). The head is K parallel CTMs, one per class; votes are scaled to logits and softmaxed, and feedback is per-pixel one-vs-rest Type I / Type II. Trained on CamVid at 512×512 with T = 50, 3×3 patches and clauses ≈ 4× channels.

What this notebook does. torchtsetlin has no U-Net, and it has no dense CTM either — so we build one, and use it to test which of the paper's ingredients actually carry the result:

  1. show concretely why a stock convolutional TM cannot segment at all;
  2. build a dense (per-pixel) TM head — the paper's "K parallel CTM heads" — in ~15 lines;
  3. train it on CamVid-like synthetic street scenes and report per-class IoU and mIoU;
  4. reproduce the paper's sky-vs-rest experiment together with the baselines the paper does not report, which is necessary to read its headline number correctly;
  5. test the Conv2D front-end that never receives a gradient — a consequence of the paper's own statement that the loss is monitored, not trained through;
  6. add multi-scale context two ways (the paper's stagewise dataflow, and a patch pyramid) and measure what U-Net's actual contribution is worth here;
  7. redo the memory arithmetic of Tables III/IV and reconcile it with the conclusion.

Runtime: a little over a minute on a GPU (RTX 3090).

docs.title: 1. Why a stock convolutional TM cannot segment¶
docs.text:
This is the obstacle the paper exists to get around, and it is worth seeing rather than assuming. In a convolutional TM a clause is a filter that slides over the image, and the clause's output for the image is the disjunction over all patch positions (Granmo et al. 2019, and the C-RTM paper's Eq. 4):

$$c_j \;=\; \bigvee_{b=1}^{B} c_j^{\,b}$$

The clause fires if it matched somewhere. That OR is exactly what makes a CTM a good classifier — it gives translation tolerance — and exactly what destroys a segmentation output, because after it there is no longer any "where" left to report.

docs.title: 2. A dense Tsetlin head¶
docs.text:
The fix is to not take the disjunction: evaluate the same clause set once per position and keep a vote vector at each one. Concretely, unfold the image into one patch per pixel and treat every patch as an independent example of an ordinary flat TsetlinMachine whose label is the class of the patch's centre pixel. Folding the predictions back gives a label map.

One thing this buys for free: the paper uses K parallel CTMs, one per class, stacks their votes into logits and softmaxes, with "Type I reinforcement if under-predicted […] Type II feedback if they wrongly predicted high activation — this mimics a one-vs-rest scheme". That is the standard multi-class TM. torchtsetlin's TsetlinMachine already gives each class its own positive/negative clause bank and trains them one-vs-rest, so n_classes=K replaces the K-head construction exactly.

docs.title: 3. CamVid-like data¶
docs.text:
CamVid is not redistributable here, so we generate street scenes with the properties that matter for the paper's argument: a wavy horizon, a large contiguous sky region, buildings standing on the horizon, trees, and a road — plus per-class texture (window grids, lane dashes, foliage noise) and a global illumination jitter, so that the classes are not separable by colour alone. Class frequencies are heavily imbalanced, as in CamVid.

Booleanization follows the paper's intent — "the RGB image grayscale values are converted to binary vectors […] with intention to remain the rich pixel and textual information". The paper uses 8 place-value bits per channel (24 planes); we use a 4-bit thermometer per channel (12 planes), which preserves ordering between levels and keeps this notebook fast.

docs.title: 4. A single-scale dense TM¶
docs.text: Matching the paper's block hyper-parameters as closely as the scale allows: 3×3 patches, clauses in the low hundreds, and a vote margin T of the same order as the paper's 50.

docs.title: 5. The sky-vs-rest experiment, read carefully¶
docs.text:
The paper's Section III-D merges the 32 CamVid classes into Sky vs. Background and reports 96.35% ± 1.99 accuracy and 86.43% ± 2.17 IoU (Table I). Those are the numbers in the abstract and conclusion. Two things need stating before they can be interpreted:

  • They are not a 32-class result. No 32-class mIoU appears anywhere in the paper, although the conclusion describes the 86.43% figure as "mIoU".
  • Table I's own comparison column shows plain U-Net at 99.99% accuracy and 99.99% IoU on the same binary task.

What the paper does not report is how hard the binary task is to begin with. Sky is a large, contiguous region that occupies the top of every frame, so two baselines that contain no learning at all set the bar:

docs.title: 6. The Conv2D front-end that never learns¶
docs.text:
The paper's CTM block is Conv2D → binarise → CTM2D → float, trained with Adam (lr = 1.5e-3, weight decay 1e-4) on a Dice + Focal loss. But Section II-E states plainly:

"this framework is introduced to monitor the training losses instead of involved in the training process"

and Section I-A gives the reason: "the Tsetlin machine (TM/CTM) is not differentiable. This hinders the information passes from a PyTorch […] conv layer with backpropagation."

Taken together, no gradient reaches a Conv2D that sits behind a CTM block. Whatever those convolutions are at initialisation is roughly what they remain. So the interesting question is not whether the block works, but whether a frozen random projection in front of the CTM helps or hurts compared to feeding the booleanized image straight in.

docs.title: 7. Adding context — what U-Net is actually for¶
docs.text:
Section 4 left buildings unsolved because a 3×3 window cannot see the horizon. U-Net's answer is to carry information down to a coarse scale and back up through skip connections. Two ways to get that inside a Tsetlin machine:

(a) Stagewise vote passing — the CTM-UNet dataflow. Train a dense TM on a 2×-downsampled image, upsample its per-pixel votes, booleanize them with a thermometer, and concatenate them with the fine-resolution patch for a second dense TM. Votes cast to float between blocks is exactly the paper's Y = float(V) step; downsampling Boolean planes with max-pooling is an OR over the window, which is the TM-native analogue of a pooling layer.

(b) A patch pyramid — skip the staging and simply give one dense TM a 3×3 patch at 1×, 2× and 4× downsampling. Same receptive field, no intermediate machine.

docs.title: 8. The memory claim¶
docs.text:
CTM-UNet's second contribution is memory. Tables III and IV report a 31–32× reduction, and the conclusion reports something else:

"CTM-UNet achieves 86.43% mIoU with 52% memory reduction compared to standard UNet"

Both figures cannot be right, so let's do the arithmetic from the paper's own tables.

docs.title: 9. Where this leaves TM segmentation¶
docs.text:
Putting the pieces together — the paper is the first to show that a TM can be trained inside a dense-prediction architecture and converge, and that is a real result. What is not yet established, by this paper or any other:

  • No multi-class segmentation number exists. The only reported accuracy is binary sky-vs-rest, on which the baseline scores 99.99%. There is no published TM Dice or mIoU on any multi-class benchmark, so anyone working on this compares against CNN baselines they run themselves.
  • The hybrid is not actually hybrid. No gradient crosses a CTM block, so the float layers between blocks are either frozen random projections or trained on a signal the paper states is not involved in training. Section 6 suggests they cost accuracy rather than adding any.
  • The architectural question is open, not incremental. A TM emits a decision from a set of matched clauses; segmentation needs a label per pixel. TM blocks in an encoder–decoder, sliding-window per-pixel TM classification (section 2), patch-wise TM plus upsampling, and convolutional-regression heads (see 04_convolutional_regression_tsetlin.ipynb) are all essentially unexplored.
  • Nothing here is medical. CTM-UNet is generic urban scene parsing; there is no TM segmentation work on MRI or cardiac imaging at all.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
1. A stock ConvTsetlinMachine cannot segment — clause outputs are OR-ed over patch positions, so a 32×32 image yields 4 numbers. Dense prediction means dropping that disjunction and evaluating per position.
  2. A dense TM head is short: unfold to one patch per pixel, run a flat multi-class TsetlinMachine, fold back. Its one-vs-rest clause banks are the paper's K parallel CTM heads.
  3. Read the paper's headline number as binary sky-vs-rest, not a 32-class mIoU, and against the trivial baselines in section 5.
  4. The Conv2D front-end receives no gradient and measurably hurts — the paper's own statements imply the first, and section 6 measures the second.
  5. Multi-scale context is what moves the hard class, building IoU roughly doubling, and it can be had entirely TM-natively with OR-pooling and thermometer-cast votes.
  6. The memory tables are analytical, not measured, over-state the advantage by pricing convolution weights rather than TA states, and do not support the conclusion's "52%".

A GraphBatch behaves like a tensor along the graph axis (len(g), g[3], g[2:10], .to(...)), so the Trainer takes it wherever it takes a tensor.

Pad the dataset to one shape. Graphs may differ in size, so a batch is stored padded to its largest graph. pad(P, E) fixes the node and edge counts for the whole dataset. On CUDA, every slice then has the same shape without looking at the data, which lets updates run on the fused kernels and be replayed from CUDA graphs (section 6). Padding nodes never match and never send, so the results do not change.

def train_graph_tm(depth, g_tr, y_tr, g_te, y_te, n_classes=2, n_clauses=4, T=40, s=2.0,
                   epochs=4, batch_size=25, **kwargs):
    tt.seed_everything(SEED)
    model = tt.GraphTsetlinMachine(
        n_features=symbols.dim, n_outputs=n_classes, n_clauses=n_clauses, T=T, s=s,
        depth=depth, message_encoding="one_hot",
        n_edge_types=2, edge_type_names=["left", "right"], **kwargs,
    )
    trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=batch_size, verbose=False)
    t0 = time.time()
    history = trainer.fit((g_tr, y_tr), epochs=epochs, val_data=(g_te, y_te))
    return model, history, time.time() - t0

The two clauses voting for AAA (0 and 3) say exactly what the task is about: this node is an A, and at both neighbours clauses 0 and 3 (an A) and clause 2 (neither C nor E) matched, i.e. the node is the middle of a triple. The clauses voting for no AAA are less tidy; clause 1, for instance, needs a node that is neither A, B nor D and has no A-message from either side.

explain_node traces one clause through one graph: which node it holds at, and, for each message literal, which neighbour sent it and why that neighbour's clause matched.

def run_task(n, max_len=10, noise=0.0, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    seqs, ys = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        L = int(torch.randint(3, max_len + 1, (1,), generator=g))
        y = int(torch.randint(0, 3, (1,), generator=g))          # run of y + 1 A's
        end = int(torch.randint(y, L, (1,), generator=g))
        s = [[] for _ in range(L)]                                # empty positions
        for p in range(end - y, end + 1):
            s[p] = ["A"]
        if float(torch.rand(1, generator=g)) < noise:
            y = int((y + torch.randint(1, 3, (1,), generator=g)) % 3)
        seqs.append(s)
        ys.append(y)
    return seqs, torch.tensor(ys)

Depth 1 stays near chance: a lone A does not know how long its run is. Depth 2 learns the task. With one-hot messages a clause names the clauses that matched next door, so the strongest clauses are read in two steps: the clause itself, then what the cited clauses test at layer 0.

docs.title: Graph Tsetlin machine — clauses that read a node and its neighbours¶
docs.text:
Paper. O.-C. Granmo et al., The Tsetlin Machine Goes Deep: Logical Learning and Reasoning With Graphs, 2025 (arXiv:2507.14874).

A flat Tsetlin machine reads one Boolean vector; a convolutional one reads every patch of an image and ORs the result. Both look at one thing at a time. The graph Tsetlin machine (GraphTM) reads a graph: each node carries a Boolean feature vector, and a clause is a deep clause, an AND over several layers. Layer 0 tests the node's own features. Every further layer tests messages: which clauses matched, one layer down, at the nodes that have an edge into this one. A depth-2 clause can therefore say "this node is an A, and an A sits on each side of it", something no single node knows.

This notebook covers:

  1. the paper's first example: does a sequence contain three consecutive A's?
  2. how sequences become graphs (SymbolTable, GraphBatch);
  3. why depth 1 cannot learn it and depth 2 can;
  4. reading the four learned clauses, and tracing one clause through the graph (explain_node);
  5. a harder sequence task: counting the length of a run;
  6. the GPU fast path for graphs (padding a dataset to one shape);
  7. images as graphs: at depth 1 a GraphTM is a convolutional machine, bit for bit.

docs.title: 1. The task: three A's in a row¶
docs.text:
The paper's Section 3.1. Each example is a sequence of five letters from A–E; about a third of them have AAA planted somewhere. The label says whether AAA occurs. Training labels get 1% noise, as in the paper, and the test labels are clean.

Any single position is uninformative: an A occurs in most sequences, with or without the triple. The answer lives in the relation between neighbouring positions.

docs.title: 2. Sequences as graphs¶
docs.text:
Two objects do the encoding:

  • SymbolTable maps symbols to node features. With encoding="one_hot" every symbol owns one feature, so the clauses stay exactly readable. ("random" hypervectors keep the width fixed for large vocabularies.)
  • GraphBatch holds a batch of graphs: node features (B, P, F), each graph's node count, and typed, directed edges. GraphBatch.from_sequences makes one node per position. Node k sends to k − 1 over edge type 0 (left) and to k + 1 over type 1 (right).

docs.title: 3. Depth 1 cannot see the triple; depth 2 can¶
docs.text:
The paper's settings: 4 clauses, T = 40, s = 2, 4 epochs. Messages are one_hot: each (clause, edge type) pair has its own inbox bit, which keeps every message readable.

At depth 1 a clause sees only its own node's letter. The machine then is a convolutional machine with a one-letter window, and the best it can do is a guess from letter counts. At depth 2, a clause can also require that given clauses matched at the left and right neighbours.

docs.title: 4. Reading the clauses¶
docs.text: clause_expression prints a deep clause in the paper's notation. Layer-0 literals are symbols. A message literal right1:3 reads "clause 3's layer-0 component matched at the node a right-going edge came from", that is, at the left neighbour. (left1:3 is the right neighbour.) The weights are the clause's votes for no AAA and AAA.

docs.title: 5. A harder task: how long is the run?¶
docs.text:
The reference implementation's sequence demo (also examples/graph_sequence.py). Sequences have 3–10 positions and a single run of 1, 2 or 3 consecutive A's; the class is the run length. Graphs now have different sizes, so padding matters.

Two settings change from section 3:

  • More clauses (40) for three classes and longer patterns.
  • A literal budget (max_included_literals=8). Early in training every clause matches everywhere and sends messages from every node, so one boosted Type Ia event can include all message literals at once. Without a budget, clauses can collapse into "everything matched around me", which holds in every graph.

docs.title: 6. The GPU fast path¶
docs.text:
Graph updates join the CUDA fast paths of the convolutional models, with nodes for patches:

  • Batched updates run in events mode: one Triton kernel computes, samples and applies the feedback.
  • Padded batches also run sequential updates (one graph at a time, the classical algorithm) through a compiled per-example commit, and replay every update from a CUDA graph.

The cell below times one epoch of sequential updates on 2,000 graphs, flat versus padded. On a CPU nothing changes with padding, so it only runs on CUDA. These are rough timings, not benchmarks.

docs.title: 7. Images as graphs: depth 1 is a convolutional machine¶
docs.text:
GraphBatch.from_images makes one node per image patch and no edges. Each node's features are the patch pixels plus thermometer-coded coordinates, exactly the features of ConvTsetlinMachine. A depth-1 clause is then an AND over one patch, and the class score ORs it over the nodes: that is the convolutional coalesced Tsetlin machine.

In torchtsetlin the two are not just equivalent on paper. With the same random stream they learn the same automata, bit for bit (depth-1 graph batches with every node present run on the convolutional kernel). The cell trains both on 10,000 MNIST digits and compares their states.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A graph Tsetlin machine clause is an AND over layers. Layer 0 reads the node, and each further layer reads which clauses matched at the in-neighbours one layer down.
  • Depth is reach. A pattern spanning h hops needs depth h + 1. At depth 1 the model is a convolutional machine over the nodes, bit for bit.
  • Clauses stay readable. clause_expression, rules and explain_node print them in the paper's notation and trace messages back to the nodes that sent them.
  • On a GPU, pad the dataset to one shape (GraphBatch.pad) to get the fused kernels and CUDA graphs.

Further reading: the Graph input guide and Graph Tsetlin machines in the documentation.

def row_prior(l_train, l_test):
    H = l_train.shape[1]
    mode = torch.stack([torch.bincount(l_train[:, r, :].reshape(-1), minlength=len(CLASSES)).argmax()
                        for r in range(H)])

def train(name, xt, xv, patch_size=3, position=False, class_p=None, patches_per_commit=128, epochs=8):
    tt.seed_everything(SEED)
    model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(
        len(CLASSES), n_clauses=300, T=60, s=10.0, patch_size=patch_size,
        position_encoding=position, patches_per_commit=patches_per_commit,
        weighted=True, n_states=100,
    ).to(device)
    model.class_names = CLASSES
    if class_p is not None:
        model.set_class_feedback_p(class_p)
    t0 = time.time()
    trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=8, verbose=False)
    trainer.fit((xt, y_tr), epochs=epochs)
    res = trainer.test((xv, y_te))
    seconds = time.time() - t0
    model.eval()                     # empty clauses are False when predicting: never skip this
    res = {k.replace("test_", ""): v for k, v in res.items()}
    res["boundary_f1"] = tt.metrics.boundary_f1(model.predict(xv), y_te, tolerance=2)
    res["seconds"] = seconds
    RESULTS[name] = res
    print(f"{name:<24} pixel acc {res['pixel_accuracy']:.3f}  mIoU {res['mean_iou']:.3f}  "
          f"building IoU {res['iou_building']:.3f}  [{seconds:.0f} s]")
    return model

  • Position literals lift building IoU from about 0.53 to about 0.87, the pyramid to about 0.84, and the two together to about 0.92 (mean IoU about 0.95, pixel accuracy about 0.993).
  • Boundary F1 rises from about 0.77 to about 0.98: the outlines, not only the regions, come right.
  • None of it costs time here: every model trains in about the same 16–19 s.

The building column is the one to read. The window could not tell building from its neighbours; knowing the row (position), or seeing a coarser picture of the surroundings (pyramid), can.

Planes 0–3 are red at levels ≥ 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8; 4–7 green and 8–11 blue likewise. y>k is a row threshold, decoded by clause_region in the last lines of the output.

In our run the strongest votes for "road" come from clauses that say only "the row is 18 or lower" (y>2 AND y>3 AND y>4): the layout prior that the row-prior baseline used, learned as single clauses. The next one is a colour statement about the 3 × 3 neighbourhood, restricted to rows 11–20: some red and blue (p[0,…], p[8,…]) but none of the brighter green and blue levels (NOT p[5,…], NOT p[6,…], NOT p[10,…]), i.e. a dim, grey pixel, which is what asphalt looks like in these scenes. Each clause can be read and checked against the image.

In our run quality degrades gently from 32 to 512 pixels per commit (mean IoU about 0.945 → 0.935 → 0.914) while training gets 3–4× faster at each step, and then collapses: at 2048 mean IoU is about 0.50, and committing a whole batch at once (None) ends at about 0.14, far below the row prior. Thousands of pixels pushing the same clauses in opposite directions before any of it is applied undo each other's learning. The default of 128 sits on the safe side of that cliff; lower it if learning looks unstable, and check the cost before raising it.

The rarest class (tree) now produces feedback from every pixel, road from one pixel in twenty. In our run this raises building IoU a little (about 0.865 → 0.881) but costs tree about 0.12 IoU (0.893 → 0.773), so mean IoU falls. Rebalancing is for a rare class that is being lost; once the model can already separate the classes, it costs accuracy. Check the per-class IoU either way.

docs.title: Semantic segmentation with a Tsetlin machine¶
docs.text:
A convolutional Tsetlin machine ORs a clause over every patch of an image: it can say that a pattern occurs, but not where. That is fine for classifying an image and useless for labelling its pixels. SegmentationTsetlinMachine keeps the patch axis instead. Every pixel is one example, classified from its k × k neighbourhood, and the prediction is a label map.

This notebook follows the documentation's segmentation example (the script examples/segmentation_scenes.py) step by step:

  1. generated CamVid-like street scenes, and booleanizing colour with a thermometer;
  2. the floor every result should be reported against: a baseline that never looks at a pixel;
  3. a single-scale model trained with the Trainer;
  4. adding context the 3 × 3 window does not contain: position literals and an OR-pooled pyramid;
  5. per-class metrics and boundary F1;
  6. why a pixel got its label: clauses as statements about named pixels;
  7. patches_per_commit, the fidelity knob of dense feedback;
  8. class-balanced feedback.

The segmentation guide covers the API and Segmentation the algorithm. Notebook 05 uses the same scenes to review the CTM-UNet paper.

docs.title: 1. The scenes¶
docs.text: tt.data.make_scenes generates street scenes: a wavy horizon, a large sky, buildings standing on the horizon, trees and a road. Each class has its own texture (window grids, foliage noise, lane markings) and every scene a random illumination, so colour alone does not separate the classes. The class frequencies are as unbalanced as in CamVid.

docs.title: Booleanizing colour¶
docs.text: A Tsetlin machine reads Boolean literals. A single threshold per channel throws away the ordering between intensities, which is most of what a segmenter needs. ColorThermometerEncoder gives each channel n_bits planes, plane k being "value ≥ k-th level". With 4 bits, the 3 colour channels become 12 Boolean planes: 0–3 red, 4–7 green, 8–11 blue.

docs.title: 2. The floor: a baseline that never looks at a pixel¶
docs.text: These scenes have a fixed layout: sky on top, road at the bottom. A "classifier" that labels every pixel with the most common class of its row in the training set needs no image at all. Its score is the floor any segmentation result on this data has to be read against.

docs.title: 3. A single-scale model¶
docs.text:
SegmentationTsetlinMachine(n_classes, n_clauses, ...) with:

  • patch_size=3: each pixel is classified from its 3 × 3 neighbourhood, 12 × 9 = 108 features;
  • n_clauses=300 clauses per class, T=60, s=10, weighted clauses with 100 states per automaton;
  • patches_per_commit=128 (the default): see section 7.

The Trainer recognises a dense model and reports segmentation metrics. batch_size counts images: a batch of 8 is 8 192 pixel-examples.

docs.title: 4. Context the window does not contain¶
docs.text:
A 3 × 3 patch of building interior and a 3 × 3 patch of road look alike once illumination varies. What separates them is where they are, relative to the horizon, and that is outside the window. Enlarging the patch grows the feature count quadratically. Two cheaper ways to add context stay within Boolean logic:

  • Position literals (position_encoding=8): each pixel also gets thermometer-coded row and column bits, so a clause can say "only below row 12". Here 8 bits per axis.
  • An OR-pooled pyramid (tt.data.PyramidEncoder(scales=(1, 2, 4), patch=3)): the planes are downsampled by OR-pooling to 1/2 and 1/4 resolution, and each pixel gets the 3 × 3 patch at every level as extra planes. The model then uses patch_size=1, because the neighbourhood is already in the features: 12 × 9 × 3 = 324 planes.

docs.title: 5. Per-class metrics¶
docs.text: tt.metrics.segmentation_report prints IoU, Dice, precision and recall per class from a label map. Boundary F1 (in the table above) scores only the class edges, within a tolerance of 2 pixels: it is the metric that shows whether the outlines are right, which mean IoU over large regions hides.

docs.title: 6. Why did a pixel get its label?¶
docs.text: Each clause is an AND of literals over the pixel's neighbourhood. Read at a given pixel, tt.interpret.explain_pixel names the literals by absolute image coordinates: p[5,20,12] is "plane 5 (green, level 2) of pixel (20, 12) is on". Position literals print as y>k / x>k. The single-scale model with position literals has the most readable clauses (12 planes rather than 324), so we ask it about a road pixel.

docs.title: 7. patches_per_commit: how much feedback is applied at once¶
docs.text: One batch of 8 images is 8 192 pixel-examples. Applying all of their feedback in a single commit is a mini-batch of 8 192, far past the point where batched feedback stops behaving like the classical one-example-at-a-time algorithm. patches_per_commit caps how many pixels share one commit; None commits a whole batch at once, and 1 is the classical algorithm. The sweep below uses the single-scale model with position literals.

docs.title: 8. Class-balanced feedback¶
docs.text: A Tsetlin machine has no loss to reweight. The lever for class imbalance is which pixels produce feedback: set_class_feedback_p gives each class a probability of contributing, and tt.data.balanced_class_probabilities equalises them (with a floor, so frequent classes still learn).

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Report the floor. On a layout-driven dataset a baseline that never sees a pixel gets 0.88 pixel accuracy. Mean IoU, and the per-class IoU of the hard classes, are the numbers to read.
  • Context beats a bigger window. Position literals and an OR-pooled pyramid both add what a 3 × 3 patch cannot see, cost nothing extra here, and compose.
  • patches_per_commit is a real hyper-parameter. Dense feedback over thousands of pixels at once destroys learning; keep the default unless you have measured otherwise.
  • Every pixel's label has an explanation in named pixels and rows, which a convolutional network does not give you.
  • model.eval() before predicting. Empty clauses are True while learning and False when predicting; the train helper above calls it for that reason.

Further reading: the segmentation guide (ignore_index, stride, real datasets such as Pascal VOC, multi-label masks) and notebook 05, which uses these scenes to test the claims of the CTM-UNet paper.

def kvasir_seg_dir(root=DATA_ROOT):

    folder = Path(root) / "Kvasir-SEG"
    if not (folder / "images").is_dir():

The frames come in many sizes (from about 330 × 490 to 1 350 × 1 920). We resize every image and mask to SIZE × SIZE. The images are resized bilinearly; the masks are resized bilinearly too and then thresholded at one half, because they are stored as JPEG and their edges carry compression noise. Kvasir-SEG has no official split, so we draw a seeded one: 780 images to train on, 100 to validate (early stopping, threshold tuning) and 120 to test.

A Tsetlin machine classifies every pixel as one example, so the resolution sets the cost: 64 × 64 is 4 096 examples per image, about 3.2 million per training epoch.

In [ ]: Copied! 
SIZE = 64


def load_kvasir(paths, size):
    images, masks = [], []
    for f in paths:
        img = Image.open(f).convert("RGB").resize((size, size), Image.BILINEAR)
        mask = Image.open(f.parent.parent / "masks" / f.name).convert("L").resize((size, size), Image.BILINEAR)
        images.append(np.asarray(img))
        masks.append(np.asarray(mask) > 127)
    rgb = torch.from_numpy(np.stack(images)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float() / 255.0
    return rgb, torch.from_numpy(np.stack(masks)).long()

def polyp_scores(pred, target):
    """Dice and IoU of the polyp class, plus mean IoU and pixel accuracy, from label maps."""
    m = tt.metrics.segmentation_metrics(pred, target, 2, CLASSES)

    return {"dice": 2 * iou / (1 + iou), "iou": iou, "mean_iou": m["mean_iou"],

In our run all background is right on 85.7% of the pixels and finds no polyp (Dice 0). The location prior is the floor to beat: knowing nothing but where polyps tend to be, it reaches a polyp Dice of about 0.43 (IoU 0.27). A model has to beat that before it can claim to read the image at all.

EPOCHS = 4


def train(name, xt, xv, xs, patch_size=3, position=False, class_p=None, epochs=EPOCHS):
    tt.seed_everything(SEED)
    model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(
        2, n_clauses=300, T=60, s=10.0, patch_size=patch_size,
        position_encoding=position, weighted=True, n_states=100,
    ).to(device)
    model.class_names = CLASSES
    if class_p is not None:
        model.set_class_feedback_p(class_p)
    stop = tt.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_iou_polyp", patience=epochs, restore_best=True)
    trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device=device, batch_size=8, verbose=False, callbacks=[stop])
    t0 = time.time()
    history = trainer.fit((xt, y_tr), epochs=epochs, val_data=(xv, y_va))
    seconds = time.time() - t0
    model.eval()                     # empty clauses are False when predicting: never skip this
    res = polyp_scores(model.predict(xs), y_te)
    res["boundary_f1"] = tt.metrics.boundary_f1(model.predict(xs), y_te, tolerance=2)
    res["best_epoch"] = stop.best_epoch + 1
    res["seconds"] = seconds
    RESULTS[name] = res
    val = [round(v, 3) for v in history["val_iou_polyp"]]
    print(f"{name:<28} val polyp IoU per epoch {val} -> test Dice {res['dice']:.3f} "
          f"IoU {res['iou']:.3f}  [{seconds:.0f} s]")
    return model

In our run the single-scale model reaches a polyp Dice of about 0.41: below the location prior. The validation IoU per epoch shows the instability, about 0.24, 0.23, 0.00, 0.17: after the third epoch the model predicted almost no polyp. Early stopping kept the first epoch.

The figure shows what the model learned: pale, bright tissue is polyp. That finds the polyp when it is the brightest thing in the frame (fourth column), and also marks the brightly lit folds close to the endoscope and the rim of the lumen (first two columns). A pale polyp on pale mucosa (last column) is missed. A 3 × 3 window of colour cannot separate them.

In our run:

  • The pyramid and position literals alone do not help: Dice about 0.39, against 0.41 for the single-scale model. Pixel accuracy and mean IoU rise (fewer false positives on the background), but the polyp itself is found less often. Its validation IoU swings even more: about 0.20, 0.12, 0.24, 0.07 per epoch.
  • With class-balanced feedback the same model reaches Dice about 0.45 (IoU 0.29, mean IoU 0.54), the only model here that beats the location prior, and its validation curve is the steadiest (about 0.28, 0.28, 0.24, 0.23). Every polyp pixel now gives feedback, and only about one background pixel in five.
  • Boundary F1 stays around 0.3 for every model: the outlines are not right, even where the region roughly is.
  • The three models train in about the same time, roughly 2 minutes for 4 epochs on an RTX 3090.

In our runs with other settings, every variation we tried ended up close to the same plateau, a test Dice of 0.40–0.47 after 4 epochs: 600 clauses, T=150, s=3 or s=20, an extra 1/32 pyramid level, 8-bit colour, patches_per_commit=32 (4× slower), and pixel_order="shuffle". Class balancing was the one setting that consistently made training steadier. The earlier, longer study in experiments/segmentation/ of the repository found the same ceiling at 128 × 128 (mean IoU about 0.54 for the best Tsetlin model, 0.75 for a U-Net).

In our run the validation-tuned threshold moves the test Dice from 0.451 to 0.454, and even the best threshold picked on the test set reaches only 0.457. The threshold is not the problem. The model's margin does not rank polyp pixels above background pixels much better than its argmax already shows. What limits it is the information in the features, not how its votes are turned into a label.

In our run Dice depends strongly on the size of the polyp: about 0.25 on average for the smaller half of the polyps and 0.52 for the larger half (median per image 0.37). 14 of 120 test images score below 0.1. The figure shows why. In the worst images a small polyp sits away from the centre and the model paints a blob of bright mucosa in the middle of the frame instead: it has learned the location prior and "pale and bright" together. The best images are the ones where those two cues happen to coincide with the polyp: a large, pale polyp in the middle of a darker frame.

LEVELS = (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8)          # thermometer level of planes 0-3 (red), 4-7 (green), 8-11 (blue)


def describe(model, j):
    """A 3x3 clause, per colour channel: the level each of its 9 pixels must reach (>=) or stay below (<)."""
    patch = model.clause_patch(j).view(3, 4, 9).cpu()       # channel, level, pixel of the window
    parts = []
    for c, name in enumerate(("red", "green", "blue")):
        lo = [max((LEVELS[k] for k in range(4) if patch[c, k, p] == 1), default=None) for p in range(9)]
        hi = [min((LEVELS[k] for k in range(4) if patch[c, k, p] == -1), default=None) for p in range(9)]
        terms = [f">={v} at {lo.count(v)}/9 px" for v in sorted({b for b in lo if b is not None})]
        terms += [f"<{v} at {hi.count(v)}/9 px" for v in sorted({b for b in hi if b is not None})]
        parts.append(f"{name}: " + (", ".join(terms) if terms else "any"))
    return " | ".join(parts)


for m in expl.matched:
    print(f"clause {m.clause} (weight {m.weight:.0f})  {describe(single, m.clause)}")

Planes 0–3 are red at levels ≥ 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8; 4–7 green and 8–11 blue likewise. Read raw, the rules are walls of literals, so the second part of the output decodes each one per colour channel.

In our run all four clauses say the same thing in slightly different words: across the whole 3 × 3 window, red is at least 0.8 at every pixel, green at least 0.6 and blue at least 0.4 at (nearly) every pixel, and no literal says "must be off". That is bright, pale pink: what the polyp in this image looks like, and also what a brightly lit fold of healthy mucosa looks like. The explanation names the shortcut that sections 3 and 7 found from the outside.

model.clause_map shows where single clauses fire over the whole image. Below: the two clauses with the largest weight among those voting for polyp, on the same image.
