In our run the strongest polyp clause (left) fires on the bright core of the polyp and nowhere else in this image. The second (right) fires on the lit rims of the colon folds, which are healthy tissue, with almost the same weight. A Tsetlin machine's mistakes can be read off as single rules: that is the argument for using one, even when its scores are not competitive.

docs.title: Polyp segmentation on Kvasir-SEG with a Tsetlin machine¶
docs.text:
Notebook 07 segmented generated street scenes, where the layout does much of the work: sky on top, road at the bottom. This notebook takes SegmentationTsetlinMachine to real medical images. Kvasir-SEG (Jha et al., MMM 2020) is 1 000 colonoscopy frames, each with a hand-drawn mask of a polyp. A polyp can be anywhere in the frame and any size, the lighting comes from the endoscope, and only about 15% of the pixels are polyp. There is no layout to lean on.

  1. downloading and loading the data, and booleanizing the colour;
  2. the floors: predicting nothing, and predicting where polyps usually are;
  3. a single-scale model, with early stopping on a validation split;
  4. context from an OR-pooled pyramid and position literals;
  5. class-balanced feedback for a minority class;
  6. is the decision threshold the problem? Tuning it on the validation split;
  7. where the model fails, image by image;
  8. why a pixel was called polyp.

Read the numbers as what a per-pixel Tsetlin machine on thermometer-coded colour reaches at 64 × 64, not as a competitive polyp segmenter: the gap to a deep encoder–decoder is large, and section 6 shows where it comes from.

docs.title: 1. The data¶
docs.text: The archive from the dataset page holds Kvasir-SEG/images/*.jpg and, under the same file names, Kvasir-SEG/masks/*.jpg. The cell below downloads and unpacks it into DATA_ROOT once. If you already have a copy, point the environment variable KVASIR_SEG_DIR at the folder that contains images/ and masks/. Check the dataset page for its terms of use, and cite Jha et al. (2020) if you use it.

docs.title: Booleanizing colour¶
docs.text: As in notebook 07: a thermometer with 4 levels per channel, so plane k of a channel says "this channel is at least the k-th level". Three channels give 12 Boolean planes, 0–3 red, 4–7 green and 8–11 blue. The features are kept as bool tensors: the pyramid in section 4 has 540 planes per pixel, which as float32 would not fit on a T4 for all 1 000 images.

docs.title: 2. The floors¶
docs.text:
Polyp segmentation is scored by the Dice coefficient and the IoU of the polyp class; mean IoU averages the polyp and background IoU. Two baselines that never look at a pixel's colour set the floor:

  • all background: predicts no polyp anywhere. It is right on about 85% of the pixels and scores 0 Dice.
  • where polyps usually are: the fraction of training masks that cover each pixel, thresholded at the value that maximises Dice on the training set. Endoscopists tend to centre the polyp, so this is a blob in the middle of the frame.

docs.title: 3. A single-scale model¶
docs.text:
SegmentationTsetlinMachine with the settings of notebook 07: each pixel is classified from its 3 × 3 neighbourhood (12 × 9 = 108 features), 300 clauses per class, T=60, s=10, weighted clauses. batch_size counts images, so a batch of 8 is 32 768 pixel-examples, committed 128 at a time (patches_per_commit, see notebook 07).

On this data the test score moves by several points from one epoch to the next: the model swings between calling too much and too little polyp. So we train with a validation split and EarlyStopping(restore_best=True), which keeps the epoch with the best validation polyp IoU, and report the test score of that epoch only.

docs.title: 4. Context: a pyramid and position literals¶
docs.text:
A 3 × 3 window of a 64-pixel image sees about 5% of its width. Whether a pinkish, shiny patch is polyp or the colon wall next to it depends on what is around it: a rounded edge, a change in texture, the dark lumen. Notebook 07 added context in two Boolean ways, and we do the same:

  • tt.data.PyramidEncoder(scales=(1, 2, 4, 8, 16), patch=3) OR-pools the planes to 1/2 … 1/16 resolution and gives each pixel the 3 × 3 patch at every level: at the coarsest level that patch covers most of the frame. That is 12 × 9 × 5 = 540 planes, and the model uses patch_size=1.
  • position_encoding=8 adds 8 thermometer bits per axis, so a clause can restrict itself to a region of the frame.

The pyramid is encoded in chunks of 50 images and stored as bool.

docs.title: 5. Class-balanced feedback¶
docs.text: Only about 15% of the pixels are polyp, so most of the feedback the machine receives is about background. A Tsetlin machine has no loss to reweight; the lever is which pixels give feedback. tt.data.balanced_class_probabilities sets the probability that a pixel of each class contributes (here: every polyp pixel, and a matching fraction of background pixels).

docs.title: 6. Is it the threshold?¶
docs.text: predict takes the class with the larger vote sum, i.e. it calls a pixel polyp when the margin votes[polyp] - votes[background] is above 0. If the model ranked pixels well but its margin were shifted, moving that threshold would fix it. We tune the threshold on the validation split, and also report the best threshold chosen on the test set itself: an upper bound that no threshold can beat, not a result.

docs.title: 7. Where it fails¶
docs.text: A dataset-level Dice hides how the errors are distributed. Per test image, against the size of the polyp:

docs.title: 8. Why was a pixel called polyp?¶
docs.text: Every pixel's label is the sum of votes of clauses, and every clause is an AND of literals about named pixels. tt.interpret.explain_pixel lists the clauses that decided one pixel. The single-scale model reads 12 planes per pixel, which is what keeps its clauses readable, so we ask it about the polyp pixel it is most confident about in one test image: p[k,r,c] is "plane k at pixel (r, c) is on".

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Beat the location prior first. On Kvasir-SEG, "where polyps usually are" reaches a polyp Dice of about 0.43. Two of the three Tsetlin models here do not beat it, and the best one (0.45) beats it only narrowly.
  • Balance the feedback for a minority class. With 15% polyp pixels, class-balanced feedback was the one change that both raised Dice and kept training from collapsing between epochs. Use a validation split and early stopping either way.
  • The limit is the features, not the decision rule. A tuned threshold adds about 0.003 Dice. A per-pixel model on thermometer-coded colour learns "bright and pale", and context from an OR-pooled pyramid does not change that here.
  • The explanations show the shortcut. Decoded per channel, the strongest polyp clauses are a colour range, and a clause map shows them firing on healthy, brightly lit folds. That is the most useful thing this notebook produces: a precise statement of what the model gets wrong.
  • Deep networks are far ahead on this data. The Kvasir-SEG paper reports a Dice of about 0.79 for its ResUNet baseline, at a much higher resolution. Closing that gap needs features that encode shape and texture (edges, curvature, local contrast) or a learned spatial composition; it does not come from tuning T, s or the number of clauses.

Further reading: notebook 07 and the segmentation guide for the API (patches_per_commit, ignore_index, multi-label masks), and Segmentation for the algorithm.

Reference. D. Jha, P. H. Smedsrud, M. A. Riegler, P. Halvorsen, T. de Lange, D. Johansen and H. D. Johansen, Kvasir-SEG: A Segmented Polyp Dataset, MultiMedia Modeling (MMM) 2020, doi:10.1007/978-3-030-37734-2_37.

docs.title: Choosing a device
docs.text:
torchtsetlin follows the PyTorch device model exactly:

model = tt.TsetlinMachine(784, 10, 2000, T=50, s=10).to("cuda")   # or .cuda(), .to("cuda:1")
model.device            # device of the automata state
model.to("cpu")         # move back
  • All learnable state (ta_state, clause weights) and caches are registered buffers, so .to(), .cuda(), .cpu() and .to(dtype)-style calls behave like any nn.Module.
  • Inputs are moved to the model's device automatically by update() / forward() (they are tiny Boolean tensors). For best throughput keep the whole Boolean dataset on the GPU and index it there — the Trainer does this when you pass (x, y) tensors.
  • Lazily initialised models (n_features=None) allocate their state on the device the module was moved to before the first batch.
  • Randomness uses the global PyTorch RNG of the device: tt.seed_everything(0) (or torch.manual_seed) makes runs reproducible per device.

docs.title: Compiled kernels
docs.text:
Large updates run part of their work through torch.compile: on the CPU the forgetting (Type Ib) step and the binomial draws of the commit, and in sequential mode on CUDA the whole single-example step of the flat models. Together with the row-sparse commit, this makes CPU training of an MNIST-sized model (20 000 clauses) about 14x faster than in 0.4.0, and GPU sequential mode about 11x faster. The kernels draw from the same distributions as the eager code.

  • The first large update of a session compiles the kernels (a few seconds; the result is cached on disk). Small models stay on the eager code, where compiling would not pay off.
  • Compiled kernels draw their random numbers from the default generator of the device, so tt.seed_everything still makes runs reproducible, but a compiled and an eager run with the same seed differ. Calls that pass an explicit generator= to the functional API stay eager.
  • Where torch.compile does not work (no C++ compiler, unsupported Python), the library warns once and uses the eager code. Turn the kernels off with TORCHTSETLIN_COMPILE=0 or torchtsetlin.functional.set_compile(False).

docs.title: The CUDA fast path (Triton kernels and CUDA graphs)
docs.text:
On CUDA, with Triton available (it ships with the Linux CUDA builds of PyTorch), a batched update runs through two hand-written kernels and is replayed as a CUDA graph:

  • One commit kernel applies all of an update's feedback in a single pass over the automata: it computes the Type Ia / Type II counts from the update's events (on tensor cores for flat models), samples them, and writes the state, the include cache and the per-clause include counts. No count tensor is materialised.
  • Convolutional models evaluate their clauses on bit-packed literals (32 per word) and OR over the patches in registers, so the (batch, patches, clauses) match tensor never exists. While learning, the same kernel picks each clause's random matching patch. Prediction of a 10x10-patch MNIST model is 4.7x faster than in 0.5.1.
  • No host synchronisation: labels that are already on the GPU are checked with a device-side assertion (an invalid label is reported as a CUDA error at the next synchronisation, as in PyTorch's own losses); labels from the host are checked there.
  • CUDA graphs: an update shape seen for the third time is captured and replayed from then on (sequential mode in blocks of 64 examples). Replays give bit-identical results to eager execution and remove the kernel-launch overhead that dominates small models and sequential mode (Noisy XOR in sequential mode: 17x faster than 0.5.1). Models with clause or literal dropout are not graphed.

Turn the pieces off with TORCHTSETLIN_TRITON=0 (Triton kernels), TORCHTSETLIN_CUDA_GRAPHS=0 or model.cuda_graphs = False (graphs), or TORCHTSETLIN_COMPILE=0 (everything compiled). Every fast path has the previous code as its fall-back, which is also what runs on the CPU, on MPS, and when Triton is missing.

docs.title: Multiple GPUs
docs.text: Different models can live on different GPUs; a single model uses one device. Because Tsetlin machine training is already massively parallel over clauses and literals, one modern GPU is usually enough for tens of thousands of clauses.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The state uses 1 byte per automaton by default (state_dtype=None picks uint8 for the default n_states=128), i.e. n_clauses_total * 2 * n_features bytes, plus a copy of the include mask in the evaluation dtype (2 bytes per automaton on CUDA, 4 on the CPU) and, on CUDA, a bit-packed one (1 bit). The CUDA fast path needs no count buffers; the other paths keep three float count buffers (12 bytes per automaton) between updates, which model.eval() releases. A 2000-clause-per-class MNIST classifier (20 000 clauses × 1568 literals) needs about 100 MB on CUDA. Intermediate tensors of an update are chunked automatically to stay within max_chunk_elements (default 2^27 elements); lower it if you hit out-of-memory errors on a small GPU.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
torchtsetlin needs Python 3.9+ and PyTorch 2.0+. Install PyTorch first (pick the CUDA or CPU build that matches your machine from pytorch.org), then:

pip install torchtsetlin

The package is published on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/torchtsetlin/.

Optional extras:

pip install "torchtsetlin[viz]"      # matplotlib for torchtsetlin.viz
pip install "torchtsetlin[vision]"   # torchvision for the MNIST helpers
pip install "torchtsetlin[sklearn]"  # scikit-learn interop in the examples
pip install "torchtsetlin[all]"      # everything, including docs and dev tools

From source:

git clone https://github.com/vlbthambawita/torchtsetlin
cd torchtsetlin
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest            # run the test-suite (uses the GPU when available)
mkdocs serve      # browse this documentation locally

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
import torch, torchtsetlin as tt
print(tt.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())
model = tt.TsetlinMachine(n_features=4, n_classes=2, n_clauses=4, T=2)
print(model)

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page walks through the complete workflow on the Noisy XOR benchmark from the original Tsetlin machine paper: 12 Boolean features of which only the first two matter (y = x0 XOR x1), with 40 % of the training labels flipped.

docs.title: 1. Data
docs.text:
Inputs must be Boolean (torch.bool, or anything that casts to it: 0/1 integers, floats, NumPy arrays). Continuous or categorical data is Booleanized first — see Booleanization. Labels are integers 0..n_classes-1.

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

x_train, y_train = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(5000, noise=0.4, seed=0)
x_test, y_test = tt.data.make_noisy_xor(2000, noise=0.0, seed=1)
x_train.shape, x_train.dtype, y_train[:5]
# (torch.Size([5000, 12]), torch.bool, tensor([0, 1, 1, 0, 1]))

docs.title: 2. Model
docs.text:
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = tt.TsetlinMachine(
    n_features=12,   # Boolean inputs (None = infer from the first batch)
    n_classes=2,
    n_clauses=20,    # clauses per class (half vote for, half against)
    T=15,            # vote margin
    s=3.9,           # specificity
    n_states=50,     # memory depth per action (default 128)
).to(device)

A TsetlinMachine is a torch.nn.Module. Its state is the integer buffer model.ta_state of shape (n_classes * n_clauses, 2 * n_features); model.to(device), model.state_dict() and torch.save work as usual. There are no gradient parameters — learning happens through feedback, not back-propagation.

docs.title: 3. A manual training loop
docs.text:
The Tsetlin machine analogue of loss.backward(); optimizer.step() is one call:

for epoch in range(60):
    model.train()
    perm = torch.randperm(len(x_train))
    for i in range(0, len(x_train), 10):
        idx = perm[i:i + 10]
        votes = model.update(x_train[idx].to(device), y_train[idx].to(device))
        # `votes` are the class sums *before* the update -> free batch metrics
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        acc = (model(x_test.to(device)).argmax(1) == y_test.to(device)).float().mean()
    print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: test accuracy {acc:.3f}")

model(x) returns the vote sums (B, n_classes) clamped to [-T, T] — treat them like logits (argmax for the class, model.predict_proba(x) for probabilities). model.train() / model.eval() matter: while learning, a clause without literals is considered True; when predicting it is False.

docs.title: 4. ... or use the Trainer
docs.text:
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, batch_size=10, callbacks=[tt.EarlyStopping(patience=20)])
history = trainer.fit((x_train, y_train), epochs=100, val_data=(x_test, y_test))
trainer.evaluate((x_test, y_test))        # {'accuracy': 0.99...}
trainer.predict(x_test[:5])               # tensor([1, 0, 0, 1, 1])
history.plot()                            # matplotlib curve of val_accuracy

The Trainer accepts (x, y) tensors, a torch.utils.data.Dataset or a DataLoader, moves batches to the model's device, and logs one line per epoch.

docs.title: 5. Read the model
docs.text:
for rule in model.rules()[:5]:
    print(rule)
# IF x0 AND NOT x1 THEN 1
# IF x1 AND NOT x0 THEN 1
# IF x0 AND x1 THEN NOT 1
# ...
print(tt.interpret.explain(model, x_test[0]))

Continue with choosing a device, the training guide or the interpretability guide.

docs.title: Benchmarking against other TM libraries
docs.text:
This guide is the protocol behind torchtsetlin's cross-library comparison (experiments/paper_experiments/). It says where the data come from, what is trained with which arguments, what is validated and tested, and what is measured and how. Follow it to reproduce the published numbers, or to put another library or another machine on the same footing.

The code lives in experiments/paper_experiments/code/; the frozen per-library arguments, with file-and-line evidence from each library's source, are in experiments/paper_experiments/config_map.md.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text: Rule What it means in practice Existing benchmarks only Every benchmark is one that another library already ships (README demo, example, performance test) or that its paper reports. Running another library on it is fair; inventing a dataset or protocol is not. No tuning Hyperparameters are the published ones. Where libraries publish different settings, one common configuration per benchmark is fixed before any run. No epoch selection The headline number is the final epoch. The best epoch is logged, never reported as the result. Identical input bits Each dataset is Booleanized once into a shared .npz. Every library reads the same bits, so encoder differences cannot pass for model differences. Booleanization time is not timed. Records, not hand-typed numbers Every number comes from a results/*.json record that carries the command line, seed, git SHA, library version, hardware and the per-epoch log. Tables are generated from the records. Exclusive timing Timing runs run one at a time on an otherwise idle machine; the load average is logged before and after each. Seed runs may share the machine, and their times are never reported. The measured library is frozen src/torchtsetlin is not changed during a run. A defect found while benchmarking is written to LIBRARY_GAPS.md, fixed between runs if at all, and every record after the fix is re-measured.

docs.title: 1. Get the data
docs.text:
cd experiments/paper_experiments
./reproduce.sh setup     # one virtualenv per external library (.cache/venv-<lib>)
./reproduce.sh data      # download + Booleanize every dataset once -> .cache/data/<bench>.npz

code/prepare_data.py follows each upstream demo script line for line and only replaces the loader by a direct download of the same file Keras or scikit-learn would fetch. It writes results/data_manifest.json with the shape, bit density and SHA-256 of every array: compare it before trusting a run on a new machine.

ID Dataset Source file Booleanization Train / test B1 Noisy XOR pyTsetlinMachine NoisyXORTrainingData.txt / TestData.txt already Boolean (12 bits, 40% train-label noise) 5000 / 5000 B2 2-D Noisy XOR pyTsetlinMachine 2DNoisyXOR*Data.txt already Boolean, 4×4 2500 / 10000 B3 Breast cancer (WDBC) sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer pyTM Binarizer(max_bits_per_feature=10) fitted on all of X 100 random 80/20 splits, split k = train_test_split(..., random_state=k) B4, B5 MNIST Keras mnist.npz pixel > 75, flattened to 784 bits 60000 / 10000 B6 MNIST (OpenML) fetch_openml("mnist_784") pixel > 75 train_test_split(test_size=10000, random_state=42) B7 MNIST Keras mnist.npz pixel >= 75, kept as 28×28 60000 / 10000 B8 Fashion-MNIST Keras Fashion-MNIST cv2.adaptiveThreshold(GAUSSIAN_C, block 11, C 2) 60000 / 10000 B9 IMDb Keras imdb.npz (num_words=5000) 1- and 2-grams with frequency ≥ 10, then SelectKBest(chi2, k=5000) fitted on the training set 25000 / 25000 B10 California housing sklearn.datasets.fetch_california_housing pyTM Binarizer(max_bits_per_feature=10) 25 random 75/25 splits

docs.title: Benchmarks and their published hyperparameters
docs.text:
C is clauses per class (pyTsetlinMachine's convention). Every value comes from the source named in PLAN.md §3; nothing is tuned.

ID Model C T s Boost TP Weighted Other Epochs Runs B1 flat 10 15 3.9 no no 200 5 seeds B2 conv 40 60 3.9 no no patch 2×2 5000 5 seeds B3 flat 800 40 5.0 yes no 25 100 splits B4 flat 2000 50 10.0 yes no 250 5 seeds B5 flat 2000 5000 10.0 yes yes 100 5 seeds B6 coalesced / per-class, as in green-tsetlin's script 10 … 5000 C/4 3.0 yes per script literal budget 20 where supported 5 3 repeats B7 conv 2000 5000 5.0 yes yes patch 10×10 30 5 seeds B8 conv 2000 5000 5.0 yes yes patch 10×10 30 5 seeds B9 flat 10000 8000 10.0 yes yes 30 5 seeds B10 regression 1000 5000 2.75 yes yes 30 25 splits

The same model is expressed differently by each library: per-class vs total clause counts, max_weight=255 as the only weighting of PyTsetlinMachineCUDA, n_clauses = C × K for green-tsetlin's shared pool, position encoding for convolution, and so on. Do not translate the arguments by hand. code/configs.py::cell_config(bench, lib, mode) returns the frozen constructor arguments of every cell, and config_map.md §(a) explains each mapping.

docs.title: torchtsetlin modes
docs.text:
torchtsetlin runs in up to three modes per benchmark, fixed in advance:

Mode Setting Meaning seq feedback_mode="sequential" the exact per-example algorithm that pyTsetlinMachine implements (B1, B2, B3, B10) batch feedback_mode="batch", batch 32 (flat) / 16 (conv) the library's recommended mini-batch range b100 feedback_mode="batch", batch 100 the number PyTsetlinMachineCUDA's demos pass as batch_size (there it is a sync window, not a mini-batch)

The whole Boolean dataset is resident on the device, which is ordinary torchtsetlin use. The other libraries are driven through their own normal fit / predict path.

docs.title: Training loop
docs.text:
The loop is the one every upstream demo uses (code/run.py):

  1. Load the shared .npz; for run k, permute the training order with np.random.default_rng(k). pyTsetlinMachine cannot be seeded, so this permutation is the common source of run-to-run variance; each library additionally gets its own seed (torchtsetlin torch.manual_seed(k), tmu 2k+1, green-tsetlin k+1).
  2. Build the model (timed separately as build_s).
  3. For each epoch: one timed training epoch (fit(..., epochs=1, incremental=True), tmu fit, torchtsetlin one shuffled pass of update() calls), then one timed prediction of the whole test set. torchtsetlin is put in eval() before predicting, because empty clauses vote differently while learning.
  4. After the last epoch: final metrics, memory peaks, model size.

One process per (benchmark, library, mode, seed) cell, each library in its own virtualenv, so no two libraries share a process or a dependency set.

docs.title: 3. What to validate, what to test
docs.text:
There is no validation split and no early stopping. The hyperparameters are the published ones, so there is nothing to select on a validation set, and reading the test set to pick an epoch would be selection on the test set. Instead, validation means checking that each library is installed and called correctly:

Stage Command Checks Pass criterion Smoke ./reproduce.sh smoke every cell runs 1 epoch (B2: 2) on seed 0: same input bits, sensible accuracy, the record is complete the record has status: "done" and a non-trivial accuracy Reproduction ./reproduce.sh repro each library on its own published configuration (R1–R4) accuracy within max(1.0 pp, 2 × seed sd) of the published number. Timing has no pass/fail (hardware differs); the ratio is reported Test every cell the upstream held-out test set, predicted after every epoch the final-epoch value is the result; best_epoch_logged_only is kept for diagnosis

A failed reproduction does not stop the comparison: the failure and its likely cause are reported under Deviations in PLAN.md.

docs.title: ML performance (test set, final epoch)
docs.text: Metric Definition (code/harness.py) Accuracy fraction of correct test predictions Precision, recall, F1 binary: positive class 1; multi-class: macro average over classes RMSE, MAE regression (B10), on the original target scale Spread mean ± sd over seeds (B3: 100 splits, B10: 25 splits)

docs.title: Efficiency
docs.text: Metric How it is measured Training time per epoch wall clock of one training epoch with the device synchronised before the timer stops (torch.cuda.synchronize(); PyCUDA calls are synchronous). Reported as the median of epochs 2…E; epoch 1 is reported separately because it includes JIT / torch.compile / PyCUDA compilation Inference time wall clock to predict the whole test set (median over epochs) Throughput test-set size ÷ inference time (examples/s) Protocol time (B6) construction + all 5 epochs including the per-epoch test prediction, as in green-tsetlin's Table I Speed-up single-thread pyTsetlinMachine time ÷ library time on the same benchmark Peak memory peak host RSS (psutil) and peak GPU memory held by the process (NVML), both sampled every 50 ms by the same probe for every library; torchtsetlin also records torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated Model size (a) the learned state in the library's own storage format (bytes), (b) the size of the saved file

docs.title: Timing hygiene
docs.text:
• One timing run at a time on an idle machine (./reproduce.sh timing runs strictly sequentially). Check env.loadavg_start / env.loadavg_end in each record and re-run cells that overlapped other work.
  • CPU threads are set with OMP_NUM_THREADS, n_jobs and torch.set_num_threads, and the process is pinned with taskset to physical cores (0–15 on the reference host; 16–31 are SMT siblings).
  • All GPU timing runs use the same card (the RTX 3090 here); the CPU governor and the driver version are recorded in env.
  • Data loading and Booleanization are outside every timer.

docs.title: 5. Run it
docs.text:
./reproduce.sh smoke                    # Phase 2: every cell, 1 epoch
./reproduce.sh repro                    # Phase 3: R1-R4
./reproduce.sh timing                   # Phase 4: seed 0 of every cell, exclusive
./reproduce.sh seeds --jobs 6           # Phase 5: remaining seeds / splits, concurrently
./reproduce.sh report                   # Phase 7: REPORT.md + LaTeX tables from the records

Every stage takes filters, so a subset can be run on its own, for example only the GPU libraries on the GPU:

./reproduce.sh smoke  --lib pytmcuda tmu tt --device cuda
./reproduce.sh timing --lib pytmcuda tmu tt --device cuda --bench B4 B7

Re-running a stage skips every cell whose record already has status: "done", so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped. To re-measure a cell, move its record away first. code/launch.py list prints the cell matrix.

docs.title: 6. Adding a library or a machine
docs.text:
• A library: write code/adapters/<lib>.py with build, fit_epoch, predict (and sync for asynchronous devices); add its constructor mapping to code/configs.py and the semantics of every argument to config_map.md before the first measured run; give it its own virtualenv in code/setup_envs.sh; then pass smoke and a reproduction check of its own published number.
  • A machine: run ./reproduce.sh data and compare results/data_manifest.json checksums, then smoke, then the timing stage. Only compare times measured on the same machine.

docs.title: Evaluation and metrics
docs.text:
Vote sums behave like logits, so any PyTorch/scikit-learn metric works. torchtsetlin.metrics keeps the common ones on the device:

votes = model(x_test)                                     # (B, K), eval() mode
tt.metrics.accuracy(votes, y_test)
cm = tt.metrics.confusion_matrix(votes, y_test)           # rows = true, cols = predicted
tt.metrics.precision_recall_f1(cm)                        # per-class tensors
print(tt.metrics.classification_report(votes, y_test, class_names))

Regression: regression_metrics(pred, y) (MAE, RMSE, R²). Multi-label: multilabel_metrics(pred_bool, y_bool) (subset accuracy, Hamming accuracy, micro-F1).

docs.title: Confidence and trustworthiness
docs.text:
Chapter 7 of the book defines the confidence of a prediction as the winning vote sum and calls a model trustworthy when accuracy increases with confidence:

model.confidence(x)                                       # (v_max + T) / 2T in [0, 1]
curve = tt.metrics.trustworthiness_curve(votes, y_test)   # accuracy at each confidence level
tt.viz.plot_trustworthiness(curve)

docs.title: Probabilities and calibration
docs.text:
model.predict_proba(x)                    # linear score (1 + v_k/T)/2, normalised
model.predict_proba(x, method="softmax")  # softmax(v / T)
tt.metrics.expected_calibration_error(model.predict_proba(x), y)

The linear score follows the uncertainty quantification literature for Tsetlin machines (P(y|x) = (1 + v/T)/2); low normalised scores flag uncertain or out-of-distribution inputs.

docs.title: Composites of several machines
docs.text:
Machines trained on different Booleanizations can be combined by dividing each member's vote sums by that member's own range and summing them (TM composites, see Confidence and composites). Fit each range once on a reference set and reuse it. A range taken from the batch being predicted would make each prediction depend on the rest of the batch.

def fit_composite(models, xs_ref):
    """One normalisation factor per member: max - min of its vote sums on a reference set."""
    alphas = []
    for m, x in zip(models, xs_ref):
        v = m(x)
        alphas.append(float((v.max() - v.min()).clamp_min(1e-6)))
    return alphas

def composite_votes(models, xs, alphas):
    return sum(m(x) / a for m, x, a in zip(models, xs, alphas))

alphas = fit_composite(models, xs_val)            # e.g. a validation split, each member's encoding
pred = composite_votes(models, xs_test, alphas).argmax(dim=1)

docs.title: Extending torchtsetlin
docs.text:
The models are thin layers over torchtsetlin.functional. To build a new variant, subclass TsetlinMachineBase and implement the output layer and feedback policy:

class MyTM(tt.TsetlinMachineBase):
    def __init__(self, n_features, n_clauses, T, **kw):
        self.T = T
        super().__init__(n_features, n_clauses, **kw)

    def _votes(self, clause_out, clamp=True):            # (B, C) bool -> (B, n_outputs)
        ...

    def _coerce_targets(self, y, n, device):             # validate / convert targets
        ...

    def _select_feedback(self, votes, y, clause_out):    # -> (type_i, type_ii, aux) masks (B, C)
        ...

Optional hooks: _accumulate_weights(acc, aux, clause_out, sel_fire_i, sel_fire_ii) and _commit_weights(acc) for clause weights; _encode, _evaluate, _feedback_counts for a different input structure (this is how the convolutional mix-in works); rules() for interpretation.

The generic update() handles input coercion, lazy initialisation, chunking, dropout masks, counting feedback events and applying them with functional.apply_feedback.

docs.title: Using the functional API directly
docs.text:
from torchtsetlin import functional as F
lit = F.to_literals(x)                                   # (B, 2F)
include = (state >= N).float()
c = F.clause_outputs(lit, include, empty_value=True)     # (B, C)
v = F.vote_sums(c, weights, T)
n_true, n_false, n_ib = F.type_i_counts(lit, sel_fire_i, sel_nofire_i)
n2 = F.type_ii_counts(lit, sel_fire_ii)
F.apply_feedback(state, n_true, n_false, n_ib, n2, n_states=N, s=s)

Everything is plain tensor code, so torch.compile, custom CUDA kernels or alternative sampling schemes can be dropped in.

docs.title: Graph input
docs.text: GraphTsetlinMachine learns from batches of graphs. This guide shows how to build them, train, and read the learned clauses. The ideas behind it (deep clauses, messages, edge types) are in Graph Tsetlin machines.

docs.title: Symbols and node features
docs.text:
Every node carries a Boolean feature vector of the same length F. The usual way to build one is a SymbolTable: each symbol (a letter, a word, a quantised value, a coordinate) owns a few positions of a sparse hypervector, and a node's vector is the OR of its symbols' vectors.

from torchtsetlin.data import SymbolTable

symbols = SymbolTable(["A", "B", "C"], encoding="one_hot")           # F = 3, exact
words = SymbolTable(vocabulary, dim=1024, bits=4, encoding="random")  # F = 1024, hashed
words.vector(["good", "movie"])     # (1024,) bool: the bundle of two symbols
words.decode(v)                     # symbols whose positions are all set in v

One-hot tables keep every symbol its own feature, which makes clauses exactly readable; hashed tables ("random", "double_hashing") keep F fixed for large vocabularies. Node features need not come from a symbol table: any Boolean vector works, such as an image patch with its position bits.

docs.title: Building a GraphBatch
docs.text:
SequencesImagesAny graph 
from torchtsetlin.data import GraphBatch

g = GraphBatch.from_sequences([["A", "B", "A"], ["C", ["A", "B"]]], symbols)

One node per element (an element may be a set of symbols). Node k sends to k − 1 over edge type 0 ("left") and to k + 1 over type 1 ("right").

g = GraphBatch.from_images(x, patch_size=10, stride=1)   # x: (B, Z, H, W) Boolean

One node per patch and no edges: the patch pixels plus thermometer-coded coordinates, exactly the features of ConvTsetlinMachine(patch_size=10). At depth 1 this graph machine is the convolutional coalesced machine.

g = GraphBatch.from_graphs(
    node_features=[f0, f1],                  # per graph, (n_i, F) Boolean
    edges=[[(0, 1), (1, 0)], [(0, 2)]],      # per graph, (source, destination) pairs
    edge_types=[[0, 1], [0]],                # per graph, one type per edge
    node_types=None,                         # optional, per graph (n_i,)
    n_edge_types=2,
    edge_type_names=["parent", "child"],
)

Edges are directed: a node hears from the nodes with an edge into it, so an undirected relation needs an edge each way, usually with two types.

A GraphBatch behaves like a tensor along the graph axis: len(g), g[3], g[2:10], g[torch.tensor([4, 1])], g.to("cuda") and GraphBatch.cat([...]). Nodes are stored padded to the largest graph of the batch, with each graph's node count in g.n_nodes.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
import torchtsetlin as tt

model = tt.GraphTsetlinMachine(
    n_features=symbols.dim,      # F, the node feature count
    n_outputs=3,                 # classes
    n_clauses=40, T=200, s=3.0,
    depth=2,                     # layers: each one reaches one hop further
    message_encoding="one_hot",  # or "random" / "double_hashing" with message_size=...
    n_edge_types=2, edge_type_names=["left", "right"],
    max_included_literals=8,     # important with message layers, see below
)
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device="cuda", batch_size=25)
trainer.fit((g_train, y_train), epochs=10, val_data=(g_test, y_test))

update(g, y), forward(g), predict(g) and the Trainer work as for every other model. The other CoalescedTsetlinMachine options (multi_label, max_included_literals, feedback_mode, ...) carry over.

Choosing the settings:

  • depth is the number of hops a pattern spans, plus one: "an A with an A on each side" needs 2. Each extra layer costs a pass over the edges and message_size more automata per clause.
  • max_included_literals. Use a budget with message layers. At the start every clause matches everywhere and sends messages from every node, and one boosted Type Ia event can include all of them; without a budget, clauses can collapse into patterns that hold in every graph (see learning).
  • message_encoding. "one_hot" gives each (clause, edge type) its own inbox bit: collision free and readable, but the inbox has n_clauses · n_edge_types bits per layer. For thousands of clauses use "random" with message_size a few times n_clauses · n_edge_types · message_bits and check model.message_collision_rate().
  • s may be one value per layer, s=(s0, s1, …). With s close to 1 use feedback_mode="sequential": forgetting then has probability close to 1, and aggregated over a batch it wipes the clauses (the reference noisy-XOR demo's s=1.0 learns only one graph at a time; s=2 learns it batched).
  • n_node_types: clause j only matches nodes of type j mod n_node_types (as in the reference implementation), which splits the clauses between kinds of node.
  • To reproduce the reference code, use feedback_mode="sequential", shared_node_draw=True, and for several classes multi_label=True with one-hot targets and negative_scale=q / (K − 1) (see the differences).

docs.title: Speed on the GPU: pad the dataset
docs.text:
On CUDA, pad the whole dataset to one shape before training:

P = max(g_train.shape[1], g_test.shape[1])                                   # nodes
E = int(max(g_train.edges_per_graph.max(), g_test.edges_per_graph.max()))   # edges
g_train, g_test = g_train.pad(P, E), g_test.pad(P, E)

A padded batch keeps that shape when it is sliced, without looking at the data, so updates can use the fused kernels and be replayed from CUDA graphs. On the sequence example (RTX 3090):

Update Flat batches Padded batches batched (25 graphs) ~0.23 ms per graph ~0.013 ms per graph sequential (one graph at a time) ~4.8 ms per graph ~0.065 ms per graph

(smoke measurements, not benchmarks). The results are the same in distribution; padding nodes and unused edge slots never match or send. What each layout gets:

  • Batched updates run in events mode (one Triton commit kernel) for flat and padded batches. Padded batches are also replayed from CUDA graphs.
  • Sequential updates use the compiled single-example commit and CUDA graphs only for padded batches, because both are built per input shape.
  • Depth 1 with full graphs (every graph has all P nodes, as with from_images) runs on the convolutional machine's bit-packed kernel: the model is then exactly a convolutional coalesced machine over the node features, and as fast.
  • Pad to one shape: every distinct (P, E) is compiled and captured on its own. A per-layer s or budget_mode="hard" keeps the eager paths. On the CPU nothing changes.

docs.title: Reading the clauses
docs.text:
for j in range(model.n_clauses):
    print(model.clause_expression(j, symbols=symbols), model.weights[j].tolist())

prints deep clauses in the paper's notation, for example

A AND left1:0 AND right1:0                [-58, 63]

"this node is an A, and clause 0's first component matched at the node a left-going edge came from (the right neighbour) and at the node a right-going edge came from (the left neighbour)". left1:0 names the edge type, the message layer and the clause the message reports. With a symbol table, node literals are decoded to symbols; hashed messages are decoded when all of their bits are included and printed raw (m1[17]) otherwise.

model.rules(symbols=symbols) gives the same as IF … THEN rules with the votes.

model.explain_node(g, clause, graph=i, symbols=symbols) explains one clause at one node of graph i (by default the first node where it holds), tracing every message back to the neighbours that sent it:

clause 1 holds at node 2 [A] of graph 0
  layer 0: A
  layer 1: left1:0 AND right1:0
    left1:0 from node 3 [A] over left: clause 0 up to layer 0
      layer 0: A
    right1:0 from node 1 [A] over right: clause 0 up to layer 0
      layer 0: A

A component that fails is marked <- fails here.

Two accessors expose what happens inside one graph:

  • model.node_clause_outputs(g, layer=i): (B, P, C), where clause components 0 … i all match. With the default last layer this says which nodes make a clause True.
  • model.node_messages(g, layer=i): (B, P, M), the inbox of every node at layer i ≥ 1.

model.evaluate_clauses(g) gives the (B, C) clause outputs, usable as Boolean features for another model.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/graph_sequence.py counts runs of consecutive A's in sequences of varying length, the reference implementation's sequence demo, and prints the learned deep clauses.

The notebook Graph Tsetlin machine walks through the same ideas: the paper's three-A's task with four readable clauses, explain_node, run lengths, the padded fast path, and MNIST as graphs learning bit for bit like ConvCoalescedTsetlinMachine. It opens in Google Colab.

docs.title: Interpreting a model
docs.text: A trained Tsetlin machine is a list of rules. torchtsetlin.interpret helps you read them, rank them and explain single predictions.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
model.feature_names = ["four_wheels", "transports_people", "wings", "yellow", "blue"]
model.class_names = ["plane", "car"]
for rule in model.rules(polarity=1):           # only clauses voting *for* their class
    print(rule)
# IF four_wheels AND transports_people AND NOT wings THEN car
model.clause_info(3)                            # dict: class, polarity, weight, n_literals, expression
model.clause_literals(3)                        # {'positive': [0, 1], 'negated': [2]}

Coalesced models list every output a clause votes on with its weight; regression models show the contribution of each clause.

docs.title: Which clauses matter?
docs.text:
act = tt.interpret.clause_activity(model, x, y)          # (K, C): firing rate per class
cp = tt.interpret.clause_precision(model, x, y)          # support and precision per clause
top = cp["precision"].argsort(descending=True)[:10]

docs.title: Feature importance (closed form)
docs.text:
Blakely & Granmo (2020) define literal importance directly from the clauses, without perturbation:

  • global: the weighted fraction of positive clauses of a class that include a literal, tt.interpret.global_feature_importance(model) → (K, 2F);
  • local: the weight of the matching clauses of the predicted class that rely on each literal for a specific input, tt.interpret.local_feature_importance(model, x) → (B, 2F).

For thermometer-encoded data, sum the bits of each original feature:

imp = tt.interpret.global_feature_importance(model, class_index=1)
groups = [i // 8 for i in range(n_columns * 8)]           # 8 bits per column
per_feature = tt.interpret.aggregate_literal_importance(imp, groups)
tt.viz.plot_feature_importance(per_feature, column_names)

docs.title: Explaining one prediction
docs.text:
print(tt.interpret.explain(model, x_test[0], feature_names=model.feature_names))
# prediction: 1  votes: [-10.0, 7.0]
#   [+1 -> output 1] clause 50: IF a>=0.12 AND NOT b>=0.41
#   ...

docs.title: Inspecting the memory itself
docs.text: model.ta_state is the raw (C, 2F) state matrix; model.included_mask() the Boolean include matrix; model.literal_frequency() counts how many clauses use each literal; model.state_summary() gives quick statistics. See Visualisation for plots of all of these.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
model = tt.RegressionTsetlinMachine(n_features=F, n_clauses=500, T=200, s=3.0, y_range=(0.0, 1.0))
trainer = tt.Trainer(model, batch_size=16)
trainer.fit((xb_train, y_train), epochs=30, val_data=(xb_val, y_val))   # logs val_mae, val_rmse, val_r2
model.predict(xb_test)                     # floats in [y_min, y_max]
model.rules()                              # 'IF x3 AND NOT x7 THEN +0.005'

All clauses are positive; the number of matching clauses (times weights) divided by T gives the position in [y_min, y_max]. T is therefore also the output resolution — choose it ≥ the number of distinct output levels you need. Pass y_range explicitly (otherwise it is inferred from the first batch with a warning). Convolutional regression: ConvRegressionTsetlinMachine.

docs.title: Multi-label
docs.text:
model = tt.CoalescedTsetlinMachine(n_features=F, n_outputs=7, n_clauses=2000, T=100, s=10, multi_label=True)
model.update(xb, y_multi)                  # y_multi: (B, 7) Boolean
model.predict(xb)                          # (B, 7) Boolean, v_i > 0
model.predict_proba(xb)                    # (B, 7) in [0, 1]

Every output is updated per example: positive labels drive Type I feedback towards their clauses, negative labels Type II (scaled by negative_scale, the q parameter of the multi-task convolutional TM literature). The Trainer reports subset accuracy, Hamming accuracy and micro-F1 for multi-label models.

docs.title: Multi-class with shared clauses
docs.text: The same CoalescedTsetlinMachine with multi_label=False is a multi-class classifier whose clauses are shared by all classes — useful when classes have common sub-patterns or when you want a smaller model than n_classes × n_clauses.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
Models are nn.Modules whose learnable state is stored in buffers, so the standard PyTorch recipe applies:

torch.save(model.state_dict(), "tm.pt")

model2 = tt.TsetlinMachine(784, 10, 2000, T=50, s=10)      # same hyper-parameters
model2.load_state_dict(torch.load("tm.pt", map_location="cpu"))

Lazily initialised models (n_features=None, or convolutional models without input_shape) allocate their state while loading, so you can restore a checkpoint without having seen data:

model3 = tt.ConvTsetlinMachine(10, 200, T=100, patch_size=10)
model3.load_state_dict(torch.load("ctm.pt"))
model3.input_shape = (1, 28, 28)          # set explicitly if you did not pass input_shape

ModelCheckpoint stores {"state_dict", "epoch", "logs"} at the best validation score.

Encoders are modules too — save them next to the model so the Booleanization thresholds travel with it:

torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), "encoder": enc.state_dict()}, "bundle.pt")

Whole-model pickling (torch.save(model)) also works but ties the file to the package version; prefer state_dict().

docs.title: Semantic segmentation
docs.text: Dense, per-pixel prediction with SegmentationTsetlinMachine. For why it is built the way it is — and why a ConvTsetlinMachine cannot do this — see Segmentation.

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text:
shape dtype input (B, Z, H, W) Boolean ((B, H, W) is treated as one plane) targets (B, H, W) long, values in [0, K-1] or ignore_index predict(x) (B, H, W) long label map vote_map(x) (B, K, H, W) float vote sums forward(x) (B·H·W, K) float, patches folded into the batch

Booleanize first. A plain threshold throws away the ordering between intensities, which is usually the information a segmenter needs; use a thermometer:

import torch, torchtsetlin as tt

rgb, labels = tt.data.make_scenes(300, 32, seed=0)          # (N, 3, H, W) float, (N, H, W) long
enc = tt.data.ColorThermometerEncoder(n_bits=4, value_range=(0.0, 1.0))
x = enc(rgb).float()                                        # (N, 12, H, W) Boolean planes

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Trainer detects a dense model and switches to segmentation metrics — pixel accuracy, mean IoU, mean Dice and per-class IoU — accumulating a confusion matrix batch by batch rather than keeping (B, K, H, W) vote tensors for a whole test set.

model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(
    n_classes=4, n_clauses=300, T=60, s=10.0,
    patch_size=3,               # the neighbourhood each pixel is classified from
    position_encoding=8,        # thermometer bits per axis of patch position (0/False = off)
    patches_per_commit=128,     # pixels per feedback commit — see below
    weighted=True, n_states=100,
).to("cuda")
model.class_names = list(tt.data.SCENE_CLASSES)

trainer = tt.Trainer(model, device="cuda", batch_size=8)     # batch_size is in IMAGES
trainer.fit((x[:220], labels[:220]), epochs=8, val_data=(x[220:], labels[220:]))
trainer.test((x[220:], labels[220:]))
# {'test_pixel_accuracy': 0.989, 'test_mean_iou': 0.935, 'test_mean_dice': 0.966,
#  'test_iou_sky': 0.999, 'test_iou_building': 0.865, ...}

Or without the Trainer:

model.update(x_batch, label_batch)     # returns pre-update folded votes (B·P, K)
model.eval()
pred = model.predict(x_test)           # (B, H, W)

model.eval() is not optional

A clause with no included literals is True while learning and False when predicting. Forgetting eval() silently changes every pixel of the output.

docs.title: patches_per_commit
docs.text: One batch of 8 images at 32×32 is 8 192 pixel-examples; committing their feedback all at once is a mini-batch of 8 192, far past where batched feedback stops matching the classical algorithm. This bounds it. The default 128 was chosen by ablation: quality is flat below it, and both the mean and the variance degrade above it. Lower it if learning looks unstable; raise it — or set None — only when you want throughput and have checked the cost. feedback_mode="sequential" is patches_per_commit=1.

docs.title: patch_size and context
docs.text:
A k × k patch is all the model sees of a pixel. When a class is not decidable from it — building interior vs. road, in the example scenes — no amount of clause budget fixes it. Add context instead of enlarging the patch (which grows the feature count quadratically):

# (a) position literals: a clause can say "only in rows 12-18"
model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(4, 300, T=60, patch_size=3, position_encoding=8)

# (b) an OR-pooled multi-scale pyramid: neighbourhood + coarse structure, patch_size=1
pyr = tt.data.PyramidEncoder(scales=(1, 2, 4), patch=3)
x_ctx = pyr(x).float()                       # (B, Z*9*3, H, W)
model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(4, 300, T=60, patch_size=1, position_encoding=8)

Both work and they compose; on the example scenes building IoU goes 0.526 → 0.837 (pyramid) → 0.865 (position) → 0.919 (both). Pass position_encoding an integer on anything bigger than about 64 px: True adds one bit per row and column, which is 1 022 extra features at 512 px.

docs.title: ignore_index
docs.text:
The void class of CamVid / Cityscapes / Pascal VOC. Pixels with this label produce no feedback and are excluded from every metric:

model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(21, 400, T=80, patch_size=3, ignore_index=255)
tt.metrics.mean_iou(pred, target, n_classes=21, ignore_index=255)

docs.title: Class imbalance
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine has no loss to reweight, so the lever is which pixels produce feedback:

p = tt.data.balanced_class_probabilities(labels, n_classes=4, floor=0.05)
model.set_class_feedback_p(p)          # per-class probability of contributing feedback

Use it when a rare class is being lost, and check the per-class IoU afterwards — it costs accuracy once the model can already separate the classes.

docs.title: stride and padding
docs.text: padding="same" with stride=1 (the defaults) keep the input resolution. A larger stride produces a coarser output grid; full-resolution label maps are subsampled to it automatically, so you can pass (B, H, W) labels either way. model.output_shape() reports the grid.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
tt.metrics.pixel_accuracy(pred, target, ignore_index=255)
tt.metrics.iou(pred, target, n_classes=4)        # (K,) per class, NaN where absent
tt.metrics.mean_iou(pred, target, n_classes=4)
tt.metrics.dice(pred, target, n_classes=4)       # medical-imaging convention
tt.metrics.boundary_f1(pred, target, tolerance=2)
print(tt.metrics.segmentation_report(pred, target, class_names=CLASSES))

All of them accept vote maps (B, K, H, W), label maps (B, H, W) or folded votes (N, K). An absent class gets NaN IoU rather than 0, and mean_iou skips it — averaging a zero there would punish the model for a class the image does not contain.

Pixel accuracy is a weak claim

On any dataset with a stable layout, a baseline that knows only a pixel's row scores well. On the example scenes it reaches 0.876 pixel accuracy — and 0.410 mIoU, with zero on two of four classes. Compute that floor and report it next to your numbers.

docs.title: Explaining a pixel
docs.text:
This is the part a convolutional network cannot do. Each matching clause decodes into a conjunction over absolute image coordinates:

print(tt.interpret.explain_pixel(model, x_test[0], row=20, col=12, target=int(y[0, 20, 12])))

pixel (20, 12) -> 3
prediction: 3  votes: [-1415.0, -445.0, -487.0, 614.0]
  [+92 -> output 3] clause 1008: IF y>2 AND y>3 AND y>4
  [+88 -> output 3] clause 1018: IF p[0,19,12] AND p[0,19,13] AND p[0,20,12] AND ...
                                    AND y>1 AND y>2 AND x>1 AND NOT p[1,20,11] AND ...

p[0,19,12] reads "plane 0 of pixel (19, 12) is set", and y>4 is a row threshold (model.clause_region(j) decodes them). Clauses get long at high s; cap them with max_included_literals if you want rules you can read at a glance. Related tools:

model.clause_map(x, clauses=[0, 5])    # (B, 2, H, W): where those clauses fire
model.clause_patch(0)                  # (Z, kh, kw): 1 = must be on, -1 = off, 0 = free
model.clause_region(0)                 # the output-grid rows/columns a clause is pinned to
tt.viz.plot_segmentation(rgb[0], target, pred, class_names=CLASSES)
tt.viz.plot_vote_map(model.vote_map(x[:1]), class_index=1, class_name="building")

docs.title: Real datasets
docs.text:
x, y = tt.data.load_voc_segmentation_boolean("./data", image_set="train", size=96)
model = tt.SegmentationTsetlinMachine(21, 400, T=80, patch_size=3, ignore_index=255)

load_segmentation_boolean takes any instantiated torchvision segmentation dataset (VOCSegmentation, Cityscapes, …), resizes masks with nearest interpolation — bilinear would invent class indices — and thermometer-encodes the images. Both need torchvision.

docs.title: Cost and memory
docs.text:
Dense evaluation is one clause evaluation per pixel: ~1000× a flat classifier on a 32×32 input. Measured on a 16-core CPU (4 planes, 4 classes, 100 clauses/class, batch of 8 images): ~35 000 px/s training, ~1 090 000 px/s predicting. Above ~64 px, use a GPU; see CPU vs GPU.

max_chunk_elements bounds the largest intermediate; the dense model budgets P · (8C + 4F) elements per image, so chunking adapts to the image size on its own. Reduce batch_size (in images) before touching it.

docs.title: Multi-label masks
docs.text:
For overlapping structures, where a pixel may belong to several classes at once:

model = tt.CoalescedSegmentationTsetlinMachine(
    n_outputs=2, n_clauses=300, T=25, patch_size=5, multi_label=True,
)
model.update(x, masks)          # masks: (B, K, H, W) Boolean
model.eval()
model.predict(x)                # (B, K, H, W) Boolean

CoalescedSegmentationTsetlinMachine also works in ordinary multi-class mode, sharing one clause pool across classes — a better fit when classes share structure, since edges and textures are the same features whichever class they belong to.

docs.title: The primitive: model.update(x, y)
docs.text:
Every model exposes one learning call. It evaluates the batch, decides feedback per clause, updates the automata in place and returns the vote sums computed before the update:

votes = model.update(x, y)            # (B, n_outputs)
batch_acc = (votes.argmax(1) == y).float().mean()

Anything you can do with a PyTorch training loop you can do here: custom schedules, curriculum, mixing data sources, logging to TensorBoard or Weights & Biases, etc. Remember to call model.train() before learning and model.eval() before measuring accuracy (empty clause semantics differ).

docs.title: The Trainer
docs.text:
trainer = tt.Trainer(
    model,
    device="cuda",                    # moves the model
    batch_size=32,
    callbacks=[
        tt.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_accuracy", patience=10, restore_best=True),
        tt.ModelCheckpoint("runs/best.pt", monitor="val_accuracy"),
        tt.CSVLogger("runs/log.csv"),
        tt.StateSummaryLogger(),      # mean literals / empty clauses per epoch
        tt.HyperparameterSchedule("s", lambda epoch: max(3.0, 10.0 - 0.2 * epoch)),
    ],
    metrics={"margin": lambda votes, y: tt.metrics.vote_margin(votes).mean().item()},
)
history = trainer.fit(train_data, epochs=50, val_data=val_data)

train_data / val_data can be:

  • an (x, y) pair of tensors or arrays — kept on the device and indexed directly (fastest),
  • a torch.utils.data.Dataset — wrapped in a DataLoader,
  • a DataLoader — used as is (e.g. with on-the-fly Booleanization via tt.data.TransformDataset).

Per epoch the trainer logs epoch_time, batch_accuracy (or batch_mae), validation metrics prefixed with val_, and anything callbacks add. history is a History with history["val_accuracy"], history.best(...), history.to_dataframe() and history.plot().

trainer.evaluate(data), trainer.test(data) and trainer.predict(data) complete the Keras-style trio; tt.evaluate(model, data) and tt.predict(model, data) are one-liners.

docs.title: Writing a callback
docs.text:
class PrintRules(tt.Callback):
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs):
        if epoch % 10 == 0:
            print(self.model.rules()[:3])

Hooks: on_train_begin/end, on_epoch_begin/end, on_batch_begin/end. Set self.trainer.stop_training = True to stop early.

docs.title: Dropout granularity
docs.text: drop_clause_p / drop_literal_p masks are resampled on every update() by default (drop_granularity="batch"). The drop-clause paper resamples once per epoch; use drop_granularity="epoch" and the Trainer will call model.resample_dropout() at the start of each epoch (do the same in a manual loop).

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: tt.seed_everything(seed) seeds Python, NumPy and all PyTorch devices. Batched updates on CUDA use index_add_ for convolutional models, which is order-nondeterministic but exact for the integer counts involved; results are reproducible up to sampling.

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
torchtsetlin.viz needs matplotlib (pip install "torchtsetlin[viz]"). Every function returns the Axes it drew on.

Function What it shows plot_history(history) metric curves per epoch plot_confusion_matrix(cm, class_names) confusion matrix heat-map plot_clause_memory(model, clause) book-style memory of one clause: bar per literal, dashed include boundary plot_ta_states(model) heat-map of all automata (clauses × literals) plot_literal_frequency(model) how many clauses include each literal plot_feature_importance(importance, names) horizontal bars plot_conv_clause(model, clause) / plot_conv_clauses(model, clauses) convolutional clause patches (black = on, white = off, gray = free) with the allowed region; 3D clauses are drawn slice by slice (depth= picks one) plot_votes(votes, y) distribution of winning vote sums, correct vs incorrect plot_trustworthiness(curve) accuracy and coverage vs confidence plot_clause_weights(model) weights of weighted / coalesced models 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
tt.viz.plot_clause_memory(model, clause=0, ax=axes[0])
tt.viz.plot_votes(model(x_test), y_test, ax=axes[1])
plt.show()
